sludge pre-treatment and solids retention time
of mesophilic anaerobic digestion on the methane
production, sludge digestion and microbial
communities in a sequential digestion process

a b s t r a c t
In this study, the changes in sludge reduction, methane production and microbial
community structures in a process involving two-stage thermophilic aerobic digestion
(TAD) and mesophilic anaerobic digestion (MAD) under different solid retention times
(SRTs) between 10 and 40 days were investigated. The TAD reactor (RTAD) was operated
with a 1-day SRT and the MAD reactor (RMAD) was operated at three different SRTs: 39, 19
and 9 days. For a comparison, control MAD (RCONTROL) was operated at three different SRTs
of 40, 20 and 10 days. Our results reveal that the sequential TADeMAD process has about
42% higher methane production rate (MPR) and 15% higher TCOD removal than those of
RCONTROL when the SRT decreased from 40 to 20 days. Denaturing gradient gel electro-
phoresis (DGGE) and real-time PCR results indicate that RMAD maintained a more diverse
bacteria and archaea population compared to RCONTROL, due to the application of the
biological TAD pre-treatment process. In RTAD, Ureibacillus thermophiles and Bacterium
thermus were the major contributors to the increase in soluble organic matter. In contrast,
Methanosaeta concilii, a strictly aceticlastic methanogen, showed the highest population
during the operation of overall SRTs in RMAD. Interestingly, as the SRT decreased to 20 days,
syntrophic VFA oxidizing bacteria, Clostridium ultunense sp., and a hydrogenotrophic
methanogen, Methanobacterium beijingense were detected in RMAD and RCONTROL. Meanwhile,
the proportion of archaea to total microbe in RMAD and RCONTROL shows highest values of
10.5 and 6.5% at 20-d SRT operation, respectively. Collectively, these results demonstrate

Microaerobic bio-pretreatment of straw with fermentation broth as 
inoculum: Enhancing hydrolysis-acidification efficiency
Chuqiao Wang a, Xiaoqian Liu a, Jialong Pan a, Shan Huang a, Xizi Long b, Yuying Hu a,  
Jiajie Zhang a,*
a School of civil engineering and architecture, East China Jiaotong University, Nanchang 330013, China
b Hunan Province Key Laboratory of Typical Environmental Pollution and Health Hazards, School of Public Health, Hengyang Medical School, University of South China, 
Hengyang 421001, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
microaerobic pretreatment
RSM
rice straw
A B S T R A C T
Anaerobic digestion (AD) has been recognized as a promising technology for the disposal of agricultural residues, 
such as straw. Nonetheless, AD encounters a bottleneck of low hydrolysis rate. Microaerobic pretreatment 
significantly enhances straw AD efficiency, but its effectiveness depends on factors like pretreatment time and 
water content, with their interactions remaining unclear. Therefore, this study employed a response surface 
methodology (RSM) to investigate the interactions among pretreatment time, water content, and volatile fatty 
acids (VFAs) concentration in inoculum during the microaerobic pretreatment. The results showed that the 
highest hydrolysis-acidification efficiency was achieved with a pretreatment time of 10 days and a VFAs con­
centration of 10,000 mg/L, and there was a notable interaction between these two factors in the inoculum. 
Additionally, microbial community analysis showed that microaerobic pretreatment altered the microbial 
community structure to adapt to micro-oxygen environments, promoting the hydrolysis-acidification of straw. 
Specifically, Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Actinobacteria became the predominant acid-producing bacteria 
following microaerobic pretreatment. Within the fungus communities, Aspergillus niger and Penicillium citrinum, 
known for lignin degradation, increased by 4.4-fold and 1.2-fold, respectively. And the Methanobacteria became 
the main group in the archaeal communities. This paper presents a new perspective on the pretreatment of 
lignocellulose in commercial anaerobic reactors.
1. Introduction
With an annual production of 1.04 billion tons, straw stands as one of 
the primary agricultural wastes in China [1]. The disposal of such a 
substantial amount of waste has posed a longstanding challenge in the 
realm of energy and environmental management. Anaerobic digestion 
(AD) is an advantageous technology for converting straw into methane, 
offering the potential to simultaneously tackle environmental issues [2]. 
However, the primary constituent of straw, lignocellulose, comprises a 
intricate structure that is intertwined with lignin, cellulose, and hemi­
cellulose, thereby impeding efficient degradation by hydrolytically 
acidifying bacteria [3,4]. Consequently, overcoming the rate-limiting 
step (hydrolysis) [5], and converting lignocellulosic biomass into solu­
ble substances are crucial for enhancing the AD process.
To address these challenges, recent advancements in biological, 
chemical, mechanical, and thermal pretreatments have been recognized 
as effective methods for achieving high substrate solubilization[6–8]. 
Among these methods, biological pretreatment has garnered consider­
able attention due to its mild reaction conditions and low cost. Notably, 
microaerobic biological pretreatment demands only minimal amount of 
oxygen, making it an economically efficient and environmentally 
friendly alternative pretreatment option [9].Recent evidence indicates 
that the introduction of small quantities of oxygen could improve the 
relative abundance and bacterial diversity of Firmicutes, thereby 
increasing the hydrolysis rate of straw [10,11]. However, this approach 
entails not only the cost of inoculants but also requires the supplemen­
tation of nutrients such as nitrogen and trace elements [12]. In addition, 
microbial pretreatment requires the additional addition of strains or

Keywords:

A B S T R A C T
Acid Red GR is a representative sulfonated azo dye frequently detected in dyeing wastewater, yet the role of 
hydrodynamic conditions in regulating its biodegradation in micro-aerobic hydrolysis acidification (MAHA) 
systems remains unclear. This study investigated how hydrodynamic conditions drive Acid Red GR trans­
formation, hydrolysis acidification, and microbial metabolic responses in the MAHA reactor. The results showed 
that a moderate stirring speed of 120 rad/min (R2) balanced turbulence intensity and flow uniformity, with 
relatively high oxygen transfer, a favorable micro-aerobic niche, and the highest biodegradability (0.50) and 
volatile fatty acid (VFA) production (140.38 mg/L). This hydrodynamic condition enriched hydrolytic, facul­
tative, and fermentative genera, including Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Bacteroides, Propionivibrio, and Bacillus, and 
was associated with higher abundances of genes encoding enzymes involved in azo reduction, aromatic inter­
mediate transformation, pyruvate generation, and acidogenic metabolism. Integrated metagenomic, metab­
olomic, and functional group evidence further indicated that Acid Red GR degradation proceeded through azo 
reduction, deamination, desulfonation, aromatic ring cleavage, and subsequent acidogenesis. These findings

1. Introduction
Acid Red GR is a representative sulfonated azo dye contaminant 
frequently detected in dyeing wastewater [1]. Its highly conjugated azo 
structure and sulfonated aromatic framework contribute to persistent 
coloration, limited biodegradability, and resistance to conventional 
biological treatment [2]. Moreover, incomplete transformation of azo 
dyes may lead to the accumulation of aromatic amines and other in­
termediates with potential ecological risks [3]. Therefore, developing 
effective strategies that not only remove dye color but also promote 
complete molecular transformation and detoxification of azo dye con­
taminants remains an important challenge in wastewater treatment.
Micro-aerobic hydrolysis acidification (MAHA) has recently emerged 
as a promising biological approach for enhancing azo dye trans­
formation and improving wastewater biodegradability [1,4]. Unlike 
conventional anaerobic hydrolysis acidification, MAHA introduces trace 
oxygen to maintain a dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration of 
0.1–1.0 mg/L, creating a micro-aerobic environment that may simulta­
neously facilitate anaerobic azo-bond reduction, aerobic oxidation of 
aromatic intermediates, and microbial carbon metabolism [5,6]. Previ­
ous studies have shown that MAHA can achieve over 80% azo dye 
decolorization, substantial organic matter removal (30–55%), and 
enhanced biodegradability (BOD5/COD = 0.36–0.50), while promoting 
volatile fatty acid (VFA) production and the further transformation of 
refractory 
aromatic 
intermediates 
through 
processes 
such 
as 
aromatic-ring cleavage [1,7,8]. However, within this narrow oxygen 
range, even subtle variations in the local micro-aerobic environment 
may substantially affect redox conditions and biological responses [9]. 
Thus, understanding microenvironmental regulation is critical for 
optimizing MAHA performance.

Treatment of petrochemical wastewater by microaerobic hydrolysis
and anoxic/oxic processes and analysis of bacterial diversity
Qi Yang a, Panpan Xiong a, Pengyuan Ding b, Libing Chu b,c, Jianlong Wang b,c,⇑
a School of Water Resources and Environment, China University of Geosciences, Beijing 100083, PR China
b Collaborative Innovation Center for Advanced Nuclear Energy Technology, INET, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, PR China
c Beijing Key Laboratory of Radioactive Waste Treatment, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, PR China
h i g h l i g h t s
 Microaerobic hydrolysis–acidiﬁcation (MHA) was used as a pretreatment.
 MHA–A/O process was developed to treat actual petrochemical wastewater.
 The total COD removal efﬁciency was 72–79% and MHA accounted for 33–42%.
 The predominant genera in MHA, anoxic and oxic reactors were determined.
a r t i c l e
i n f o

Received 20 June 2015
Received in revised form 20 July 2015
Accepted 21 July 2015
Available online 29 July 2015
Keywords:
Microaerobic hydrolysis
Petrochemical wastewater
Microbial community
Wastewater treatment
a b s t r a c t
Microaerobic hydrolysis–acidiﬁcation (MHA)–anoxic–oxic (A/O) processes were developed to treat actual
petrochemical wastewater. The results showed that the overall COD removal efﬁciency was 72–79% at
HRT = 20 h, and MHA accounted for 33–42% of COD removal, exhibiting good efﬁciency of acidogenic fer-
mentation. Ammonium removal was more than 94%. The main pollutants in the inﬂuent were identiﬁed
to be benzene, ketone, alcohols, amine, nitrile and phenols by GC–MS, and the majority of pollutants
could be removed by MHA–A/O treatment. Proteobacteria was the most dominant bacteria in the system,
accounting for more than 55% of the reads. The predominant genera in MHA, anoxic and oxic reactors
were Anaerolineaceae and Sulfuritalea, Lactococcus and Blastocatella, and Saprospiraceae uncultured and
Nitrosomonadaceae, respectively. This treatment system exhibited good performance in degrading the
complex compounds in the petrochemical wastewater.

1. Introduction
A large amount of petrochemical wastewater was generated in
the petroleum reﬁning industry and the manufacturing processes
of numerous organic chemicals and raw materials, which has
become one of the most serious issues. Usually wastewater
released from the petrochemical industry contains hazardous
chemicals such as petroleum hydrogen, aromatic compounds, phe-
nolic substances and heavy metals, which are highly toxic and bio-
logically recalcitrant (Wang, 2002; Liu et al., 2014).
The treatment processes used for petrochemical wastewater
generally include pretreatment to improve the biodegradation
and reduce toxicity, followed by biological treatment involving
activated sludge process, anoxic–oxic (A/O) process, ﬂuidized bed
reactor, membrane bioreactor and bioﬁlm process (Wang et al.,
2000; Guo et al., 2009). Among the biological treatment processes
available, the A/O process is highly effective in removing organics
and nutrients with low operational costs, and has been a promising
alternative to conventional activated sludge process (Wang et al.,
2002, 2004). The pretreatment processes include several physico-
chemical methods such as ultrasonic, ﬂocculation, Fenton and
ozone oxidation as well as anaerobic hydrolysis–acidiﬁcation (Lin
et al., 2001).
Anaerobic hydrolysis–acidiﬁcation is the ﬁrst two stages of
anaerobic digester, serving for solubilization of complex macro-
molecular and particular organic compounds into micromolecular
and simple soluble compounds such as volatile fatty acids (VFAs).
Recent studies found that the hydrolysis–acidiﬁcation process
could occur under microaerobic conditions by adding a small
amount of oxygen (air) into the reactor, which is termed as
microaerobic hydrolysis–acidiﬁcation (MHA) (Lim et al., 2014).

a b s t r a c t
Thermophilic microaerobic pretreatment (TMP) was recently reported as an efﬁcient pretreatment
method of anaerobic digestion (AD). In this study, the chemical properties and microbial community
were characterized to reveal how TMP working. Compared with thermophilic treatment under anaerobic
condition (TMP0), cellulase activity obviously improved under microaerobic condition (TMP1), which
was 10.9–49.0% higher than that of TMP0. Reducing sugar, SCOD and VFAs concentrations of TMP1 were
2.6–8.9%, 1.8–4.8% and 13.8–24% higher than those of TMP0, respectively. TMP gave obvious rise to phy-
lum Firmicutes, which associated with extracellular enzymes production. The proportion of class Bacilli
(belongs to phylum Firmicutes and mainly acts during hydrolysis) in TMP1 was 124.89% higher than that
of TMP0, which reﬂected the greater hydrolytic ability under microaerobic condition. The improved
abundance of phylum Firmicutes (especially class Bacilli, order Bacillales) under microaerobic condition
could be the fundamental reason for the improved AD performance of thermophilic microaerobic pre-
treated corn straw.

the higher facultative bacteria grow rate, more cellulase produc-
tion and higher enzyme activity under microaerobic condition
which then led to the higher hydrolysis could be the mechanism
behind microaerobic pretreatment. Botheju and Bakke (2011) also

nanobubble water: Performance improvements and microbial mechanisms 
under thermophilic and mesophilic conditions

A B S T R A C T
High-solid anaerobic digestion (HSAD) is a promising strategy for cattle manure (CM) valorization, but its ef­
ficiency is often limited by slow hydrolysis, acid accumulation, and ammonia inhibition. This study investigated 
the effects of air nanobubble water (Air-NBW) on HSAD of CM under thermophilic (55 ± 1 ◦C) and mesophilic 
(37 ± 1 ◦C) conditions. Batch digesters were operated at CM-to-liquid mass ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 1:4, with 
distilled water as the control. Air-NBW promoted soluble chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) release and volatile 
fatty acids (VFAs) formation, indicating enhanced hydrolysis and acidogenesis. Under thermophilic conditions, 
Air-NBW accelerated both soluble organic matter production and subsequent VFAs conversion, whereas under 
mesophilic conditions it mainly facilitated later-stage VFAs turnover after transient acid accumulation. 
Compared with the corresponding controls, cumulative methane yield increased by 23.1%, 10.2%, and 31.9% at 
thermophilic CM-to-liquid ratios of 1:1, 1:2, and 1:4, respectively, and by 21.4%, 15.7%, and 17.4% under 
mesophilic conditions. The modified Gompertz model further indicated improved methane production kinetics. 
Microbial analysis showed that Air-NBW was associated with the enrichment of hydrolytic bacteria and 
hydrogenotrophic methanogens, supporting the coordinated conversion of particulate organics to methane. 
Correlation analysis linked Corynebacterium with SCOD and Methanosphaera with methane production under 
thermophilic conditions, while mesophilic enhancement was more related to VFAs turnover and methanogenic 
recovery. These findings demonstrate that Air-NBW can improve HSAD performance and provide a practical 
strategy for enhancing renewable energy recovery from CM.
1. Introduction
The global intensification of livestock production has led to vast 
accumulations of manure, among which cattle manure (CM) pre­
dominates [1]. Improper handling and disposal of CM can cause air 
emissions, groundwater pollution, soil degradation, and the propagation 
of pathogenic microorganisms [2]. At present, direct land application 
remains the predominant CM management practice [3]; however, CM 
often harbors low levels of heavy metals—which, upon repeated soil 
application, can accumulate (e.g., Cd, Hg), and ultimately threaten crop 
safety [4]. Consequently, devising strategies for CM volume reduction, 
detoxification, and resource recovery has emerged as an urgent priority. 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) represents a leading manure-treatment tech­
nology that concurrently reduces waste, detoxifies contaminants, facil­
itates nutrient recovery, and produces renewable biogas [5]. Operating 
temperature and total solids (TS) content critically influence AD per­
formance [6]. Mesophilic AD (25–40 ◦C) is widely implemented due to 
its operational stability [7], whereas thermophilic AD (> 45 ◦C), despite 
its higher energy demands and potential stability issues, offers faster 
hydrolysis rates, increased biogas yields, and enhanced methane

A B S T R A C T
The widespread adoption of anaerobic digestion for pig manure treatment is limited by malodorous gas emissions 
and low energy recovery efficiency. This study systematically examined the effects of micro-aeration pretreat­
ment over a range of intensities (0-13.9 mL/g(TS)/d) on odor abatement and digestion performance. Micro- 
aeration reduced emissions of eight key malodorous gases, including sulfide (H2S), ammonia (NH3), meth­
anethiol (CH4S), and ethanethiol (C2H6S), by 14.0-100%. Complete sulfide mineralization was achieved at in­
tensities ≥9.3 mL/g(TS)/d. Mitigation of nitrogen- and sulfur-containing compounds was likely driven by 
selective enrichment of facultative aerobic consortia (e.g., unclassified_f__Bacillaceae and unclassi­
fied_c__Gammaproteobacteria) and the upregulation of sulfur oxidation and nitrogen transformation pathways. 
Methane production increased by 37.6-95.5%, owing to enhanced hydrolysis and acetogenesis resulting from 
upregulated fatty acid β-oxidation and acetyl-CoA synthesis. Moreover, syntrophic bacteria (Syntrophomonas) 
and key methanogens (Methanothrix and Methanosarcina) were selectively enriched. An aeration intensity of 
4.6 mL/g(TS)/d was identified as optimal, as it balanced effective odor control and maximal methanogenic 
activity. These findings provide a theoretical foundation and a viable strategy for improving energy recovery and 
environmental sustainability in swine manure management.
1. Introduction
The rapid expansion of the global pig industry has led to a severe 
accumulation of manure, presenting a severe environmental manage­
ment challenge [1]. Consequently, developing efficient treatment and 
resource recovery strategies for pig manure is essential for environ­
mental protection and sustainable agricultural development [2]. 
Although rich in organic matter and nutrients, pig manure is charac­
terized by an imbalanced carbon-to-nitrogen ratio [3]. Its improper 
disposal poses significant environmental risks, such as water eutrophi­
cation, soil contamination with heavy metals, and atmospheric pollution 
[4]. Among these concerns, the emission of intense and complex 
malodorous gases during microbial degradation represents one of the 
most immediate and perceptible hazards [5]. The emission of these 
malodorous gases not only creates a public nuisance and restricts the 
siting of farming and processing facilities, but also poses health risks to 
onsite workers [6].
Anaerobic digestion (AD) has been widely recognized as a promising 
technology for treating pig manure, achieving simultaneous stabiliza­
tion, volume reduction, and energy recovery in the form of methane 
(CH4) [7]. Nevertheless, the traditional anaerobic digestion process is 
often plagued by inherent limitations, such as low CH4 yield and the 
persistent release of substantial amounts of malodorous gases [8,9]. 
Sulfur and nitrogen-containing compounds are key contributors to these 
foul-smelling gases [10,11]. These compounds are formed due to the 
incomplete microbial degradation of sulfur-containing amino acids and 
nitrogen-rich organic matter in pig manure under anaerobic conditions 
[12]. These malodorous gases not only impeded the broader adoption of 
AD technology but also compromises the safe handling and utilization of 
its by-products [13].

Impact of Microaeration and the Redox Mediator
Anthraquinone-2,6-Disulfonate on Azo Dye Reduction
and By-Products Degradation
Amanda N. de Barros, Marcos E. R. da Silva, Paulo I. M. Firmino,
Eduardo A. F. de Vasconcelos, and Andre B. dos Santos*
This work assessed the impact of microaeration and the redox mediator
anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonate (AQDS) on both azo dye reduction and
by-products degradation (aromatic amines) in a mesophilic reactor. The
experiment was carried out in an up-flow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB)
reactor with 3.2 L of working volume and hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 24h.
The synthetic effluent contained 50 mg L1 of the dye Reactive Red 2 (RR2). The
reactor was initially operated under anaerobic conditions and, subsequently, was
microaerated with atmospheric air (1 mLmin1) and then supplemented with the
redox mediator (AQDS) at a concentration of 25 μM. The microaeration effect on
dye reduction and by-products formed was not evident. However, AQDS
considerably enhanced RR2 reduction, and its regeneration was not affected by
the presence of oxygen. It seems that the cleavage of the double bond between
nitrogen groups is a much easier way to start the attack of the azo dye, and it is
independent of the presence of oxygen. Thus, the introduction of hydroxyl groups
into the aromatic ring was not playing a role in the color removal process. In
terms of ecological parameters, the ecological niches were maintained, and the
distribution of species increased, despite the majority being generalists, i.e., not
specialized in dye degradation. Furthermore, anaerobic species are dominant over
facultative species, which explains why there was no population diversity recovery
after the microaeration started.
1. Introduction
The textile sector is one of the most representative segments in
industry due to its importance to the economy of developed
countries and because it represents a “ﬂagship” in several
developing countries. In 2015, it was responsible for US$ 291
billion of world exports, in which China, the European Union,
and India remained the top three exporters
of textiles. Altogether, they accounted for
66.4% of world exports.[1] The Brazilian
demand for textile products is still high,
generating wastewater with high amounts
of dyes, organic matter, chemicals, etc.,
which
poses
a
risk
when
discharged
without treatment into surface water. The
difﬁculty to treat efﬁciently colored waste-
water in treatment plants is a constant in
textile industry, as small amounts of dyes
and pigments produce intense coloring.[2]
It is estimated that 109 kg of dyes are
produced every year in the world, among
which 70% are azo dyes (N55N).[3,4]
These dyes are molecules soluble in water,
which can contain one or more ionic
groups, and the most common used are
sulfonic acid and amine groups. These are
considered recalcitrant and non-biodegrad-
able.[5,6] Large amounts of dyes are lost
during industry process and goes to the
environment as wastewater. Efﬂuents con-
taminated with dyes are considered toxic to
aquatic
environment
and
symbiosis
process, and interfere negatively in photo-
synthesis and primary production, because
transparency is reduced.[5]
Some works show that the application of
quinone-based compounds, such as anthraquinone-2-sulfonate
(AQS) and anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonate (AQDS), vitamins,
such as riboﬂavin, or even yeast extract can accelerate electron
transfer and increase color removal.[7,8] Biological azo dye
reduction usually requires anaerobic operation because the
redox condition achieved is more effective for color removal,
whereas removal or biodegradation of the by-products (aromatic
amines) occur commonly in aerobic environment, in which the
products are used as sources of carbon, nitrogen, and energy.[9]
The addition of microaeration, i.e., introduction of low oxygen
concentrations (< 1 L O2 L1 feed),[10] can facilitate the initial
degradation of some aromatic compounds, including BTEX
(benzene, toluene ethylbenzene, and xylenes), hormones, and
pharmaceuticals, because, under microaerobic conditions, some
microorganisms can use oxygen to introduce hydroxyl groups
into the aromatic ring, as in the classical aerobic pathway,
subsequently facilitating cleavage by anaerobic pathway.[11] By

desulfurization and biomethane generation in a centralized sewage sludge 
digestion plant 
Nicola Di Costanzo a, Francesco Di Capua b,*, Alessandra Cesaro a, Federica Carraturo c, 
Michela Salamone c, Marco Guida c, Giovanni Esposito a, Andrea Giordano d

A B S T R A C T   
The biogas produced in a centralized digestion plant treating high-solid sewage sludge under thermophilic 
conditions was biologically desulfurized via in-situ headspace micro-oxygenation. The removal of hydrogen 
sulfide (H2S) from the produced biogas was evaluated for 84 days under decreasing injection flows of oxygen 
(O2), resulting in O2 doses from 0.96(±0.03) to 0.19(±0.01) NL/Nm3 biogas. A stable H2S removal efficiency of 
98.2(±1.3)% was obtained with an O2 dose of 0.96(±0.03) NL/Nm3 biogas, whereas removal efficiencies of 67.4 
(±0.7)% were observed at the lowest O2 dose tested. The response time of the biological desulfurization system 
to transient oxygen conditions was evaluated through intermittent O2 injection. Headspace micro-oxygenation 
did not negatively impact the digestion performance, and the optimization of O2 dose allowed to reach a 
biogas quality complying with the specification for biomethane in terms of both O2 and H2S contents. Lenti­
microbiaceae, Caldicoprobacteraceae, DTU014, Syntrophomonadaceae, and Rhodobacteraceae were the main 
microbial families responsible for biological H2S oxidation in digester headspace.   
1. Introduction 
AD is a biological process by which complex organic substrates, such 
as sewage sludge, are transformed into biogas, an energy vector, and 
digestate, a semi-solid residue that is nowadays considered a valuable 
source of organic matter and nutrients and can be used as a fertilizer [1, 
2]. The biogas is a well-known energetically valuable product that can 
be further processed to produce biomethane and/or thermal/electrical 
energy [3]. It typically contains 55–65% of CH4, 35–45% of CO2, and 
small concentrations of other gases, including H2S in the range 50–5000 
ppm [4]. H2S in biogas commonly occurs due to the anaerobic 
fermentation of sulfur-containing organic molecules (i.e., proteins) and 
the activity of sulfate-reducing bacteria [5]. The presence of H2S in 
biogas is often a limitation for downstream processing to generate en­
ergy, as H2S oxidation can release harmful SOx in flue gases and create 
corrosive condensates that reduce the operational life of gas pipelines, 
CHP units, boilers, and biogas upgrading systems [6]. Moreover, 
dissolved sulfide is toxic to methanogens already at concentrations 
above 50 mg/L and may cause the inhibition of the AD process [7]. 
Depending on the use of biogas and required desulfurization per­
formance, several biogas desulfurization technologies have been pro­
posed: biological systems, as biotrickling filters and microaeration [8,9], 
adsorption media such as granular activated carbon [10,11], hybrid 
solvent [12] or wet scrubbing systems [13,14]. Physical-chemical pro­
cesses typically require large amounts of chemicals or water as well as 
the replacement and disposal of spent media, making operation and 
maintenance more complex and expensive [6,7]. In contrast, biological 
methods involve lower operational costs with no need for chemical 
addition [15]. Among these methods, the in-situ biological desulfur­
ization consists in the injection of a limited flux of air or O2 into the 
digester headspace, which triggers the biological oxidation of the H2S 
contained in the biogas to SO4
2−and/or S0 by the SOB growing on the 
internal surfaces exposed to O2 [16]. The redox reactions described 
above are shown by Eqs. (1) and (2) [5,17].

Many fermentation products are produced under microaerobic or anaerobic conditions, in which oxygen is
undetectable by dissolved oxygen probe, presenting a challenge for process monitoring and control. Extracellular
redox potentials that can be detected conveniently affect intracellular redox homeostasis and metabolism, and
consequently control proﬁles of fermentation products, which provide an alternative for monitoring and control
of these fermentation processes. This article reviews updated progress in the impact of redox potentials on gene
expression, protein biosynthesis and metabolism as well as redox potential control strategies for more efﬁcient
production of fermentation products, taking ethanol fermentation by the yeast Saccharomyces under microaerobic
conditions and butanol production by the bacterium Clostridium under anaerobic conditions as examples.

anaerobic digestion of swine manure under nano-bubble water addition

A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Nano-bubble water
Anaerobic digestion
Swine manure
Methane production
Hydrolysis
A B S T R A C T
Nano-bubble water (NBW) refers to water with a large number of nanoscale particle bubbles. The aim of this
work was to study the mechanism of NBW addition into the anaerobic digestion (AD) of swine manure (SM). The
results showed that the cumulative methane production from the NBW added reactor was 192–225 mL/g-VS and
19–39% higher than the control group (without NBW addition). Based on the analysis of soluble organics, NBW
addition not only accelerated hydrolysis rates of proteins and carbohydrates, but also enhanced the production
of VFAs. Moreover, mechanism analysis reveals that NBW with higher spin–spin relaxation time and absolute
value of zeta potential might promote enzyme activity and the hydrolysis of organic solids. Simultaneously, the
electron transport system activity of the methanogenic communities and electric conductivity were enhanced by
NBW addition. This work implies that NBW addition is promising for enhancing AD for enhancement of methane
production.
1. Introduction
Globally, a large amount of livestock manure from animal hus-
bandry needs to be scientiﬁcally and eﬀectively processed. The annual
livestock waste produced in Japan is about 80 million tons, of which
swine manure (SM) is as high as 21 million tons (MAFF, 2018). If these
huge amounts of SM are not treated properly, not only the biomass
resources are wasted, but also the surrounding environments are pol-
luted. Composting is a widely applied method to handle livestock
manure since it is capable of stabilizing organic matters, increasing the
manure fertility and sterilizing weed seeds and pathogens (Yuan et al.,
2017). However, composting has some disadvantages like excessive
nutrients loss, greenhouse gases emission, and high eutrophication
potential (Yuan et al., 2018).
Anaerobic digestion (AD) has been widely used in the treatment of
SM. AD involves a series of biochemical processes, in which anaerobic
microorganisms can degrade and stabilize organic matters and produce
biogas and other valuable intermediates as well (Raposo et al., 2009).
Compared with other traditional treatment methods such as com-
posting, AD of SM has many advantages, such as water pollution re-
duction, generation of valuable bioenergy and fertilizer, odor control,
pathogen inactivation (Atandi and Rahman, 2012). Although the AD
process also produces CO2, the carbon source is not derived from fossil
fuel but from biomass, which is considered as carbon neutral (Kothari
et al., 2014). Therefore, AD has become a hot topic in the treatment of
SM. However, AD of SM also has some shortcomings, such as prone to
inhibition, low hydrolysis rate, low biogas and methane production
(Burton et al., 2003; Carrère et al., 2009).
Many methods can be used to increase methane production and to
improve AD performance, such as chemical (González-Fernández et al.,
2008), thermal (Wu et al., 2017), thermal steam explosion pretreatment
(Ferreira et al., 2014), co-digestion (Dennehy et al., 2016), initial pH
adjustment (Zhang et al., 2015), additives addition (Wang et al., 2017;
Yang et al., 2018), or applying a proper inoculum ratio (González-
Fernández and García-Encina, 2009). Although these methods show
some improvement eﬀects on AD performance, most of them have not
been applied in industry. The main reason is most probably due to the
consumption of chemicals and energy or the complexity of operations,
partly counteracting its environmental-friendliness and cost-eﬀective-
ness. As known, water is critical in the AD process, which can facilitate
the transfer of hydrolyzed products to the site where the bacteria can
utilize them (Bollon et al., 2013). In this aspect, most studies have been
focusing on water content, namely, AD performance under diﬀerent
total solids (TS) contents (dry or wet AD) (Li et al., 2015; Chen et al.,

Dose-dependent effects of micro-aeration on methane production and 
lignocellulose degradation during continuous anaerobic digestion of 
food waste
Ziyu Xiong a,1, Yutong Wu a,1, Jinglin Li b, Yafan Cai c, Xingyao Meng a,*, Pan Wang a,  
Lianhai Ren a
a School of Light Industry Science and Engineering, Beijing Technology and Business University, Beijing, 100048, China
b China IPPR International Engineering Co, Ltd., Beijing, 100089, China
c School of Chemical Engineering, Zhengzhou University, Zhengzhou, 450001, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Bioenergy
Micro-aeration
Waste valorization
Methane recovery
Microbial functional potential
A B S T R A C T
While micro-aeration is a promising strategy to enhance hydrolysis and acidogenesis in anaerobic digestion (AD), 
its dose-dependent effects on lignocellulose degradation and methane production under different total solids (TS) 
conditions remain unclear. This study investigated continuous AD of food waste (FW) at TS levels of 6% and 10% 
under oxygen loading rates of 0, 2.625, 5.25, and 10.50 mLO2/LR/d. At TS = 6%, 2.625 mLO2/LR/d modestly 
increased methane yield from 527.2 to 561.9 mL/gVSadded and increased cellulose removal to 60.16%. At 5.25 
mLO2/LR/d, biogas production increased further, whereas methane content decreased, indicating enhanced 
upstream substrate conversion rather than proportionally enhanced methanogenesis. At TS = 10%, improved 
methane production was observed only at 2.625 mLO2/LR/d, while higher oxygen loading impaired process 
performance. Excessive aeration caused volatile fatty acid (VFA) accumulation, increased oxidation reduction 
potential (ORP), and reduced lignocellulose degradation. Microbial community analysis showed oxygen- 
dependent shifts in lignocellulose-associated bacteria and methanogens, while PICRUSt2-based prediction sug­
gested changes in hydrolysis-related functions, energy metabolism, and oxidative-stress-response potential. 
Overall, the effective oxygen-loading window narrowed with increasing TS, and low oxygen input modestly 
improved methane production, whereas moderate oxygen loading mainly enhanced upstream substrate 
conversion.
1. Introduction
FW management has become a critical issue in sustainable waste 
treatment, resource recovery, and greenhouse gas mitigation. In 2022, 
approximately 1.05 billion tonnes of food were wasted globally, 
contributing an estimated 8–10% of global greenhouse gas emissions [1,
2]. Anaerobic digestion is widely recognized as an effective technology 
for FW treatment because it enables organic stabilization, methane re­
covery, and nutrient recycling [3,4]. However, FW contains lignocellu­
losic fractions such as vegetable stalks and fruit peels, in which cellulose, 
hemicellulose, and lignin are embedded in a recalcitrant matrix that 
limits enzymatic accessibility and hydrolysis efficiency [5,6]. As hy­
drolysis is generally regarded as the rate-limiting step in FW AD, 
improving lignocellulose solubilization while maintaining stable meth­
anogenesis is essential for enhancing the overall conversion of FW into 
methane.
Several studies have explored ways to improve the performance of 
AD, including substrate pretreatments, optimizing process parameters 
and introducing additives. However, the pretreatment or supplementary 
additives usually required extra energy and chemicals, thereby 
increasing operational costs and process complexity and potentially 
causing environmental concerns. Recent studies have shown that micro- 
aeration, which involves injecting small amounts of air or oxygen into an 
anaerobic system, has attracted increasing attention as a cost-effective 
strategy for improving digestion performance by accelerating hydroly­
sis and acidogenesis and providing more available substrates for

A B S T R A C T   
This research studied the conversion of alkaline-pretreated oil palm empty fruit bunch (OPEFB) into volatile fatty 
acids (VFA) through anaerobic fermentation (AF). In AF, the methanogens that consume VFAs must be sup­
pressed to increase the accumulated VFA as an intermediate product of AF. In-depth research has not been 
conducted on the effects of temperature and micro aeration to maximize the VFA accumulation. To investigate 
the temperature effect, the experiment was run at mesophilic (RM) and thermophilic conditions (RT). The impact 
of the micro aeration dose was studied in the thermophilic reactor set to the ORP −50 mV (RTM −50) and ORP 
−150 mV (RTM −150). The experimental data were fitted to the Anaerobic Digestion Model 1 (ADM 1) using 
AQUASIM®. The khyd.ch value of the RT reactor is higher than that of the RM, suggesting that high temperatures 
encourage hydrolysis and enhance hydrolase activity. Based on the simulation results, RT reactors without micro- 
aeration had a substantially higher specific growth rate of methanogens compared to RM. Therefore, micro 
aeration should be applied in RT to suppress the potentially faster growth of methanogen bacteria at elevated 
temperature. The result of this study indicated that both temperature and micro-aeration were important process 
variable to be further optimized to make VFAs production from OPEFB attractive.   
1. Introduction 
Over the last few decades, palm oil production has grown very 
rapidly. Consequently, the amount of oil palm empty fruit bunch 
(OPEFB) as the solid wastes in palm oil industries has increased signif­
icantly, posing a severe environmental burden. Based on Indonesia’s 
Central Statistical Bureau (Badan Pusat Statistik/BPS) data, in 2020, 
Indonesia produced more than 44 million tons of palm oil annually [1]. 
For every ton of fresh fruit bunches used in the oil extraction process, 
lignocellulosic biomass was produced, including oil palm empty fruit 
bunches (OPEFB) (23%), mesocarp fiber (12%), decanter cake (6%), and 
shell (5%) [2]. Untreated OPEFB contained 15.2% hemicellulose, 25.8% 
lignin, 40.9% cellulose, and 18.1% miscellaneous components [3]. The 
rich carbon source in lignocellulosic biomass makes it a highly ideal 
substrate feedstock for anaerobic processes, which produce carboxylic 
acids and biogas [4,5]. However, before being used as a substrate, 
OPEFB must be pretreated because lignin in the biomass forms an 
impermeable/resistant layer, making it difficult to biodegrade [6]. In 
another study, pretreated OPEFB could be a source of fermentable 
sugars [7], such as 2,3-butanediol (2,3-BDO). Other interesting pathway 
of utilizing lignocellulose waste is anaerobic fermentation (AF) to collect 
the intermediate product, i.e. volatile fatty acids (VFA) [8,9]. 
VFAs are low-molecular-weight carboxylates containing 2–6 carbon 
atoms with primary components of propionic acid, acetic acid, butyric 
acid, and valeric acid [10]. Some of the potential substrates to produce 
VFAs include citrus waste [11], activated sludge waste [12], tuna waste 
[13], household food waste [14], and vegetable waste [15]. VFAs can be 
utilized as attractive carbon sources for the removal of ammonia, ni­
trogen, and phosphorus during wastewater treatment [16,17]. They can

A B S T R A C T   
Micro-aeration has been shown to be favorable for anaerobic digestion (AD) process. However, the underlying 
mechanisms are not fully revealed. In this study, the effects of micro-aeration on AD process were investigated, 
the underlying mechanisms were also explored by comprehensively analysis of the substrate degradation, in­
termediate products, electron-transfer capacity, key enzymes and microbial communities. Results showed micro- 
aeration could benefit the AD process, and the beneficial effects were oxygen intensity-dependent. Maximum 
methane yield (262.0 ± 6.0 mL/(g⋅VS)) was achieved at micro-aeration of 0.2 mL/(g⋅VS⋅day), which was 7.8% 
higher than that of the control (without micro-aeration). The volatile fatty acids concentration, cellulase activity, 
soluble humic acids (SHAs) concentration and substrate degradation rate were all enhanced under micro- 
aeration condition. Moreover, micro-aeration could regulate the bacterial and archaeal communities: bacterial 
diversities and relative abundances of facultative and acetate-oxidizing bacteria (e.g., Firmicutes, Synergistota and 
Spirochaetota) increased, leading to higher substrate utilization rate; archaeal diversities decreased while oxygen- 
tolerating methanogens (e.g., Methanobacterium) became dominant to promote the methanogenesis. AD system 
with micro-aeration showed higher electron-transfer capacity and better conductive environment due to the 
increased SHAs concentration. The increased relative abundance of direct-interspecies-electron-transfer (DIET)- 
associated microbes could be favorable to DIET-based syntrophic methanogenesis which promotes AD under 
micro-aeration.   
1. Introduction 
Lignocellulosic biomass, such as agricultural and forest residues, 
energy crops, and grasses is the most abundant renewable bioresource 
on the Earth [1]. Corn is one of the most important grain crops in China, 
and the yearly yield of corn crop is estimated to be 520 million tons, 
which yields 260 million tons of corn straw as a major by-product [2,3]. 
Corn straw has been proved to be a potential substrate for biogas pro­
duction via anaerobic digestion (AD). Many biogas plants that use corn 
straw as feedstock are built every year in China. Although promising, 
some barriers still exist in AD of corn straw, among which the low hy­
drolysis efficiency caused by the recalcitrant structure of corn straw is 
generally regarded as the rate-limiting step [4]. 
In order to enhance the AD efficiency of corn straw, various substrate 
pretreatment methods have been extensively studied, including phys­
ical, chemical and biological pretreatments as well as their combinations 
[5–8]. However, these pretreatment methods have their respective 
inherent shortcomings, e.g., need of chemicals, high energy consump­
tion and/or long residence time. Another choice to improve the AD ef­
ficiency of cellulosic substrate is to manage or alter the microbial 
community composition through bioaugmentation, enrichment and/or 
stimulation of specific indigenous microorganisms [9]. Micro-aeration 
by introducing limited amount of oxygen into the AD system has been 
proved to be a potential strategy to address the challenge of low hy­
drolysis efficiency associated with AD of cellulosic substrate [10,11]. As 
reported, micro-aeration during AD can stimulate the growth of facul­
tative anaerobes which excrete more extracellular enzymes to improve 
hydrolysis and fermentation of lignocellulosic biomass, thus enhancing

Improved methane production from corn straw using anaerobically digested
sludge pre-augmented by nanobubble water
Xuezhi Wanga, Zhongfang Leia,⁎, Kazuya Shimizua, Zhenya Zhanga, Duu-Jong Leeb,c
a Graduate School of Life and Environmental Sciences, University of Tsukuba, 1-1-1 Tennodai, Tsukuba, Ibaraki 305-8572, Japan

A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Corn straw
Anaerobic digestion
Methane production
Pre-augmentation
Nanobubble water
A B S T R A C T
Nanobubble water (NBW) has been proven to efficiently improve methane production from organic solid wastes.
However, the increase in reactor volume due to addition of NBW hinders its practical applications. In this study,
anaerobically digested sludge was first pre-augmented by N2-NBW and O2-NBW using corn straw as sole sub-
strate for methane production with electron transfer activity being monitored. 20%, 33% and 38% of cellulose
and 29%, 35% and 35% of hemicellulose were reduced respectively from the control, N2-NBW and O2-NBW pre-
augmented sludge reactors. N2-NBW and O2-NBW pre-augmented sludge reactors achieved methane yields of
127 and 142 mL/g-VS, about 10% and 22% higher than that from the control. Results show that use of NBW pre-
augmented anaerobically digested sludge as inoculum can remarkably enhance methane yield from corn straw,
providing a novel concept for NBW-based anaerobic digestion system with no increase of reactor volume and
construction cost in practice.
1. Introduction
The irregular climate change and energy crisis are considered to
closely associate with excessive use of non-renewable fossil fuel, and
biofuel may be a good solution for these issues (Robertson et al., 2017).
Biofuel generation from renewable resources can solve the energy
shortage as well as the associated environmental problems. In recent
years, agricultural wastes, such as crop straws have gained great at-
tention due to their abundant distribution, carbon neutrality and ability
to sidestep competition with food crops for land. They have also de-
monstrated significant potential to satisfy the feedstock targets for the
advanced 2nd-generation biofuels (Cornejo et al., 2019).

Anaerobic digestion (AD) of lignocellulosic biomass is a promising
approach for bioenergy (mainly methane) production (Xu et al., 2019).
Corn straw is a typical agricultural waste that is produced in large
quantities globally for food, feed and industrial applications. Corn
productions in the US and China account for 40% and 20% of the world,
respectively (Veljković et al., 2018). In China, the annual production of
corn straw is about 216 million tons, which shows high potential for
methane production (Wei et al., 2020). Although AD of lignocellulosic
biomass has been widely applied to achieve the sustainable manage-
ment of agricultural wastes, the low energy conversion efficiency limits
its application mainly due to the following two aspects: 1) the low
metabolic activity of microbes, and 2) the rigidity and recalcitrant
structure of lignocellulose (Huang et al., 2019).
To cope with the above problems, various pretreatments including
physical, chemical and biological methods have been attempted to
enhance biogas production from AD of lignocellulosic biomass. For
physical methods, steam explosion pretreatment could decrease the
hemicellulose content of corn straw by 28% and increase the neutral
detergent solute by 24% (Shi et al., 2019). Some chemical methods like
phosphate addition could accelerate the biogasification process of rice
straw particles and total solids or volatile solids reduction to a certain
extent (Lei et al., 2010). In addition, biological methods such as Tri-
choderma reesei addition could effectively remove lignin by 23% com-
pared to the untreated rice straw (Mustafa et al., 2016). However, the
improvement of methane production is difficult to balance the addi-
tional energy consumption, high process cost and secondary pollution
potentials due to the additives addition. Thus, environment-friendly
methods are still urgently required to meet the sustainable development
goals (SDGs).
Most recently, nanobubble water (NBW) has been proven to en-
hance methane production from AD of waste activated sludge and lig-
nocellulosic biomass (Wang et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2019; Wang et al.,
2019a). NBW is defined as the water containing gas nanobubbles (NBs)
with diameter less than 1000 nm that have some special physico-
chemical properties, such as negative surface charge, low buoyancy,
high gas solubility (Lyu et al., 2019), rapid mass transfer rate (Agarwal
et al., 2011) and better stability (dispersed in liquids or adhered to solid
surfaces) (Ghadimkhani et al., 2016). The NBs in NBW could improve
the contact areas between the solid and liquid phases (Lyu et al., 2019).

anaerobic digestion of chicken manure wastewater 
Krailak Fakkaew a,*, Chongrak Polprasert b 
a Environmental Health Program, School of Health Science, Mae Fah Luang University, Thailand

Keywords: 
Air stripping 
Chicken manure 
Anaerobic digestion 
Biogas production 
Ammonia 
A B S T R A C T   
Anaerobic digestion is typically applied for water and air pollution control and energy recovery from chicken 
manure wastewater. Unfortunately, high nitrogen content of the chicken manure could be prohibitive to efficient 
anaerobic digestion. In this study, air stripping was employed as a pre-treatment process for ammonia removal 
from a chicken manure wastewater. Laboratory-scale experiments of air striping were conducted at various 
temperatures, initial pH values, air flow rates, and stripping times. The experimental results showed that the high 
ammonia removal efficiencies of more than 80% could be achieved from the air stripping process operating at the 
initial pH, temperature, and air flow rate of 11, 80 ◦C, and 4.0 L/min, respectively. The ammonia removal ki­
netics were found to fit with the first-order reaction. Bio-methane potential tests suggested that air stripping pre- 
treatment of the chicken manure wastewater resulted in about 25% increase in biogas production.   
1. Introduction 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a cost-effective and environmentally- 
friendly method which can treat and recover bio-energy from various 
types of organic wastes. AD of livestock wastes such as chicken and 
swine manures could yield considerable environmental and economic 
benefits, including water and air pollution control, and renewable en­
ergy production (Blumenstein et al., 2016; Cowley and Brorsen, 2018; 
Scarlat et al., 2018). Although chicken manure is rich in organic matters 
and has higher potentials for biogas production than swine and cow 
manures (Owamah et al., 2014; Qiao et al., 2011), its high nitrogen 
content could be prohibitive to efficient anaerobic digestion. During 
microbial degradation, organic nitrogen is converted to ammonia which 
could act as a strong inhibitor on microbiological conversion in the AD 
process (Angelidaki and Ahring, 1993; Nielsen and Angelidaki, 2008). 
Total ammonia nitrogen concentration greater than 3 g/L could result in 
a decreased methane production (Bi et al., 2020; Calli et al., 2005; Chen 
et al., 2008; Yenigün and Demirel, 2013). To overcome the ammonia 
inhibition of AD, various ammonia reduction techniques have been 
developed including: substrate dilution, co-digestion with high‑carbon 
substrates, pH and temperature setting, use of additives with adsorptive 
capacity such as activated carbon, bentonite and zeolite, use of trace 
elements 
such 
as 
selenium, 
microflora 
acclimation 
and 
bioaugmentation, stripping, membrane processes, struvite precipitation, 
ultrasonication and microwave irradiation, and biological process such 
as Anammox (Fuchs et al., 2018). 
Ammonia stripping is considered to be a cost-effective technique that 
requires relatively low energy inputs in which free ammonia is trans­
ferred from the wastewater into the gas phase (Li et al., 2018). Ammonia 
stripping experiments have been carried out by using a variety of 
techniques at different operating conditions such as pH, temperatures, 
and stripping agents (air, nitrogen, steam, or biogas) (Bonmati and 
Flotats, 2003; Georgiou et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Jiang et al., 
2013; Ledda et al., 2013; Li et al., 2018; Nie et al., 2015; Serna-Maza 
et al., 2015; Walker et al., 2011; Zeng et al., 2006). Successful applica­
tions of ammonia stripping have been reported both as a pre-AD process 
to various feedstocks, such as: domestic and industrial wastewaters, 
piggery and poultry wastes (Georgiou et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2019; Li 
et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2012), and as a post-AD process to the effluent 
of anaerobic digestion and digested dairy manure supernatant (Huang 
et al., 2016; Jiang et al., 2014; Lei et al., 2007; Serna-Maza et al., 2015). 
Currently, ammonia stripping methods are based on pH and/or 
temperature of substrate. Because pH directly affects the distribution of 
ammonia forms (NH4
+/NH3) in aqueous solutions, raising pH to more 
than 11 results in the conversion of almost all the ammonium ions (NH4
+) 
into dissolved ammonia gases (NH3) (Tchobanoglous et al., 2003).

Eﬀect of incubation conditions on the aerobic pretreatment of the organic solid wastes and
the volatile fatty acids production
Efecto de las condiciones de incubación en el pretratamiento aeróbico de los residuos
sólidos orgánicos y la producción de ácidos grasos volátiles
J.E. Jiménez-Rodríguez, F.J. Martínez-Valdez, R. Estrada-Martínez, O. Monroy-Hermosillo,
G. Saucedo- Castañeda, F. Ramírez-Vives*
Metropolitan Autonomous University Campus Iztapalapa, Biotechnology Department, Mexico City, Iztapalapa, Z.C. 09340,
Mexico.
Received: September 10, 2019; Accepted: November 19, 2019
Abstract
In the present work, the eﬀect of an aerobic pretreatment on the hydrolysis and acidogenesis of the organic solid wastes (OSW)
was evaluated. The aerobic pretreatment was carried out under three incubation conditions: the ﬁrst condition was at 30 °C for
24 hours (isothermal), the second condition was at 30 °C for 12 hours followed by 12 hours at 35 °C, and the third condition
was at 35 °C for 12 hours followed by 12 hours at 40 °C. The enzymatic activity was analysed during the aerobic pretreatment,
and the product obtained was subsequently fermented in anaerobic hydrolytic leach bed reactors (AHLB) to obtain volatile fatty
acids (VFA). The best hydrolysis results were achieved with the aerobic pretreatment at 30 °C for 24 hours, obtaining activities
of xylanases and pectinases of 115 and 73 U g−1 dry matter (DM) respectively, after 18 hours and 100 U g−1 DM of proteases
at the beginning of the process; values that are 2.7, 2 and 4 times higher than previously report. Also, a hydrolysis constant (k)
of 0.081 d−1 was obtained, with the productivity of VFA of 0.82gLr−1d−1, with predominance in acetate, the main precursor of
methanogenesis in the ﬁnal stage of anaerobic digestion.
Keywords: Organic Solid Wastes (OSW), aerobic pretreatment, hydrolysis, leachate, volatile fatty acids.
Resumen
En el presente trabajo, se evaluó el efecto de un pretratamiento aeróbico sobre la hidrólisis y la acidogénesis de los residuos
sólidos orgánicos (RSO). El pretratamiento aeróbico se llevó a cabo bajo tres condiciones de incubación: la primera condición fue
a 30 °C durante 24 horas (isotérmica), la segunda condición fue a 30 °C durante 12 horas seguido de 12 horas a 35 °C, y la tercera
condición fue a 35 °C durante 12 horas seguido de 12 horas a 40 °C. Se analizó la actividad enzimática durante el pretratamiento
aeróbico y el producto obtenido se fermentó posteriormente en reactores hidrolíticos anaerobios de lecho escurrido (RALE) para
obtener ácidos grasos volátiles (AGV). Los mejores resultados de hidrólisis se lograron con el pretratamiento aeróbico a 30 °C
durante 24 horas, obteniendo actividades de xilanasas y pectinasas de 115 y 73 U g−1 materia seca (MS) respectivamente después
de 18 horas y 100 U g−1 MS de proteasas al inicio del proceso; valores que son 2.7, 2 y 4 veces más altos que los reportados
previamente. Además, se obtuvo una constante de hidrólisis (k) de 0.081 d−1, con una productividad de AGV de 0.82gLr−1d−1,
con predominio en acetato, el principal precursor de la metanogénesis en la etapa ﬁnal de la digestión anaerobia.
Palabras clave: Residuos sólidos orgánicos, pretratamiento aerobio, hidrólisis, lixiviado, ácidos grasos volátiles.

Keywords:

A B S T R A C T
Tetracycline is widely present in sludge, and its residual concentration can vary substantially under different 
contamination scenarios. Nanobubble water (NBW) has been shown to promote sludge anaerobic digestion (AD), 
but its effects on tetracycline removal and changes in antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) during sludge AD remain 
unclear. This study evaluated the effects of NBW on sludge AD under different tetracycline concentrations (0, 2, 
and 20 mg L−1). The addition of NBW reduced tetracycline concentrations by 10.4%–23.1% and ARG abundance 
by 1.8%-14.3%, while mitigating the potential risks associated with ARG transmission. In addition, NBW may 
enhance antioxidant enzyme activities by upregulating the abundance of antioxidant-related functional genes, 
thereby strengthening the antioxidant capacity of the system. At the same time, NBW reduced the abundance of 
type IV secretion system-related functional genes, suggesting a reduced dissemination potential of ARGs asso­
ciated with mobile genetic elements (MGEs). These changes may contribute to the reduction of ARGs during 
sludge AD. Overall, NBW improved the removal efficiency of tetracycline and ARGs during sludge AD, providing 
novel perspectives for mitigating the potential environmental risks associated with the final digestate.

1. Introduction
Tetracycline ranks among the most extensively utilized antibiotics 
globally in aquaculture sectors, human medicine, and animal husbandry 
(Wang et al., 2025b). Over 50% of tetracycline cannot be fully metab­
olized during usage, resulting in the frequent detection of significant 
amounts of tetracycline in industrial wastewater, medical wastewater, 
and livestock manure (Xu et al., 2021). During wastewater treatment, 
tetracycline tends to be adsorbed onto sludge due to its high affinity for 
solid phases (Zhao et al., 2020), thus leading to its accumulation in the 
sludge. However, the levels of tetracycline residues in sludge vary 
greatly. A multi-city survey of sludge found that the total tetracycline 
concentrations could reach 0.6–37.9 mg kg−1 dry weight, while in some 
pharmaceutical wastewater treatment plant dewatered sludge, tetracy­
cline concentrations could be as high as 300–2790 mg kg−1 dry weight 
(Cheng et al., 2014; Hou et al., 2016; McClellan and Halden, 2010). The 
treatment of tetracycline-containing sludge is both highly important and 
challenging.
As a typical selective pressure, tetracycline in the sludge can drive 
the generation and enrichment of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs)- 
particularly tetracycline resistance genes, which are the most prevalent 
and diverse ARG subsets associated with tetracycline exposure (Wang 
et al., 2025b). As emerging environmental pollutants, ARGs can be 
horizontally transferred between microorganisms via mobile genetic 
elements (MGEs) such as plasmids and transposons (Zhang et al., 2026). 
The residual tetracycline exhibits a positive correlation with ARGs 
abundance, which not only reduces the efficacy of subsequent antibiotic 
treatment but also poses a persistent threat to ecological stability and 
human health via the dissemination of ARG-carrying microorganisms 
across diverse environmental media (Bai et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023). 
Consequently, the mitigation of tetracycline-induced ARG pollution has

experiences
Lucie Pokorna-Krayzelova,

Eveline I. P. Volckebc and Pavel Jeniceka
Microaeration, a biological method to remove H2S from biogas by oxidizing it to elemental sulfur, has been
shown to be highly efficient, simple and reliable. However, dosing air directly into an anaerobic fermenter
results in the dilution of biogas with nitrogen and oxygen and can cause clogging of biogas pipes by ele-
mental sulfur. These disadvantages can be overcome by the use of a biomembrane, i.e. a membrane cov-
ered with a biofilm that separates air and biogas. Experiments with bare, wet and biofilm membranes were
conducted with a commercially available PVDF LM-P2 membrane to evaluate the chemical and biological
oxidation rates of H2S. Different amounts of air were dosed through the biomembrane to determine the
optimum air-to-biogas ratio, to evaluate methane losses and to evaluate biogas contamination with nitro-
gen and oxygen. The H2S content decreased from 3000 ppm to less than 100 ppm within two days. The
loss of methane was 3.7% of the total methane production and the specific H2S removal rate was 32 mg
m−2 d−1.
1. Introduction
During the anaerobic treatment of wastewater with high sulfate
concentrations,
sulfate-reducing

fur dioxide from biogas combustion.3 Because of these negative
effects, hydrogen sulfide has to be removed from biogas.
The available methods for desulfurization are physico-
chemical (e.g. absorption, precipitation) or biological (e.g.
biochemical oxidation of sulfide) methods.4,5 Biological pro-
cesses are often simpler and more cost-effective compared to
physico-chemical methods.3 One of the options for biological
H2S removal from biogas, which has been used on a full-
scale,6 is microaeration, i.e. the controlled dosing of a small
amount of air into an anaerobic reactor.7–9 In microaeration,
sulfide is oxidized to elemental sulfur by sulfide-oxidizing
bacteria, at low oxygen concentrations. The elemental sulfur
produced is insoluble and could be possibly removed from
the system. Both the total concentration of sulfide in the ef-
fluent and the concentration of hydrogen sulfide in biogas
can be significantly decreased with this process.10
The possible drawbacks of microaeration are the dilution
of biogas with nitrogen and little or no control over the exact
location where elemental sulfur is deposited. Elemental sul-

space11 or in the liquid effluent.12 However, sulfur could also
accumulate in the three-phase separators of anaerobic high-
rate bioreactors or in gas pipes, which may cause serious
clogging problems. These problems could be overcome by
using a biomembrane, where air needed for microaeration is

Pre-aeration was investigated for enhancing biodegradation of recalcitrant lignocellulosic structure of
rice straw under various low temperatures regimes (25, 35 and 45 C) and aeration durations (0, 2, 4,
6 and 8 days). It was demonstrated aerated rice straw for 2 days at 35 C resulted in highest hydrolytic
efﬁciency and biochemical methane potential (BMP) (355.3 ± 18.7 ml CH4/gVS). Furthermore, both
methane yields and initiation speeds of the solid-state anaerobic digestion (SS-AD) were inversely pro-
portional to substrate-to-inoculum ratios due to the accumulation of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) and poor
mass transfer. The highest methane yield achieved under SS-AD was 234 ml CH4/gVS at TS of 16% which
72% of the BMP. Inoculum dilution with recycled water improved buffering capacity and mitigated accu-
mulation of VFAs, resulting in an improved SS-AD performance. The combined pre-aeration and SS-AD
was therefore established as a viable option to accelerate methane production for lignocellulosic biomass.

1. Introduction
Nowadays, increasing attention has been devoted on various
strategies for the bioconversion of biomass into methane-rich bio-
gas due to increased global warming, the need for sustainable
waste management and high energy costs (Li et al., 2016b). The
anaerobic digestion (AD) or biomethanation is an attractive
approach to biodegradable waste treatment which has a dual-
advantage of volumetric reduction of organic wastes in the
oxygen-free condition and renewable energy generation such as
biogas, containing 60–70% of methane (Yan et al., 2015). AD of bio-
waste and sludge is a well-developed technique in European coun-
tries. In Germany, which is the leading country in this ﬁeld, >50% of
the biogas potential results from energy crops treated in over 7000
biogas plants (Li et al., 2011). Furthermore, it was reported by
Swedish Energy Agency that there are over 260 biogas plants in

(SS-AD) has several predominances including smaller digester vol-
ume, higher solid loading capacity with total solids (TS) content of
15%–35%, free of ﬂoating and stratiﬁcation of ﬁbrous materials,
reduced energy requirements for agitation, minimal material wear
by fewer detachable machine parts to handle. SS-AD may also be
less susceptibility to detrimental substances and over acidiﬁcation
especially when the new substrate is mixed with the digestate
from the bottom of the reactor (Weiland, 2010). SS-AD has been
used to manage municipal solid waste since the 1990s and pre-

2013). Moreover, various types of organic wastes with lignocellu-
losic structure of high solid contents are also treated by SS-AD to

difference in methane yields in both SS-AD and L-AD when treating
lignocellulosic biomasses such as wheat straw, switch grass and
corn stover (Brown et al., 2012).
Rice straw is one of the major agricultural wastes and the dry
content of global rice straw reached approximately 741 million
tons in 2014 (FAO, 2016). The waste management of rice straw

it is complicated to adjust substrates ratio in co-digestion and the

H I G H L I G H T S  
• Hydrolysis and BMP performance of various biological pretreatments were studied. 
• Different pretreatment conditions have resulted in different microbial diversity. 
• PCA analysis identified no correlation between hydrolysis and BMP. 
• BMP showed good correlation with sN, sP, sCOD, and propionic acid formation. 
• Total VFAs were correlated to VS removal and levels of acetic and butyric acid.  
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Temperature-phased anaerobic digestion 
Microalgae 
Biomethane potential 
Volatile fatty acids 
Microbial community 
A B S T R A C T   
Parameters of temperature-phased anaerobic digestion (TPAD) were varied to study their effects on hydrolysis, 
biomethane potential (BMP), and microbial diversity of microalgae biodegradation. Anaerobic pretreatments at 
85 ◦C demonstrated the release of soluble carbohydrate and protein molecules under low microbial metabolic 
activity. However, at 55 ◦C, anaerobic pretreatments showed superior performance in methane yield, nutrient 
release, and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production due to dominant Clostridium. Furthermore, the highest 
destruction of volatile solids (VS) was observed during aerobic pretreatments at 55 ◦C under the influence of 
various quantities of these genera – Luteimonas, Symbiobacterium, Soehngenia, Thermobacillus, and Ureibacillus. 
Statistical analysis revealed that hydrolysis and BMP were not correlated. However, soluble nitrogen and 
phosphorous showed strong correlation with methane (r = 0.623 and 0.948, respectively) under thermo- 
anaerobic pretreatment, while VS removal and concentrations of acetic and butyric acids and lipids were posi­
tively correlated with each other under thermo-aerobic pretreatment.   
1. Introduction 
As a potential alternative energy source to fossil fuels, third-gen­
eration biofuels derived from microalgae have shown promise for bio- 
energy production due to their high quantum yield, high biomass per 
unit area, and low competition for arable land (Marsolek et al., 2014). 
Growing algae using wastewater effluent offers multiple benefits such as 
the recovery of nutrients, removal of heavy metals, and production of 
biogas as a renewable energy source. It also has the potential of coupling 
CO2 mitigation to wastewater recycling (Barrag´an-Trinidad et al., 
2017). 
However, digestion of algae requires pretreatment to breakdown 
resistant cell walls to render them susceptible to microbial attack 
(Gonzalez-Fernandez et al., 2015). Various technologies have been 
suggested as pretreatment including physical, thermal, chemical, me­
chanical, and biological processes (Passos et al., 2014). Biological 
degradation of microalgae using anaerobic digestion offers the most 
cost-effective, environmental-friendly option, is feasible for large-scale

application, and is energy-efficient, requiring few chemicals, while 
producing non-inhibitory byproducts (Sindhu et al., 2016). It requires 
microorganisms such as fungi, protozoa, and bacteria, and costly in­
dustrial enzymatic cocktails (Barrag´an-Trinidad et al., 2017). 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is generally regarded as a potential means 
to recovery energy via biogas production. Among the various types of 
AD setups, the current study utilized temperature-phased anaerobic 
digestion (TPAD) due to its excellent reactor stability, methanogen ac­
tivity, and the abundance and diversity of the microbial community (Ge 
et al., 2011; Jang et al., 2014). The biggest advantage of TPAD is its 
potential to combine both enhanced hydrolysis and stability while uti­
lizing moderate energy input and completely removing pathogens 
(Pervin et al., 2013). Moreover, TPAD provides both high destruction of 
solids along with an increased rate of gas production at a relatively low 
capital cost (Ge et al., 2011). This increased removal of volatile solids 
(VS) thereby reduces the costs associated with subsequent sludge dew­
atering and sludge disposal (Lv et al., 2010). 
However, applications of these biological methods to microalgae 
pretreatment have been limited, to date, due to insufficient knowledge 
and uncertainties about the process performance. Among these, the

(iii) only sequences that overlap longer than 10 bp were assembled according to their overlap sequence. Reads which could not be assembled were discarded. The reduction of sulfate to sulfide is a critical factor limiting the efficiency of anaerobic digestion in treating 
sulfate-containing organic wastewater. This study proposes a synergistic operational strategy that combines 
nitrate addition and microaeration to inhibit sulfate reduction and enhance anaerobic digestion performance.

strategy improved chemical oxygen demand removal efficiency and methane production by 48.2–49.8 % and 
138.5–141.5 %, respectively, surpassing the enhancements achieved by nitrate addition alone (28.5–36.0 % and 
69.2–86.2 %) or microaeration alone (38.3 % and 87.7 %, respectively). This synergistic approach inhibited the

1. Introduction
Sulfate-containing organic wastewater (SOW) is generated by 
various industrial sectors, including the petrochemical, pharmaceutical, 
textile dyeing, mining processing, and food processing industries 
(Cetecioglu et al., 2019; Jung et al., 2019; Zak et al., 2021). Directly 
discharging untreated SOW can severely disrupt aquatic ecosystems and 
threaten aquatic organisms and human health. Therefore, the effective 
treatment of SOW is of significant importance for environmental pro­
tection and sustainable development.
Biological treatment methods, particularly anaerobic digestion, are 
widely used to manage organic wastewater because of their operational 
simplicity and cost-effectiveness. Anaerobic digestion offers multiple 
advantages over aerobic treatment technologies, including reduced 
aeration requirements, lower operating costs, a high organic loading 
capacity, minimal sludge production, and generating secondary energy 
in the form of methane (Fang et al., 2019). However, the chemical ox­
ygen demand (COD) removal efficiency in the treatment of SOW 
generally remains below 80 % (Deng et al., 2022; Li et al., 2022), pri­
marily because of the proliferation of sulfate-reducing bacteria (SRB).

Enhanced heavy metal stability of sludge anaerobic digestion by different 
dosages of air nanobubble water
Tianfeng Wang a,*, Ziying Xu a, Jie Wang a, Siqi Ren a, Cheng Peng a, Dan Luo a, Xuemei Zhang b,

A R T I C L E  I N F O
Editor: Wenshan Guo
Keywords:
Nanobubble water
Anaerobic digestion
Heavy metal speciation
Valence state
Potential ecological risks
A B S T R A C T
Nanobubbled water (NBW) can improve the performance of sludge anaerobic digestion (AD) to enhance 
digestate dewaterability. However, the effects of different doses of NBW on the stability of heavy metals (HMs) 
remain unknown. This study found that NBW increased the ultimate methane production of sludge AD by 11.7 
%–16.0 %. Compared with the corresponding control groups, the 40 % Air-NBW group (A40) presented the best 
improvement in methane production and digestate dewaterability of the three different dose groups (20 %, 40 %, 
and 60 % NBW: mixed substrates). NBW contributed to decreasing the proportion of HMs in the unstable 
exchangeable/acid-soluble fraction and promoting the conversion of heavy metal ions to stable low-valence 
states and low-energy levels. These low-valence states and low-energy levels of HMs were positively corre­
lated with digestate dewaterability and methane production. NBW reduced the potential ecological risk index 
(RI) of HMs by 4.2 %–42.0 %, with the A40 showing the greatest reduction in ecological risks. The RI of HMs was 
negatively correlated with methane production and digestate dewaterability. NBW can simultaneously improve 
methane production, digestate dewaterability, and heavy metal stability in sludge AD, with 40 % NBW being the 
optimal dose. This study provides a new sludge treatment strategy for controlling HMs pollution.
1. Introduction
The global production of sewage sludge is projected to reach 
approximately 130 million tons by 2030 (with a moisture content of 80 
%) [1]. As the final product of municipal sewage treatment plants, 
dewatered sludge (DS) is rich in biodegradable organic matter, 
including proteins, polysaccharides, and lignocellulose, which are ad­
vantageous for agricultural applications after treatment [2]. However, 
DS also contains certain heavy metals (HMs), which can significantly 
diminish its usability and pose serious risks to environmental and 
ecological security [3]. Anaerobic digestion (AD) has emerged as the 
predominant technology for treating DS [4]. This process not only 
generates clean energy and reduces sludge volume but also stabilizes 
HMs within the sludge to some extent [2,5]. Nevertheless, conventional 
AD still encounters several challenges, such as low methane production, 
poor dewaterability, and limited stabilization of HMs [6].
To improve sludge AD performance and enhance the stability of 
HMs, exogenous additives have been widely employed [6,7]. Nanoscale 
zero-valent iron used in the sludge mesophilic AD process increased 
cumulative methane production by 45.8 % and simultaneously 
increased the residual states of zinc (Zn) (from 15.1 % to 27.5 %) and 
nickel (Ni) (from 15.1 % to 26.0 %) [7]. Using biochar for sludge AD 
increased the oxidizable (from 23.0 % to 27.0 %) and residual (from 9.5 
% to 17.5 %) states of lead (Pb) [6]. However, these approaches may 
inadvertently contribute to secondary environmental pollution, thereby 
restricting the subsequent agricultural utilization of digestate [8]. In

Anaerobic Digestion of Dairy Dissolved Air Flotation Sludge:
Assessment of Enhancement Strategies
Iin Parlina[1], Asaf Rachmani[2], Saeid Baroutian[1,3],*
Abstract
Dissolved air flotation (DAF), a primary treatment
for high-strength waste (HSW) dairy wastewater,
generates sludge with a high organic content, pos-
ing disposal challenges. Anaerobic digestion (AD)
offers a solution to promote renewable energy use
and enhance the circular economy of the dairy indus-
try by converting this sludge into biogas. However,
DAF sludge has low digestibility, potential inhibitory
risks, nutritional imbalances, and other challenges.
This study identified potential technological solu-
tions to optimize DAF sludge use by enhancing
AD performance, including pretreatment, anaer-
obic co-digestion (ACoD), additives, and process
modifications, which have been successfully imple-
mented for other organic substrates. Using modi-
fied weighted scoring analysis (WSA), microaeration
pretreatment was found to be a superior method,
waste-activated sludge was identified as the most
suitable co-substrate, and bentonite was selected as
the most promising additive. Two-stage anaerobic
digestion (TSAD) emerged as the most promising
comprehensive solution for process modifications,
addressing predominant DAF sludge AD issues and
other subsidiary challenges.
Keywords: Anaerobic digestion, Biogas, Dairy industry, Dissolved air flotation, Weighted scoring analysis

Introduction
The dairy industry is a key global sector, with production reach-
ing 965.7 million tonnes in 2023, marking a 1.5 % increase
from 2022, according to the Food and Agriculture Organiza-
tion (FAO) [1]. The rapid growth of dairy products has led
to significant environmental challenges, particularly in waste
management, where addressing organic pollutants is critical for
reducing their environmental impact. As the industry grows, so
does the volume of wastewater, with 2.5–10 L produced for every
1 L of processed milk [2, 3]. Although these pollutants typically
do not cause severe issues, mismanagement can lead to prob-
lems, making strict control essential, preventing system failures
and environmental harm [4].
Dairy wastewater (DWW) is rich in organic matter, such as
carbohydrates, proteins, and fats, as shown by its high chem-
ical oxygen demand (COD) from 0.79 to 68.6 g L−1 [5]. It
offers recycling potential, but its composition varies with the
processing methods, technologies, and cleaning procedures [5].
This wastewater often contains residual cleaners such as nitric
acid and sodium hydroxide [5, 6]. The use of acidic and alka-
line cleaning agents impacts pH levels and turns nutrient-rich
wastewater into an environmental problem, contributing to
eutrophication, acidification, emissions, soil degradation, and
health risks [7–9].
To effectively treat their high-strength waste (HSW), dairy
industries utilize the dissolved air flotation (DAF) process to
primarily separate solids, organic matter, fat, oil, grease (FOG),
and proteins before discharge or directed to further subsequent
treatment [10–13]. However, this process generates DAF sludge,
also known as DAF waste, DAF float, DAF slurry, DAF solid, or
flotation sludge (FS) [7, 12, 14, 15]. Land spreading is the most
widely applied disposal method for DAF sludge after dewater-
ing [13, 16]. However, due to its high COD, high solid content,
