with strict anaerobic conditions, thereby reshaping the
microbial community in the digester. Facultative anaerobes
involved in the hydrolytic-acidification process exhibit higher
activities under these conditions. Fu et al.5 demonstrated that
introducing microaeration at an air load of 12.5 mL/LR per day
in the AD of corn stover enhanced the biodiversity of
facultative hydrolytic and acidifying bacteria. Furthermore,
according to Yu et al.,12 appropriate microaeration (5 mg O2/
L-reactor/cycle) not only enhanced the hydrolytic-acidification
process in the digestion of black water but also improved the
methanogenesis efficiency. The ORP variation induced by
microaeration also had domestication effects on the archaeal
community. Higher abundance of hydrogenotrophic metha-
nogens with stronger toxic tolerant ability was commonly
observed in the microaerated digesters.
In addition, the syntrophic interaction between bacteria and
methanogenic archaea is another crucial factor determining the
AD efficiency.13 These microorganisms have unique yet
complementary metabolic capabilities, exchanging electrons
via H2 as electron shuttles for energy.

a b s t r a c t
In controlled ecological life support system (CELSS), 100% water recycle efﬁciency is needed. Both water
and nutrients in wastewater needs reclaiming. In an anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) designed
to hydrolyze organic matters and convert organic nitrogen, accumulation of anionic surfactants and
organic compounds was observed in the supernatant. To solve the problem, microaeration which had
rarely been reported to enhance surfactants biodegradation in anaerobic process was introduced and it
was proved to be an effective approach that resulted in concentrations of surfactants and soluble
chemical oxygen demand (SCOD) in the supernatant decreasing from 9000 mg/L and 40000 mg/L to
2000 mg/L and 10000 mg/L, respectively. And the degradations followed the kinetic characteristics of
zero order reaction with R2 values of 0.9472 and 0.949. Three-dimensional excitation emission matrix
(3D-EEM) analysis revealed that some activities of microbes were activated and enhanced by microa-
eration, which resulted in the disintegration of aggregates of large molecules, indicated by the size
exclusion chromatography (SEC). After the introduction of microaeration, the emerging genera Aqua-
microbium, Flaviﬂexus, Pseudomonas and Thiopseudomonas in the microbial community might be
responsible for the effective biodegradation of the surfactants.

1. Introduction
Controlled ecological life support system (CELSS) is an artiﬁcial
closed ecosystem built for long-term space exploration which
provides humans (astronauts) with enough breathable air, clean
water, essential food and safe working-living places (Dai et al.,
2018). In the CELSS, urine and greywater need properly treating
and a 100% water recovery rate is essential to ensure the material
closure of the whole system. And all the waste treatment systems
have to feature high performance, small foot prints, and as little
consumables and by-products (such as gas emission and excess
sludge) as possible. In 1990s, National Aeronautics and Space
Administration (NASA) made an estimation of 20e30 L/(d$person)
wastewater in the CELSS (Wieland, 1994; Wydeven and Golub,

China, 2002), the much lower water consumption in the CELSS
results in higher concentration of surfactants contained in personal

600 mg/L surfactant (Igepon TC-42) in the inﬂuent (Levine et al.,
2000).
Anionic surfactants, as core components of detergent and
cosmetic products formulations, contribute signiﬁcantly to the

not suitable for the CELSS. Though surfactants are degradable or

for validation of optimized hydrolysis conditions for reduction in
ammonia accumulation

a b s t r a c t
Ammonia accumulation above the inhibitory level is the major cause of failure of anaerobic digesters
(AD) treating kitchen waste (KW). In the present investigation a biphasic system (hydrolysis and
methanogenesis) was evaluated for validation of previously optimized hydrolysis conditions [pH 7.2e7.5,
Aeration 0.19e0.22 vvm (volume of air per unit volume of media per minute), Temperature 44 - 48 C]
for reduction in ammonia accumulation in the methanogenic digester. The pre hydrolyzed KW was fed to
methanogenic reactor with the organic loading 1.16 gVS/L - 2.97 gVS/L. Speciﬁc biogas and methane yield
were 0.589 L biogas/gVSfeed and 0.321 L methane/gVSfeed under mesophilic condition, and 0.633 L biogas/
gVSfeed and 0.329 L methane/gVSfeed under thermophilic condition, respectively. The ammonia concen-
tration in the methanogenic phase remained below 250 ppm and 550 ppm under mesophilic and ther-
mophilic conditions, respectively, validate the optimized conditions for hydrolysis of KW for reduction in
ammonia accumulation in methanogenesis phase. The Microbial diversity analysis of methanogenic
phase was carried out to monitor the shifting of microbial population under mesophilic and thermophilic
conditions. Results on these aspects have also been presented and discussed in this paper.

1. Introduction
Municipal solid waste (MSW) includes waste from households,
commercial and institutional establishments, markets and street
sweepings [1]. Safe and cost-effective management of organic
fraction of MSW (OFMSW), such as kitchen waste (KW) is a sig-
niﬁcant environmental challenge for modern society. Inadequately
managed KW disposal has the potential to affect the health and
environment [2]. KW is a readily available organic-rich waste, and
has great potential for anaerobic digestion [3]. Conversion of KW
into biogas using anaerobic digestion is one of the promising ap-
proaches for solving the OFMSW management problem, since, it
also provides clean energy in the form of methane [4].
Despite the advantages of biogas production through anaerobic
digestion of KW, accumulation of by-products viz. ammonia,
hydrogen sulﬁde and long chain fatty acids has been well known for
inhibiting the process of biomethanation. Ammonia accumulation
in the biogas digester treating substrate having low C/N ratio has
been reported as a major cause of digester failure. However, there is
a large variation in the reported inhibitory ammonia concentration
(1.7e14 g/L) which depends on the inoculum, substrate, inoculum
acclimatization and environmental conditions (pH and tempera-
ture) [5,6]. Kayhanian [7] explained the theoretical relationship
between the concentrations of free ammonia and total ammonia,

concentration is six times greater than mesophilic system. The
most widely accepted mechanism explaining ammonia inhibition
is that elevated ammonia level causes change of intracellular pH,
increase in maintenance energy requirement, depletion of intra-
cellular potassium, and inhibition of enzyme reactions involved in
methanogenesis [8]. Accumulation of ammonia in the digester
causes shifting in the biochemical pathways towards syntrophic
acetate oxidation from aceticlastic methanogenesis [9].

in a monophasic system, where all the four steps are carried out in a
single digester, or in a biphasic system, in which the fermentative

Fate of sterols, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, pharmaceuticals,
ammonia and solids in single-stage anaerobic and sequential
anaerobic/aerobic/anoxic sludge digestion
M. Ahmad, C. Eskicioglu ⇑
UBC Bioreactor Technology Group, School of Engineering, University of British Columbia, Okanagan Campus, 1137 Alumni Ave., Kelowna, BC V1V 1V7, Canada
a r t i c l e
i n f o
Article history:
Received 6 September 2018
Revised 14 March 2019
Accepted 12 May 2019
Available online 21 May 2019
Keywords:
Emerging contaminants
Pharmaceuticals
Sterols
Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
Sequential digestion
a b s t r a c t
Emerging contaminants (ECs), such as pharmaceuticals, sterols and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons
(PAHs) are frequently detected in the environment. ECs are refractory, toxic, tend to bioaccumulate
and have a potential to disrupt the endocrine system of living organisms. These compounds are only par-
tially eliminated in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs). Due to their hydrophobic nature, they tend to
accumulate in sludge. However, the fate of the majority of ECs in sludge treatment processes is not fully
understood. In this study, the effect of a sequential anaerobic/aerobic/anoxic (AN/AERO/ANOX) digestion
and a conventional single-stage AN digestion (as control) was investigated on mixed primary and sec-
ondary sludge. Digesters were operated at an overall solid retention time (SRT) of 18 days. The steady-
state results have shown that sequential AN/AERO/ANOX digestion conﬁgurations improved the removal
of three classes of ECs (e.g., sterols, PAHs and pharmaceuticals) by either reducing their accumulation or
enhancing their removal. Moreover, sequential AN/AERO/ANOX digestion also achieved 45% less ammo-
nia generation, 20% faster digestate dewaterability and 4% enhanced volatile solids removal compared to
single-stage AN digestion.

1. Introduction
Over the last few decades, the occurrence of emerging contam-
inants (ECs), such as pharmaceuticals, sterols and polycyclic aro-
matic hydrocarbons (PAHs), have gained considerable attention
due to their regular occurrence in the environment and their
potential to cause harmful effects in the environment and living
organisms. ECs are naturally occurring or synthetic chemicals that
are not usually monitored in the environment. They have a poten-
tial to disrupt the endocrine system, can cause infertility as well as
expedite the maturation in females and bioaccumulation in aquatic
organisms (mainly ﬁsh) (Vanderford et al., 2003; Jakimska et al.,
2014). Moreover, these compounds are part of many products that
are consumed daily (medicines, over the counter therapeutic
drugs, painkillers and industrial agents) at home or used in indus-
trial processes. ECs are refractory compounds. Due to an increase in
the consumption of ECs, their rate of introduction into the environ-
ment surpasses their degradation rate and hence, they are detected
worldwide in the environment.
As one of the major groups in ECs, pharmaceuticals have a cru-
cial role in disease treatment and prevention in both humans and
animals. They encompass a wide and diverse group of chemicals
designed either to be very toxic to infectious organisms or highly
active to interact with receptors in humans and animals. The usage
and consumption of pharmaceuticals have increased signiﬁcantly
because of population increase and aging, the discoveries of new
drugs and the availability of less expensive generics. After inges-
tion, signiﬁcant fractions of the parent compounds either as
active/inactive metabolites or in unmetabolized form are excreted
from the body and are then found in raw wastewater (Ternes et al.,
2001; Celiz et al., 2009). Moreover, pharmaceuticals along with
their metabolites are constantly entering wastewater via disposal
of unused or expired drugs or directly from pharmaceutical dis-
charges (Gros et al., 2006).
Another set of compounds, known as sterols, are also recur-
rently detected in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs). A major
fraction of municipal wastewater consists of organic matter, 20–

of

64% of the lipids in municipal wastewater are from fecal sources
(Mahmood-Khan, 2005). Coprostanol accounts for 40–60% of
the total fecal sterols excreted in human wastes and has been

Bench-Scale Liquid-Phase Microaeration and Iron Dosing
Comparison for In Situ Biogas Desulfurization and Antibiotic
Resistance Management in Mesophilic Anaerobic Digestion
Seyed Mohammad Mirsoleimani Azizi, Basem S. Zakaria, Nervana Haffiez, Parisa Niknejad,
Rasha Maal-Bared, Saif Molla, and Bipro Ranjan Dhar*

ABSTRACT: Microaeration and iron dosing are promising in situ
desulfurization methods for anaerobic digestion (AD). However, limited
reports exist on their systematic comparison. Consequently, this study
investigated liquid-phase microaeration (60−106 mL air/Lreactor/d) and
ferric chloride (250−650 mg FeCl3/L) dosages in mesophilic AD of
sewage sludge operated at a solid residence time of 20 days. Both
methods provided up to 88% H2S removal and moderate siloxane
removal (30−37%) but had no apparent impact on mercaptan removal
from biogas. However, the control and test reactors demonstrated
equivalent AD performance in terms of biomethane yields, chemical
oxygen demand, and total/volatile solids degradation efficiencies,
indicating that air and iron dosages were primarily utilized for biogas
desulfurization. Still, both methods resulted in substantial changes in
microbial community composition. Notably, the indication of syntrophy between facultative microbes and hydrogenotrophic
methanogens was intensified by both methods. For both methods, antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) and mobile genetic element
(MGE) abundances in digestate decreased considerably due to the decrease in the abundance of potential ARG hosts. Compared to
iron dosing, MGE removal was slightly higher in the microaeration reactor. These findings provide valuable insights into the efficacy
of these two approaches in desulfurization and the reduction of antibiotic resistance in AD.
KEYWORDS: anaerobic digestion, sludge, in situ biogas desulfurization, siloxanes, mercaptans, microaeration, iron dosing,
antibiotic resistance genes
■INTRODUCTION
In most centralized water resource recovery facilities (WRRFs)
worldwide, mesophilic or thermophilic anaerobic digestion
(AD) is widely practiced for sludge stabilization.1,2 Biogas from
AD can be used to co-generate heat and electricity or can be
upgraded to renewable natural gas (RNG). However, extensive
purification requirements of biogas to remove hydrogen sulfide
(H2S), mercaptans, and volatile organic compounds (e.g.,
siloxanes) limit its conversion to heat/electricity/RNG,
resulting in ubiquitous biogas flaring instead.3 Particularly,
excessive H2S and mercaptans in the biogas can cause
corrosion of metal pipes, combustion engines, and biogas
utilization equipment.3 Moreover, silicon dioxide particles
produced from the combustion of siloxanes can cause extensive
damage to process equipment by erosion or blockage.4 The
release of sulfur oxides (SOx) in flue gases is increasingly
becoming subject to air quality monitoring and permit
restrictions. Thus, regardless of biogas end use, reducing
sulfides allows WRRFs to maintain high operational and safety
standards and better odor control.
Established biogas desulfurization methods include various
end-of-the-pipe, ex situ approaches, such as scrubbing, biofilter,
biotrickling filters, absorption, and adsorption, where the
biogas is cleaned ex situ in a separate downstream treatment
unit.5 Despite being commercially available and implemented
to full-scale, ex situ methods (e.g., absorption) are usually
considered expensive (US $0.244−2.38/m3 biogas).5 Thus,
researchers have explored the use of in situ approaches, such as
microaeration and iron salt addition, for biogas desulfurization.
Microaeration is operated via controlled injection of a small
amount of air or pure oxygen into the headspace or liquid
phase of digesters.6 At low oxygen levels, sulfide can be
biochemically oxidized to elemental sulfur and/or sulfate. Iron

REVIEW PAPER
Microaeration for hydrogen sulﬁde removal
during anaerobic treatment: a review
Lucie Krayzelova . Jan Bartacek . Israel Dı´az . David Jeison .
Eveline I. P. Volcke . Pavel Jenicek
Published online: 14 November 2015
 Springer Science+Business Media Dordrecht 2015
Abstract
High sulﬁde concentrations in biogas are a
major problem associated with the anaerobic treat-
ment of sulfate-rich substrates. It causes the corrosion
of concrete and steel, compromises the functions of
cogeneration units, produces the emissions of unpleas-
ant odors, and is toxic to humans. Microaeration, i.e.
the dosing of small amounts of air (oxygen) into an
anaerobic digester, is a highly efﬁcient, simple and
economically feasible technique for hydrogen sulﬁde
removal from biogas. Due to microaeration, sulﬁde is
oxidized to elemental sulfur by the action of sulﬁde
oxidizing bacteria. This process takes place directly in
the digester. This paper reviews the most important
aspects and recent developments of microaeration
technology.
It
describes
the
basic
principles
(microbiology, chemistry) of microaeration and the
key technological factors inﬂuencing microaeration.
Other aspects such as process economy, mathematical
modelling and control strategies are discussed as well.
Besides its advantages, the limitations of microaera-
tion such as partial oxidation of soluble substrate,
clogging the walls and pipes with elemental sulfur or
toxicity to methanogens are pointed out as well. An
integrated mathematical model describing microaera-
tion has not been developed so far and remains an
important research gap.

sulfur  Hydrogen sulﬁde removal  Microaeration 

1 Introduction
Under anaerobic conditions, dissimilatory sulfate-
reducing bacteria (SRB) use sulfate as the terminal
electron acceptor for the degradation of organic
compounds while producing hydrogen sulﬁde (H2S).
H2S ends up in both the liquid efﬂuent and biogas
formed through the anaerobic digestion of organic
material. High concentrations of hydrogen sulﬁde in
biogas reduce its quality, since it causes corrosion of
concrete and steel, compromises the functions of
cogeneration units, produces emissions of unpleasant
odors, is toxic to humans and generates emissions of
sulfur dioxide during combustion. In addition, the
presence of sulﬁde in the liquid phase causes corrosion
of water transport systems and the accumulation of
inert material in the sludge (e.g. metal sulﬁdes).
Moreover, sulﬁde is toxic to methanogens (already at
concentrations above 50 mg L-1) and may cause the
inhibition of anaerobic processes (Buisman et al.
1990a; Hao et al. 1996; Hulshoff Pol et al. 1998;
Khanal and Huang 2003b; Stucki et al. 1993; Zhou
et al. 2007). For all of these reasons, the production of
sulﬁde is a major problem associated with the
anaerobic treatment of sulfate-rich wastewater and
organic wastes.
Available methods for sulﬁde removal from biogas
can be classiﬁed into physico-chemical and biological
methods, as summarized in Table 1. Many commer-
cial technologies are available on the market, such as
SulfaTreat (solid scavenger, iron sponge technol-
ogy),
SOXSIA
(sulfur
oxidation
and
siloxane
adsorption), THIOPAQ (physical–chemical absorp-
tion with biological regeneration), DMT Sulfurex
(water scrubber), Sulfur-rite (iron sponge technol-
ogy), and Media-G2 (iron sponge technology).
Operation at high temperature and pressure, as well
as the need for additional equipment and chemicals,
make
physico-chemical
methods
energetically
demanding and expensive (Appels et al. 2008). In
contrast, biological methods based on the biochemical
oxidation of sulﬁde to sulfate, thiosulfate and elemen-
tal sulfur involve lower operational costs with lower or
no need for chemical addition (Buisman et al. 1989;
Syed et al. 2006). Biological removal of H2S from
biogas in closed anaerobic reactor (or digester)
requires an electron acceptor. Therefore, a small
amount of pure oxygen or air must be provided into
the reactors for biological desulfurization.
Among the biological desulfurization methods,
microaeration has recently gained growing attention.

Eﬀect of Propane Addition and Oxygen Enrichment on the Flame
Characteristics of Biogas
Xi Wang, Ligang Zheng,* Jian Wang, Rongkun Pan, Wen Yang, Hongwang Jin, and Yuanpeng Fu
Cite This: Energy Fuels 2021, 35, 5015−5025
Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
Article Recommendations
*
sı

ABSTRACT: Mixing biogas with other fuels or increasing the oxygen
fraction in the oxidizer can improve the combustion performance of
biogas. In this study, we investigated the eﬀects of propane addition and
oxygen enrichment on the ﬂame characteristics of biogas with a constant
heating value in a half-open duct. The evolution of the ﬂame structure
revealed that the tulip structure took on two types of patterns at the
oxygen fraction θ = 0.21. However, there was no salient tulip ﬂame
formation when θ > 0.21. Oxygen enrichment signiﬁcantly increased the
ﬂame propagation velocity (V) and explosion pressure (P). Propane
addition signiﬁcantly reduced Vmax at θ = 0.25 and 0.29. The maximum
rate of pressure rise [(dP/dt)max] exhibited a nonlinear dependence on
the maximum ﬂame velocity (Vmax). A similar trend was observed for
the dependence of (dP/dt)max on the laminar burning velocity (LBV). Therefore, the LBV is an important parameter to predict Vmax
and (dP/dt)max values of mixtures. Furthermore, by using the PREMIX code and the UC San Diego mechanism, we simulated
laminar ﬂame burning properties to reveal the macroscopic ﬂame propagation characteristics. The rate of propane consumption was
higher than the rate of methane consumption. Additionally, oxygen enrichment played an important role in the entire reaction
process, leading to an increase in the molar concentrations of microscopic free radicals and a promotion of the rates of production
(ROP) of free radicals. In contrast, the addition of propane decreased the molar concentrations of microscopic free radicals and
inhibited the ROP of free radicals.
1. INTRODUCTION
Currently, more than 85% of the world’s energy demands is
met by fossil fuels.1 The emission of CO2 and NOx is
increasing continuously, which has led to a signiﬁcant
greenhouse eﬀect and air pollution.2 Growing concerns
regarding the amount of these gases emitted into the
environment and predictions of the exhaustion of petroleum-
derived fuels have motivated the development of clean energy.3
Biogas is produced through bacterial conversion of organic
matter under anaerobic conditions and is a mixture of CH4 and
CO2, with small amount of H2S, N2, CO, and O2.3,4 Compared
with traditional fossil fuels, biogas has the advantages of
abundant availability and lower pollution.3 It is also very
appropriate for power generation, heating systems, and other
applications.4 Interest in the use of biogas as an increasingly
renewable and sustainable energy source has been promoted
recently.5 Dupont and Accorsi6 investigated biogas explosion
characteristics at various temperatures (30−70 °C) and at
atmospheric pressure. Anggono et al.7 determined the
ﬂammability limits of biogas−air mixtures using spherically
expanding ﬂames propagating. Ratna Kishore et al.8 studied the
adiabatic burning velocities for natural-gas-like mixtures over a
range of equivalence ratios at atmospheric pressure. Hinton
and Stone9 measured the laminar burning velocity (LBV) of
biogas over a wide range of temperatures and pressures. Zeng
et al.10 investigated the main factors inﬂuencing the
combustion stability and LBV of biogas in laminar burning
inside a constant-volume combustion chamber using a
schlieren system.
However, biogas has an extremely low energy density, low
propagation velocity, and narrower ﬂammability ranges based
on large amounts of inert gas (i.e., CO2).11 These character-
istics have hindered the popularization of biogas. On the basis
of these shortcomings, two methods have been developed to
improve the combustion performance of biogas: mixing biogas
with other fuels with superior characteristics or increasing the
oxygen fraction in the oxidizer.12 To evaluate both methods,
this study raises the possibility of investigating the eﬀect of
propane addition and oxygen enrichment on the explosion
characteristics of biogas.
A well-established alternative to gasoline is liqueﬁed
petroleum gas, where propane is a major component.13−15

a b s t r a c t
There is a growing trend toward considering municipal solid waste (MSW) with a large organic fraction as
a source of renewable energy using a dry anaerobic digestion (AD) process. Pre-aeration is effective in
improving the dry AD of MSW. However, due to a lack of information regarding the modiﬁcation of
organic components during pre-aeration and the relationship with the subsequent AD, the mechanisms
and optimum strength of this process remain unclear.
In this study, the role of different short-term pre-aeration durations (4, 8, and 14 days) in dry AD of
MSW was evaluated in batch-tests, with a focus on changes in the organic components during pre-
aeration and their impact on the subsequent spectral evolution of dissolved organic matter (DOM) and
bulk performance. Dry AD of MSW operated effectively after the 8-day pre-aeration. The accelerated
degradation of proteins during pre-aeration is critical for the subsequent AD, by reducing the organic
loading and providing a buffer for the ammonia generated. A favorable methanogenesis, facilitated by
pre-aeration, rapidly decreased protein-like ﬂuorescent matter by 2.8 times, by converting it to stable
humic- and fulvic-like groups. MSW with an 8-day pre-aeration produced the highest biogas yield
(192.4 NL/kg dry matter), representing 24.9% of the initial carbon recovered as methane. Excessive
pre-aeration of 14 days decreased the biogas yield by 33%. An insufﬁcient pre-aeration led to an exces-
sive butyric-type acidiﬁcation, with protein-like matter dominating the bulk DOM (81% of total ﬂuores-
cence intensity). Multivariate analysis methods conﬁrmed that spectroscopic indicators could evaluate
the stability of dry AD.

1. Introduction
The generation of municipal solid waste (MSW) in China has
increased due to rapid socioeconomic and population growth. It
has been reported that MSW collected in China amounted to
1.79 million tons in 2014 [1], with an estimated increment of
3–10% per year [2]. MSW generated in developing countries is
characterized by a high content of biodegradable organics and
moisture, with food waste usually accounting for more than 50%
by weight [3,4]. The improper processing and/or disposal of MSW
can have serious adverse effects on the surrounding environment.
However, the special chemical characteristics of MSW have gener-
ated interest in its use as a substrate for methane-rich gas via
anaerobic processes, such as dry/wet anaerobic digestion (AD) or
anaerobic bioreactor landﬁlling [5–8]. This could provide a solution

relative technical simplicity, the minimal capital cost and energy

MSW with a large easily degradable fraction, may be especially
sensitive to the inhibition caused by excessive acidiﬁcation due
to organic overloading of the system. This will result in low oper-
ational stability and hinder the actual application [6,11,12]. To
overcome this problem, a large amount of inoculum or hydroxide
is usually applied in the early AD phase [8,10,13]. However, there
are disadvantages with these approaches because the efﬁciency
of the digester is decreased as some of the volume capacity is lost,
due to the presence of inoculum, and the salt content increases
dramatically in the digester.
Therefore, to improve the digestion performance in a dry AD
system (including MSW bioreactor landﬁlls), a short-term biologi-

A B S T R A C T
During the anaerobic digestion (AD) of cellulosic substrate, an economical and environmental friendly pre-
treatment method should be selected to improve the AD performance. In this study, ﬁve pretreatment methods
include four traditional pretreatment methods (alkali hydrogen peroxide pretreatment, NaOH pretreatment, HCl
pretreatment and hot water pretreatment) and one new developed pretreatment (microaerobic pretreatment)
method were selected to study the eﬀects of pretreatment on the AD of Miscanthus ﬂoridulus. In addition, pre-
liminary economic analysis of diﬀerent pretreatment methods was also conducted. Results showed pretreatment
could signiﬁcantly improve the AD performance of Miscanthus. After alkali hydrogen peroxide pretreatment,
microaerobic pretreatment, NaOH pretreatment, HCl pretreatment and hot water pretreatment the methane
yields of Miscanthus were 41.1%, 25.5%, 18.7%, 15.7% and 10.2% higher than that of untreated sample. Though
all these ﬁve pretreatment methods could improve the methane yield signiﬁcantly, their action sites were dif-
ferent. H2O2 pretreatment and NaOH pretreatment were eﬃcient in removal lignin from Miscanthus ﬂoridulus.
Hemicellulose structure was also partly destroyed during H2O2 pretreatment and NaOH pretreatment. HCl
pretreatment was eﬃcient in destruction of hemicelluloses structure and partly destroyed the cellulose structure.
Microaerobic pretreatment and hot water pretreatment were mainly acted in partly destruction of hemicelluloses
and cellulose components. Preliminary economic analysis showed compared with un-pretreated group only
microaerobic pretreatment was economically feasible. In addition, compared with other pretreatment methods,
microaerobic pretreatment just needs limited amount of oxygen, which is more environmental friendly.
1. Introduction
Due to the energy shortage and environmental pollution, bio-me-
thane production from organic waste through AD method has attracted
increasing attention [1–3]. Miscanthus is a tall perennial grass with high
water and nitrogen use eﬃciency [4–6]. In addition, biomass yields of
Miscanthus is much higher, Miscanthus can also well adapt to diﬀerent
climate and soil conditions [4,6]. These all make Miscanthus to be a
potential substrate for biogas production. Miscanthus is a lignin rich
substrate, and the hemicellulose in Miscanthus was encircled by com-
pact lignin structure. Therefore, the AD of Miscanthus is always in-
eﬃcient [7]. During the AD of Miscanthus, appropriate pretreatment is
essential to destroy the compact structure and improve the AD eﬃ-
ciency [5].

A B S T R A C T   
Tobacco straw is an abundant biomass in China’s agricultural ecosystems, and has high potential for methane 
production. However, the anaerobic digestion (AD) efficiency is limited by the recalcitrant lignocellulose 
structure of the tobacco straw. In this study, three microaerobic pretreatments were performed for the AD of 
tobacco straw to increase methane production. Among them, microbial pretreatment with biogas slurry at an 
oxygen concentration of 4 mL/g VS resulted in the highest methane production of 349.1 mL/g VS, increasing by 
19.8 % than that of untreated. During this pretreatment, the relative abundances of Enterococcus and Clostridium 
sensu stricto 12, which are closely related to acetic acid production and cellulose degradation, were high, and 
these bacteria might have an important contribution to substrate hydrolysis and the methanogenesis efficiency of 
the AD process. This study advances the understanding of microaerobic pretreatment processes and provides 
technological guidance for the efficient utilization of tobacco straw.

Tobacco plays an important role in China’s economy, due to the first 
planting area and output worldwide. Based on the Statista data, the 
estimated tobacco production in 2022 is approximately 2.19 million 
metric tons. Zhang et al. (2023) had reported that tobacco straw ac­
counts for more than 48 % of tobacco production. As a result, over 1.05 
million metric tons of tobacco straw are generated a year and are either

may migrate into the soil to decrease the yield and quality of tobacco for 
the next season. Therefore, a disposal measure that is effective and eco- 
friendly must be developed. 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) refers to the process in which anaerobic 
and facultative microorganisms transform biodegradable organics into 
methane and carbon dioxide through a series of biochemical reactions 
under oxygen-free conditions. Due to its low cost and environmental 
advantages, AD has frequently served as a method to recycle agricultural 
wastes. Like conventional agricultural residues, tobacco straw is pro­
duced in large quantities and is abundant in lignocellulose components. 
Therefore, tobacco straw may function as an effective supplement to 
existing feedstocks, but the recalcitrance of lignocellulosic structure 
presents a bottleneck for the utilization of the available organic matter 
in tobacco straw. 
Pretreatment strategies, such as physical and chemical pre­
treatments, are indicated measures to reduce the naturally recalcitrant 
structure of lignocellulosic biomass and increase hydrolysis rate. While a 
good consequence is received, the investment of physical and chemical 
pretreatments on the equipment and chemical reagent is relatively high, 
which may bring significant difficulties for commercial practice (Chen 
et al., 2022). Recently, microaerobic pretreatment achieved by intro­
ducing a small amount of oxygen or air into a pretreatment reactor 
before AD has gradually attracted increasing attention due to its ease of 
operation, low cost, and potential effectiveness (Huili˜nir et al., 2023). To 
the best of our knowledge, good AD performance after microaerobic 
pretreatment has been established for corn straw (Zhen et al., 2021), 
giant grass (Wang et al., 2021), rice straw (Amin et al., 2021b), and so 
on, but negative outcomes also exist (Díaz et al., 2011; Lim and Wang, 
2013; Okuda et al., 2007). The effect of microaerobic pretreatment 
varies with feedstock, and little research has been conducted to provide 
insights with respect to the pretreatment of tobacco straw. Considering

A R T I C L E I N F O

A B S T R A C T
In this study biogas production eﬃciency was evaluated by adding ultra-ﬁne bubble water (UFBW) into waste
activated sludge (WAS) through anaerobic digestion (AD). Four kinds of gases, i.e. Air, N2, CO2 and H2 were
introduced into tap water (TW) to prepare the UFBW with their properties being ﬁrst investigated. Results show
that hundreds of millions of nanoscale bubbles with the negative zeta potential could be stable in the UFBW for
longer than two weeks whereas almost no nanometer bubbles could be detected in the raw TW. As for their
impact on subsequent AD of WAS, the cumulative methane production with the addition of UFBW was 14–21%
higher than that from the raw TW addition group. Interestingly, the Air-UFBW also could promote the biogas
production in this study, which is diﬀerent from the common understanding of AD, an obligate anaerobic
process.
1. Introduction
Waste activated sludge (WAS) produced from the wastewater
treatment plant is rich in organic matters and nutrients that can be
recycled and reused, whereas it brings about a lot of serious environ-
mental problems due to its huge production amount, toxic and harmful
substances contained and diﬃcult to dispose of (Zhen et al., 2014).
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is recognized as the most eﬃcient technique
for destroying and stabilizing municipal wastes like WAS, which is
basically a microbiological degradation process to convert organic
matters under oxygen free conditions into biogas (with methane as the
major component), a form of fuel that could reduce handling costs

(Khan et al., 2016).
In addition to the optimization of operating parameters and en-
hancement of AD performance via co-digestion, additives addition to
the AD system is also an eﬀective way to increase the biogas production
(Brown and Li, 2013; Khan et al., 2016). For example, the addition of
zero valent iron (ZVI) to AD system has been reported by several re-
searchers. Feng et al. (2014) achieved increased biogas productivity by
43.5% at ZVI of 20 g/L; Jia et al. (2017) pointed out that ZVI could
enhance the degradation of chemical oxygen demand (COD) and pro-
mote volatile fatty acids (VFAs) generation; and the results from Puyol
et al. (2018) indicated that ZVI addition could increase methane pro-
duction and accelerate the formation of siderite and vivianite. Besides,
the addition of ZnO nanomaterials (Zhang et al., 2017), metallic wastes
(Montalvo et al., 2018), ferroferric oxide (Yin et al., 2018), CaO2 (Ping
et al., 2018) and bentonite (Ma et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2018a) has
also been reported to promote AD process because of the enhanced
microbial hydrolysis, acidiﬁcation and metabolism under the ambient
conditions. In recent years, some researchers have tested the eﬀect of
the addition of emerging carbon-based functional materials on AD,
including graphene, biochar, activated carbon and carbon cloth due to
the key roles of carbons in improving cell growth, enrichment and ac-
tivity, and accelerating their co-metabolisms (Zhang et al., 2018b). In
the research work of Dang et al. (2016), carbon cloth was used as an
electron transfer mediator to promote the direct interspecies electron
transfer, therefore achieving faster recovery of soured reactors and
stimulated methane production than the control. The addition of bio-
char, on the other hand, might provide temporary substrates to support
microbial metabolism and growth that could shorten the lag phase by
21.4% and increase methane production potential by 9.6% (Sunyoto
et al., 2016). In addition, ozone was found to initially and temporarily
reduce biomass viability and activity, while after the lag phase, me-
thane yield from the ozone-treated sludge could be enhanced by 52%
(Chacana et al., 2017). Up to the present, however, most of the above-
mentioned methods haven’t been applied in practice, probably due to
the large amount of chemicals consumption and thus low environ-
mental-friendliness.

optimized micro-aeration pretreatment
Xiang Li a, Yi-Juan Yan a, Hong-Ming Wu a, Samir Ibrahim Gadow b, Hongyu Jiang c, Zhe Kong d,  
Yong Hu a,*

A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Micro-aeration pretreatment
Anaerobic digestion
Lipid-rich environment
Methanogenesis pathway
Microbial composition
A B S T R A C T
Micro-aeration pretreatment has emerged as a promising technology for improving the performance of anaerobic 
bioreactors in the treatment of lipid-rich organic waste, particularly in mitigating the accumulation of long-chain 
fatty acids (LCFAs). Micro-aeration intensity is a critical factor in optimizing substrate hydrolysis and meth­
anogenesis efficiency. In this study, optimal micro-aeration intensities for acetoclastic (30 mL-air/g-COD) and 
overall methanogenesis (7.5 mL-air/g-COD) were initially determined using acetate and glucose as substrates, 
respectively. Subsequently, the addition of 0.5 mM oleate (a typical LCFA) increased cumulative methane pro­
duction by 22.1 % when acetate was used as the substrate after 30 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration pretreatment. 
Conversely, it decreased cumulative methane production by 17.3 % when glucose was used as the substrate after 
7.5 mL-air/g-COD micro-aeration pretreatment. Additionally, the population of facultative hydrolysis microor­
ganisms, such as the genus Pseudomonas, increased by 25.7 % and 27.8 % when acetate and glucose were used as 
substrates, respectively. Furthermore, the predominant methane-producing archaea, including the genus Meth­
anosarcina, increased by 27.3 % when acetate was used as the substrate, while the genus Methanosaeta decreased 
by 65.3 % when glucose was used as the substrate. Collectively, these findings provide insights into the meth­
anogenesis pathway under optimal micro-aeration pretreatment conditions, guiding future research in this field.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a promising technology for treating 
lipid-rich organic waste (Hu et al. 2022). Theoretically, 94.8 % of lipids 
can be converted into methane during the AD process, according to the 
McCarty equation (Jeganathan et al. 2006). This makes lipids a more 
potent methane-producing substrate (1010 mL CH4/g VSS) compared to 
cellulose (379 mL CH4/g VSS), protein (496 mL CH4/g VSS) and glucose 
(351 mL CH4/g VSS) (Raposo et al. 2012). During lipid hydrolysis, long- 
chain fatty acids (LCFAs) are produced. Nevertheless, LCFAs are 
recognized as common inhibitors and pollutants in AD process 
(Elsamadony et al. 2021). Previous studies have shown that LCFAs often 
accumulate in AD reactors due to the thermodynamically unfavorable 
and energy-requiring β-oxidation pathway, which required a prolonged 
duration (Saha et al. 2019). Additionally, LCFAs can adhere to microbial 
cell membranes, disrupting microbial homeostasis and hindering the 
vital movement of methane-producing archaea (MPA) (Amha et al. 
2017, Kurade et al. 2019). To mitigate LCFA accumulation, researchers 
have explored strategies such as the supplementation of cations and 
natural adsorbents (Dereli et al. 2014, Nordell et al. 2013). However, the 
precise dosing of metal cations and the potential decomposition of 
insoluble compounds formed under thermophilic conditions can 
compromise the long-term stability of AD bioreactors (Soltan et al. 
2019). Moreover, the dosage of natural adsorbents will augment 
accompanied by LCFAs enrichment, and the adsorbents completed by 
adsorption required subsequent treatment (Reeve and Fallowfield 
2018). Therefore, it is worthwhile to investigate alternative approaches, 
such as enriching the abundance of functional microorganisms, to alle­
viate LCFA accumulation and enhance the overall efficiency of lipid-rich 
waste AD.

ABSTRACT: Microaeration has been reported to improve anaerobic digestion, which is generally attributed to increased microbial
diversity, but a thorough explanation is lacking. In this study, it was found that intermittent microaeration (IMA) supplied to an
anaerobic digester could oxidize Fe(II) produced by dissimilatory iron reduction (DIR) to form a Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle and generate
extracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) to improve anaerobic treatment of phenol-containing wastewater. The results showed
that compared to the control group without IMA, the removal rates of COD and phenol increased by 29.54 and 49.68 percentage
points, respectively, and daily average methane production increased by 85.44%. The Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle slowed down the loss of
iron (13.97%) released from sludge due to the lower solubility of Fe(III) and facilitated •OH generation (1.22 ± 0.04 μM) via
Fenton-like reactions. The DIR and the generation of •OH accelerated phenol degradation. Metagenomic analysis revealed that the
abundance of methanogens and antioxidant enzymes-encoding genes in response to oxidative stress significantly increased in the
IMA group compared to the control, enabling methanogenesis to proceed smoothly under microaeration. This study investigated the
extracellular ROS generation induced by microaeration during anaerobic digestion and their roles in promoting anaerobic
performance, thereby providing a new perspective for optimizing anaerobic systems with microaeration.
KEYWORDS: dissimilatory iron reduction, Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycle, reactive oxygen species, antioxidant defense,
direct interspecies electron transfer
1. INTRODUCTION
Anaerobic digestion is considered one of the most widely used
technologies to treat high-concentration organic wastewater
due to its effectiveness in recovering biomass energy
(methane) from organic matter.1,2 However, anaerobic
digestion is challenged by low operational stability and slow
hydrolytic acidification of complex substrates. Additionally,
numerous toxic organic pollutants, such as phenol in industrial
organic wastewater, impede anaerobic digestion and methane
production.3,4 Phenol is widely present in industrial wastewater
from coal chemical processing, pharmaceutical manufacturing,
and other industries, and has been listed as one of the priority
control pollutants by the United States Environmental
Protection Agency due to its high toxicity.5 It has been
reported that phenol over 2000 mg/L inhibits biological
processes including anaerobic digestion due to the toxic
accumulation of phenol.6,7 Consequently, accelerating the
decomposition of phenol is essential for improving the
anaerobic treatment of phenol-containing wastewater.
The addition of iron (hydro)oxides has been extensively
reported to promote the degradation of complex organic
matter through microbially dissimilatory iron reduction
(DIR).8,9 It also can facilitate the syntrophic metabolism
between dissimilatory iron-reducing bacteria and methanogens
capable of direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) to
increase methane production.3,10 DIR, also known as iron

Corn straw (CS) was pretreated by ultrasonic combined aerobic with biogas slurry as medium for anaerobic 
digestion (AD), that strengthened the degradation efficiency CS, varied in the composition of digestion slurry, 
thereby the methane production was increased. Central combinatorial design (CCD) test was used to treat CS at 
ultrasonic power (200, 400, and 600 W), time (10, 20, and 30 min) and AD for 25 days, at 37 ± 1℃. According to 
data showed that the pH and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) affected methane production directly. With an ultrasonic 
power 309 W, time 26 min, it reached the maximum content of VFAs with 16.24 g/L, the cumulative methane 
production achieved the highest with 198.56 mL/g VS, which was 46.73% higher than unpretreated raw material 
as CK. Ultrasonic-aerobic hydrolysis pretreatment can obtain higher VFAs and methane production content in a 
short period of time that is great significance to biogas engineering.   
1. Introduction 
Since 2014, China has made great efforts to solve the adverse impact

liquid hot water pretreatment (Zhong et al., 2018; Syaftika and Matsu­
mura, 2018; Zou et al., 2016; Li et al., 2017).

with production wastewater from furfural plant could increased the

ABSTRACT  
To investigate the effects of aeration pretreatment on the anaerobic digestion (AD) of swine 
manure, five pretreatment groups were established with dissolved oxygen (DO) in each group 
set to 0.0, 0.4, 0.8, 1.4, and 2.0 mg/L, respectively. The results demonstrated that compared to 
the non-aeration group, methane production increased to varying degrees with different 
aeration pretreatments (AP), with a maximum increase of 27.98% (DO = 2.0 mg/L). AP reduced 
the hydrogen sulfide (H2S) content of biogas. The H2S concentration in the DO = 2.0 mg/L was 
only 0.209%, and this represented an increased H2S removal rate of 49.27% compared to that of 
the DO = 0.0 mg/L (0.412%). Simultaneously, AP increases the hydrolysis rate. When the DO 
concentration reached 2.0 mg/L, the hydrolysis rate reached its maximum. An increase in the 
hydrolysis rate further enhanced the removal rate of organic matter. The organic matter 
removal rate was highest (36.96%) at DO = 2.0 mg/L. AP effectively prolonged the methane 
generation time and shortened the lag time of methane generation. AP creates a brief micro 
aerobic environment, accelerates substrate hydrolysis, and promotes the production and 
consumption of total volatile fatty acids, particularly acetic acid. Additionally, AP promoted the 
symbiotic relationship between Caldicoprobacter (20.93%–34.96%) and Metanosaeta (14.73%– 
18.45%).

1. Introduction
With increasing demand for meat, eggs, and dairy pro­
ducts, the livestock industry has developed rapidly in 
recent years. Pork is a major source of human food, 
accounting for over 40% of the total meat consumed 
worldwide [1]. The rapid development of pig farming 
has produced large amount of manure, and swine 
manure (SM) contains large amounts of organic 
matter, nitrogen, and phosphorus. If not handled and 
stacked properly, it can cause environmental pollution, 
affect human health, and can easily cause eutrophica­
tion of water bodies when discharged into water [2,3]. 
Anaerobic digestion (AD) provides a new method for 
treating SM and is an important technology for 
organic waste treatment and biomass energy utilisation. 
AD protects the environment and reduces pollutants 
while reducing the use of fossil energy using the pro­
duced biogas as a fuel, and the digestate can be used 
as an organic fertiliser for agricultural production, thus 
facilitating the recycling of resources and energy [4].

A B S T R A C T   
In this study, different micro-aeration (MA) strategies for anaerobic digestion (AD) of poultry litter (PL) and 
wheat straw (WS) were examined. MA at different stages (pretreatment, middle, pretreatment plus middle, and 
daily) in batch AD of WS showed that daily MA had the highest increase (16.5 %) of the cumulative methane 
yield (CMY) compared to the control. Batch co-digestion (Co-AD) of WS and PL with daily MA obtained a fur­
therly improved (15.1 %) CMY of 225.44 N mL CH4/g vS added. The modified Gompertz model and Cone model 
were good in fitting the methane yield kinetics of MA engaged AD process (R2 greater than 0.99). Daily MA 
shortened the lag phase of Co-AD by 3.4 %. The sequencing batch reactor for the Co-AD of WS and PL showed an 
increased (21.5 %) daily methane yield when 0.5-h/d MA was employed. The results provided support for the 
application of micro-aeration in the AD of agricultural wastes.

remediating agricultural wastes for producing methane containing 
biogas as a renewable energy resource, as reviewed by previous workers 
(Chen et al., 2008; Karki et al., 2021), the common AD process has

However, it has been reported recently that all these problems could be 
overcome through applying micro-aeration to the AD process as previ­
ously reviewed by Nguyen and Khanal (2018). Micro-aeration was 
defined as an advanced technology by dosing small quantities of air or 
oxygen into the AD reactor to enhance the process efficiency (Botheju 
et al., 2010). The air or oxygen might be dosed either one time by in­
jection, intermittently (pulse-mode), or continuously, and the air or 
oxygen dosing might be conducted at different stages of the AD process 
(pretreatment, during digestion, or post digestion) (Girotto et al., 2018). 
Many researchers reported that with a small amount of energy input, 
micro-aeration showed great promise for improving AD process per­
formance in organic degradation and methane production (Lim & Wang, 
2013; D. Nguyen et al., 2019a; Xu et al., 2021). Zhen et al. (2021) 
applied micro-aeration pretreatment to the thermophilic (55 degrees 
Celsius (◦C)) anaerobic digestion of corn stalk in a batch reactor (0.5 L) 
and found that micro-aeration promoted the generation of volatile fatty 
acids (VFA), and the digesters with a micro-aeration rate of 1 mL O2/g 
volatile solids (VS) increased cumulative methane production by 13.2 
%. While Fu et al. (2015) conducted oxygen injection to a batch AD (37 
℃) of corn straw after experiencing an obvious decrease in methane 
yield and observed an increase in the yield by 28.5 % and an improve­
ment in the volatile solids (VS) removal efficiency by 29.4 %. Moreover, 
Fu et al. (2016) conducted another study on batch thermophilic AD of 
corn straw with daily micro-aeration and reported that the group with 
air injection rate of 12.5 mL/LR per day improved the methane yield 
(16.5 %) and the vS removal efficiency. However, no direct comparisons 
between these micro-aeration strategies in terms of improving methane 
yield have been made. In addition, the substrate used for micro-aeration 
assisted AD process was mostly single substrate including primary 
sludge, wastewater, food waste or straw. There was a lack of research on 
the application of micro-aeration for anaerobic co-digestion (Co-AD) of 
agricultural waste, neither in batch nor in continuous flow operation 
mode. Thus, the effect of micro-aeration on methane yield efficiency and 
reaction kinetics of batch AD of agricultural wastes needs to be inves­
tigated. Also, the application of micro-aeration in continuous-flow AD of

A B S T R A C T
The performance of the microaeration hydrolytic acidification (MAHA) process and microbial community were
investigated under different organic loading rates (OLRs) for the pretreatment of 2-butenal manufacture was-
tewater (2-BMW). Results indicated that OLRs had different impact on the performance of MAHA process. More
than 23.7 ± 2.3% of the chemical oxygen demand (COD) removal and the highest acidification degree
(20.9 ± 3.1%) were obtained when OLRs were less than 4.0 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d. However, further increasing
OLRs to 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d subsequently led to the significant reductions of COD removal and acidification
degree. In addition, it could be preliminarily inferred that 2H-pyran-2-one tetrahydro-4-(2-methyl-1-propen-3-
yl), 5-formyl-6-methyl-4,5-dihydropyran and ethyl sorbate were the main refractory and toxic organics for
microorganisms in the wastewater. The soluble microbial product (SMP) and extracellular polymeric substance
(EPS) contents (protein, polysaccharide, nucleic acid) had obvious changes under different OLRs. With parallel
factor (PARAFAC) model, four fluorescent components were identified. The Fmax of protein-like substances in
SMP significantly decreased with increasing OLRs to 6.1 ± 0.1 kgCOD/m3 d, which might attribute to fluor-
escence quenching. Illumina MiSeq sequencing revealed that Pseudomonas, Longilinea, T78, Clostridium, WCHB1-
05, Acinetobacter, SHD-231 and Oscillospira were dominant genera at different OLRs.

1. Introduction
2 -Butenal (also named crotonaldehyde) is an important industrial
chemical for synthesizing sorbic acid. Sorbic acid as food preservative,
which is recognized as safe substance in certain degree, has become one
of the most common preservatives in the food industry throughout the
world [1]. With increasing demand on sorbic acid, the yield of 2-bu-
tenal presents an increasing trend. In China, 2-butenal is mainly pro-
duced by aldehyde condensation technology [2]. With this production
technology, aldehyde, acetic acid and polymerization inhibitor are
needed during the production process, which leads to a toxic, refractory
and highly concentrated 2-butenal manufacture wastewater (2-BMW).
Untreated wastewater released directly into the biological treatment
processes could cause severe damage to microbial activity. At present,
the effective technologies for wastewater pretreatment have been rarely
reported in the literature. Thus, it is necessary to explore an efficient
and economical pretreatment process for 2-BMW.
Hydrolytic acidification (HA) is an economical and effective pre-
treatment way, which plays an important role in breaking refractory/
toxic organic matters and improving the biodegradability [3,4].
Therefore, HA process has been widely used in pretreatment field of
toxic and refractory wastewater [5]. However, hydrolysis is usually a
rate-limiting step for wastewater containing complex pollutants. To
solve this situation, some new methods for enhancing hydrolysis effi-
ciencies were proposed. Recently, literature reported that microaera-
tion was an alternative method to enhance hydrolysis of complex or-
ganic matter [6]. Under anaerobic conditions metabolites (lactic acid
and ethanol) are usually formed to oxidise nicotinamide adenine di-
nucleotide (NADH2). However, microaeration could effectively reduce
the formation of toxic metabolites and increase formation of the desired
products [7]. In addition, microaeration could help in the synthesis of
certain lipids that are required for the cellular growth [8]. Moreover,
the study of Charles et al. revealed that microaeration could enhance
the cellulase and protease exoenzyme activities [9]. Until now, micro-
aeration has been predominantly used for the desulphurization of
biogas [10]. Besides, some researches have examined the effect of mi-
croaeration on the solid waste anaerobic digestion [11,12]. However,
there are few research available with regard to the application of

a b s t r a c t
The effect of various micro-aeration strategies on the anaerobic digestion (AD) of wheat straw was thor-
oughly examined using a mixture of inocula, containing compost and well digested sludge from biogas
plant. The aim was to determine the most efﬁcient oxygen load, pulse repetition and treatment duration,
resulting in the highest methane production. The oxygen load had the largest impact on the biodegrad-
ability of straw, among the examined variables. More speciﬁcally, a micro-aeration intensity of 10 mL O2/
g VS was identiﬁed as the critical threshold above which the AD performance was more susceptible to
instability. The highest enhancement in biogas production was achieved by injecting 5 mL O2/g VS for
a consecutive 3-day treatment period, presenting a 7.2% increase compared to the untreated wheat straw.
Nevertheless, the results from optimisation case study indicated a higher increase of 9% by injecting
7.3 mL O2/g VS, distributed in 2 pulses during a slightly shorter treatment period (i.e. 47 h).

1. Introduction
During the recent years, the annual production of wheat is stea-
dily increasing, reaching 729 Mt in 2014 (Faostat, 2016) with 20%
of the global amount being produced in Europe. Unfortunately, the
entire harvest cannot be utilized for food production, resulting in a
residue to crop ratio of 1.3:1.0 (Milbrandt, 2005). Thus, the signif-
icant amount of biomass which is typically disposed could be
exploited for alternative purposes, such as energy generation in
the form of biogas via the anaerobic digestion (AD) process.
It is well known that pretreatment methods are typically
applied to all lignocellulosic substrates in order achieve efﬁcient
AD performance. These methods target to improve the hydrolysis
step and thus enhance substrate’s degradability (Carrere et al.,
2015). However, the existing pretreatments are usually associated
with speciﬁc drawbacks, such as the need for an increased energy
supply (e.g. for mechanical pretreatment), the possibility of inhibi-
tor formation (e.g. for chemical pretreatment) or difﬁculties in the
application at an industrial scale (e.g. for biological pretreatment)
(Zheng et al., 2014). As a result, even if these methods can initially
increase the biogas production, the ﬁnal economic balance is not
always positive. Alternative techniques are lately developed to
enhance the hydrolysis of complex organic polymers, without the
need for increased energy carriers or without the production of
undesirable by-products (e.g. furfural, 5-hydroxymethylfurfural
and phenols).
Accordingly, providing the digester with small amounts of oxy-
gen or air has been considered an alternative tool to improve the
overall AD (Krayzelova et al., 2015). The synthesis of unique extra-
cellular hydrolytic enzymes has been reported to be higher in the
presence of oxygen (Lim and Wang, 2013); thus, the creation of
micro-aerobic conditions is an interesting solution to promote

into hydrolysis, acidogenesis, and methanogenesis processes

A B S T R A C T
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is an effective approach for the resource and energy recovery of straw biomass. 
However, the process faces challenges such as poor hydrolysis efficiency, slow startup, and lower overall effi­
ciency. Nanobubble technology offers a promising solution to enhance methane production without causing 
secondary pollution. This study investigates the effects of nanobubble water (NBW) prepared using different 
gases (N2-NBW, O2-NBW, H2-NBW, CO2-NBW, and Air-NBW) on the methane production characteristics and 
microbial communities during AD of corn straw. The results showed that methane production increased by 
11.86 %–24.08 % compared to the control group, with the maximum cumulative methane yield reaching 189.36 
± 5.32 mL/g VS. The modified Gompertz equation effectively fitted the cumulative methane production curves, 
with a high correlation coefficient (R2 > 0.99). Total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) removal rates improved 
by 9.70 %–26.28 % and 11.87 %–24.09 %, respectively. Microbial community analysis revealed an increased 
relative abundance of bacteria such as Ruminofilibacter, which facilitates hydrolysis and acidogenesis. Addi­
tionally, the relative abundance of methanogenic archaea such as Methanosarcina and Methanobacterium also 
increased to varying degrees. Consequently, the addition of NBW promotes the processes of hydrolysis, aceto­
genesis, and methanogenesis, providing new opportunities for the efficient utilization of straw biomass.
1. Introduction
With growing global energy demand and increasing severity of 
environmental issues, the development of renewable energy has become 
a research hotspot in today’s society [1]. Straw, as a widely distributed 
agricultural waste, has an annual production of approximately 1 billion 
tons in China [2]. Its resource utilization through AD can not only 
reduce environmental pollution but also convert it into cleaner biogas, 
alleviating the dependence on fossil fuels and reducing carbon emissions 
[3,4]. However, the efficient bioconversion of straw is hindered by its 
pronounced recalcitrance, which stems from the complex physico­
chemical structure of lignocellulosic biomass. At the structural level, 
cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin are tightly interwoven to form a 
rigid plant cell wall, creating a natural barrier to microbial and 
enzymatic attack [5]. The high crystallinity of cellulose and the presence 
of extensive hydrogen bonding networks reduce the accessibility of 
hydrolytic enzymes, while hemicellulose acts as a cross-linking matrix 
that further restricts degradation. Lignin, with its highly hydrophobic 
and aromatic polymeric structure, not only provides physical rigidity 
but also exerts non-productive binding with enzymes, thereby inhibiting 
hydrolysis. In addition, the low porosity and limited surface area of 
straw cell walls hinder the penetration of microbial consortia and 
enzymatic systems into the substrate. Collectively, these physicochem­
ical barriers make hydrolysis the rate-limiting step of straw anaerobic 
digestion, emphasizing the need for effective pretreatment and 
enhancement strategies to overcome recalcitrance and improve overall 
bioconversion efficiency [6]. In addition, maintaining a dynamic bal­
ance between hydrolysis and methanogenesis during anaerobic

 Microaerobic conditions are applied in order to control the H2S content of biogas.
 The S0-rich deposits found in the HS of two microaerobic reactors are removed.

a b s t r a c t
O2-limiting/microaerobic conditions were applied in order to control the H2S content of biogas. The S0-
rich deposits found all over the headspace of two pilot reactors (R1 and R2) as a result of operating under
such conditions for 7 and 15 months (respectively) were sampled and removed. After restarting micro-
oxygenation, H2S-free biogas was rapidly obtained, and the O2 demand of R2 decreased. This highlighted
the need for a cleaning interval of less than 14 months in order to minimise the micro-oxygenation cost.
The H2S removed from R2 after approximately 1 month was recovered from its headspace as S0, thus indi-
cating that the biogas desulphurisation did not take place at the liquid interface. Denaturing gradient gel
electrophoresis indicated that the composition, species richness and size of the sulphide-oxidising bacte-
ria population depended on the location, and, more speciﬁcally, moisture availability, and indicated
increasing species richness over time. Additionally, a possible succession was estimated.

1. Introduction
H2S is a common biogas compound arising from the anaerobic
digestion of proteins and S-containing compounds. It can exceed
concentrations of 0.05% v/v and up to 2.0% v/v, which inevitably
causes corrosion problems in combustion engines, and the release
of SOx in ﬂue gases (Fortuny et al., 2008). Therefore, most manufac-
turers of combined heat and power installations recommend a
biogas sulphide content of less than 0.01% or 0.03% v/v, depending
on the equipment concerned (Peu et al., 2012).
H2S can be controlled either at the source, by controlling the
feedstock, at the end, by desulphurising the biogas in a later stage,
or at process level, directly inside the anaerobic digester (Peu et al.,
2012). The ﬁrst solution is not realistic, and it is in fact the latter
H2S removal from biogas which is the most established method
in practice, as it can be carried out during digestion or in an
additional unit (Cirne et al., 2008). The most common end-of-pipe
techniques for H2S removal are based on physical–chemical
processes. However, their high costs of both operation and by-
product disposal have encouraged research and the application of
biological processes (Park et al., 2011). Speciﬁcally, biological des-
ulphurisation has been reported to be approximately 62% cheaper
than chemical absorption (Burgess et al., 2001). Furthermore, it can
achieve more complete removal due to the extremely high afﬁnity
of sulphide-oxidising bacteria (SOB) for the substrate (Kobayashi
et al., 2012).

A little breath of fresh air into an anaerobic system: How microaeration
facilitates anaerobic digestion process
Duc Nguyen, Samir Kumar Khanal⁎
Department of Molecular Biosciences and Bioengineering, University of Hawai'i at Mānoa, 1955 East-West Road, Honolulu, HI 96822, USA
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Microaeration
Oxygen
Process control
Bioenergetics
Microbial communities
Metabolic pathway
Syntrophic activity
A B S T R A C T
Exposure of a small amount of oxygen/air (microaeration) has been reported to beneﬁt the anaerobic digestion
(AD) process in enhancing hydrolysis, improving methane yield, stabilizing the process and scavenging hydrogen
sulﬁde among others. The underlying mechanism of enhancing AD process via microaeration is the augmen-
tation of activity and diversity of the microbial consortia that promotes syntrophic interactions among diﬀerent
microbial groups, thereby creating a more stable process. To design and implement a microaeration-based AD
process, fundamental insights about the mechanism of the AD system at process, microbial and molecular levels
must be fully explored. This review critically examines microaeration-based AD processes through our recent
understandings of the eﬀect of oxygen on microbial community structure, enzymatic, energetic, physiological,
and biochemical aspects of the microbial-mediated process. Syntrophic interactions between hydrolytic, fer-
mentative, sulfate reducing, syntrophic bacteria and methanogens under microaerobic conditions are examined
to reveal putative mechanism and factors that need to be considered when implementing microaeration in AD
process. Further studies are needed to better understand the microbial pathways and bioenergetics of the mi-
croaerobic AD process by adopting advanced molecular techniques such as metagenomics, transcriptomics, and
proteomics.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD), a mature technology originally employed
for waste stabilization and waste (water) remediation, has gained sig-
niﬁcant attention in recent years for producing bioenergy from diverse
feedstocks. Besides the source of renewable energy resources, AD pro-
cess has also been used for production of diverse biobased products
such as biopolymers, valuable biochemicals via carboxylic acids plat-
form and organic fertilizer among other products using bioreﬁnery
platform (Sawatdeenarunat et al., 2016; Surendra et al., 2015). More-
over, AD process can also curtail greenhouse gases (GHGs) emissions by
replacing part of fossil fuels, minimizing deforestation for ﬁre woods in
developing countries, and diverting food wastes, and organic fraction of
municipal solid waste from landﬁlls. These inherent merits make AD
process highly desirable technology for remediating organic wastes,
with concomitant production of renewable energy and value-added
products.
Despite the aforementioned merits, the AD process has several
drawbacks such as low hydrolysis rate, unstable at high organic loading
rate (OLR), and release of toxic/corrosive hydrogen sulﬁde; however,
all these issues could be overcome through micro-aeration. AD process
could suﬀers from volatile fatty acids (VFAs) built-up due to involve-
ment of highly sensitive microbial communities and delicate balance
among interrelated biochemical processes, especially at high organic
loading rates (Nguyen et al., 2015). The anaerobic degradation of or-
ganic matters follow a series of interdependent biochemical steps (i.e.,
hydrolysis, acidogenesis, syntrophic acetogenesis, and methanogenesis)
carried out by diverse microbial groups, in which metabolic products
excreted by one group of microorganisms are vital substrates for an-
other group of microorganisms (Khanal and Li, 2017). For eﬀective
performance and stable operation of an AD system, all these inter-
dependent stages should be kept kinetically and energetically at equi-
librium by maintaining the syntrophic activities among the micro-
biomes. For example, in case of AD of highly recalcitrant feedstocks
such as lignocellulosic biomass (e.g., agricultural waste/residues, forest
residues and energy crops), enhancing hydrolysis is critical to solubilize
these complex substrates into simple organic substrates for further
downstream conversion (Mathews et al., 2015; Shrestha et al., 2017).
On the other hand, AD of readily degradable substrates such as food
wastes and food processing wastewater at high organic loading rate
(OLR) is challenging due to the rapid production of fermentative pro-
ducts, especially VFAs. The accumulation of VFAs inhibits methanogens

A B S T R A C T
Linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS) is one of the most widely used anionic surfactants and is frequently detected 
in wastewater, while its removal under anaerobic conditions remains limited and unstable. This study evaluated 
the independent and combined effects of the redox mediator anthraquinone-2-sulfonate (AQS) and controlled 
microaeration on LAS biodegradation in upflow anaerobic sludge blanket (UASB) reactors. Two reactors treating 
synthetic wastewater containing 15 mg L−1 LAS were operated for 90 days: R1, a strictly anaerobic UASB, and 
R2, a micro-aerated UASB. Each reactor was assessed without (Period I) and with AQS addition (50 μM, Period 
II). Under strictly anaerobic conditions without AQS, LAS removal was low and highly unstable (32 ± 16%), with 
pronounced performance fluctuations. The addition of AQS alone significantly improved LAS removal to 65 ±
4% without affecting methane production, indicating enhanced LAS transformation via electron shuttling rather 
than changes in methanogenic activity. Microaeration combined with AQS yielded the best overall performance, 
increasing LAS removal to 77 ± 1%, COD removal to 92.3 ± 3.8%, total methane production to 5.6 ± 0.7 L/day, 
and specific methane yield to 0.50 ± 0.11 LCH4⋅gCODapp
−1 . Microaeration without AQS improved process stability 
but did not achieve LAS removal comparable to AQS. Microbial analyses showed that AQS promoted the 
enrichment of hydrogenotrophic methanogens, particularly Methanobacterium, and syntrophic taxa such as 
midas_g_2229, while microaeration increased microbial richness. The combined condition exhibited the highest 
archaeal enrichment and microbial richness. Results demonstrate that AQS and microaeration act through

1. Introduction
Linear alkylbenzene sulfonate (LAS) is the most widely used anionic 
surfactant (Palmer and Hatley, 2018; Wang et al., 2024). It is a primary 
ingredient in many household and industrial products, including 
laundry detergents, cleaning agents, and personal care products (Ran 
et al., 2024; Zhu et al., 2020). Because LAS is widely used and not 
completely removed by conventional wastewater treatment plants 
(WWTPs), it is often found in final effluents and in nearby water bodies. 
Even low concentrations in aquatic environments raise concerns about 
persistence, toxicity, and bioaccumulation. Research shows toxicity at 
levels of at least 15 μg/L (Luo et al., 2023).
LAS is biodegradable under certain conditions, but its degradation in 
WWTPs is often incomplete, especially under anaerobic conditions 
(Ogawa and Kawase, 2021). Commercial LAS mixtures are complex, 
containing homologues of varying alkyl chain lengths and positional 
isomers, which make the compounds resistant to biological treatment, 
particularly in the absence of oxygen (Terreros-Mecalco et al., 2024). At 
moderate to high concentrations, LAS can inhibit microbial activity and 
affect treatment performance (Wu et al., 2020). Concentrations around 
2 mg/L are already sufficient to inhibit nitrifying bacteria (Dereszewska 
et al., 2015), while denitrifying microorganisms are inhibited at 15 
mg/L (Andrade et al., 2020).
In anaerobic systems, which are increasingly used for wastewater 
treatment due to their energy-efficient operation and biogas production, 
LAS removal is typically lower and more variable than in aerobic pro­
cesses (Cui et al., 2022). Their efficiency decreases when treating 
wastewater containing poorly biodegradable compounds, such as LAS, 
which can compromise effluent quality and microbial stability (Costa 
et al., 2024; Teran et al., 2022). Only 20% of the surfactant is bio­
degraded by anaerobic digestion; the low biodegradation is likely due to

A B S T R A C T   
Micro-aeration hydrolysis acidification (HA) is an effective method to enhance the removal of toxic and re­
fractory organic matter, but the difficulty in stable dosing control of trace oxygen limits its wide application. 
Membrane-based bubbleless aeration has been proved as an ideal aeration method because of its higher oxygen 
transfer rate, more uniform mass transfer, and lower cost than HA. However, the available information on its 
application in HA is limited. In this study, membrane-based bubbleless micro-aeration coupled with hydrolysis 
acidification (MBL-MHA) was exploited to investigate the performance of 2,4-dinitrophenol (2,4-DNP) degra­
dation via comparing it with bubble micro-aeration HA (MHA) and anaerobic HA. The results indicated that the 
performances in MBL-MHA and MHA were higher than those in HA during the experiment. 2,4-DNP degradation 
rates under redox microenvironments caused by counter-diffusion in MBL-MHA (84.43~97.28%) were higher 
than those caused by co-diffusion in MHA (82.41~94.71%) under micro-aeration of 0.5–5.0 mL air/min. The 2,4- 
DNP degradation pathways in MBL-MHA were nitroreduction, deamination, aromatic ring cleavage, and 
fermentation, while those in MHA were hydroxylation, aromatic ring cleavage, and fermentation. Reduction/ 
oxidation-related, interspecific electron transfer-related species, and fermentative species in MBL-MHA were 
more abundant than that in MHA. Ultimately, more reducing/oxidizing forces formed by more redox proteins/ 
enzymes from these rich species could enhance 2,4-DNP degradation in MBL-MHA.   
1. Introduction 
Nitrophenols have been extensively used as essential raw materials 
for dyes, plasticizers, pesticides, herbicides, paints, pharmaceuticals, 
explosives, and leather preservatives in the global chemical industry 
(Wu et al., 2015; Fajardo et al., 2015; Arora et al., 2014). Among the 
nitrophenols, 2,4-dinitrophenol (2,4-DNP), a representative nitro­
phenol, has been ranked as a priority-controlled pollutant by the United 
States Environmental Protection Agency (2003) and must be appropri­
ately treated because of its high toxicity, oncogenicity, and biological 
accumulation (Sasidharan Pillai et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2021). 
Several methods to treat 2,4-DNP-containing wastewater via physi­
cochemical treatment processes, for example, adsorption methods 
(Azari et al., 2021), advanced reduction (Yang et al., 2011), advanced 
oxidization (Hedayat et al., 2018), and various other methods (Xiong 
et al., 2019), have been investigated in the literature. Although they 
have achieved remarkable effects, these methods have disadvantages, 
such as the necessity to recycle chemicals, the complex processes 
involved, the high cost, and the resultant secondary pollution (Naidu 
et al., 2016). Therefore, in recent decades, biological treatment methods 
have been widely used because of their high degradation efficiency and 
uncomplicated treatment or extraction processes. 
Hydrolytic acidification (HA) is an effective, economical bio­
treatment method that plays a crucial role in changing refractory com­
plex macromolecules, such as aromatic hydrocarbons or heterocyclic 
substances, into small molecules, such as small-molecule organic acids 
and alcohols, and improving biodegradability via biological hydrolysis 
and acid production (G Song et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2021). Therefore,

Rapid hydrogen generation from cotton wastes by mean of dark 
fermentation
Gaweł Sołowski1 · Izabela Konkol1 · Marwa Shalaby2 · Adam Cenian1

Abstract
Dark fermentation of textile wastes is discussed in the paper. In the experiment cotton wastes were fermented. Before 
fermentation the cotton was hydrolyzed using 0.1 M HCl acidic solution. The inoculum was pretreated by means of heat 
shock for 0.5 h at 105 °C. The fermentation was carried out under mesophilic conditions at a load of 5 g VSS/L, and pH 5. 
Oxygen was added in small quantities during fermentation. The oxygen flow rates (OFR) were between 0.3 and 1.0 mL/h. 
The fermentation was carried out for a few days at temperatures between 40 and 43 °C. Hydrogenesis prevailed at the 
lower temperature (40 °C) and methanogenesis at the higher (43 °C). Conversion of cotton waste to methane (3.4%) was 
slightly higher than conversion to hydrogen (2.6%). The highest hydrogen production was obtained for OFR 0.8 mL/h and 
the percentage of hydrogen in biogas was 43%. At higher temperatures (43 °C) no hydrogen production was observed
Keywords  Dark fermentation · Hydrogen · Methane · Cotton
1  Introduction
Cotton waste constitute a high proportion of textile 
wastes, which account for 50% of world biomass waste [1]. 
Its utilization, complying with demands of circular econ-
omy, can solve a problem especially in the Middle East, 
including Syria [2] but also in Europe [3]. Poland gener-
ates around 236 661 Mg of cotton waste annually, which 
is clearly a huge amount to process [4]. On the other hand, 
there exists a high demand for energy [5] and industrial 
raw materials [6], that increasingly will not be easily met 
by fossil resources [7]. So, the role of renewable fuels like 
hydrogen produced from biomass will grow continuously 
[8]. Cotton plantations can contribute to global world sus-
tainability [9], oil from its seeds may serve as biofuel or 
lubricant [10, 11], and cotton wastes may be transformed 
into biodiesel [12, 13] or as an additive to other biofuels 
[14, 15] with properties similar to FAME [16]. Cotton wastes 
are used for PET or insulating material production [17] or 
serve as important substrate for pyrolysis [16, 17].
An interesting issue, undertaken in this research, is 
related to the possibility of using cotton waste, including 
cotton stalk [18] as a source of hydrogen. Fast depletion 
of fossil fuels [19] means that there is a growing need to 
seek renewable ways of hydrogen production, an impor-
tant resource for chemistry [20] and carbon free fuel [8]. 
Taherzadeh works [2, 21] proved that cotton wastes are 
a good source of methane generation, but the process 
includes expensive chemical pretreatment using NMMO, 
highly concentrated sulfuric acid or sodium hydroxide [2,
