A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Lignocellulosic substrate 
Microaeration microbial pretreatment 
Hydrolysis 
Microbial community 
Methane 
A B S T R A C T   
The effects of various microaeration strategies and process parameters on anaerobic digestion (AD) of ligno­
cellulosic substrates have received increased attention; however, different results have been reported. To 
determine optimal conditions and clarify the mechanisms influencing this process, the effect of pretreatment of 
microaerobic microbial on corn stover decomposition and AD was investigated with real-time pH control. Fresh 
cow manure was chosen as the inoculum, as it has the strongest cellulose hydrolysis capacity under microaer­
ation conditions. Microaeration microbial pretreatment effectively promoted the hydrolysis and acidogenesis of 
corn stover, and pH considerably affected total solid reduction, volatile fatty acid (VFA), and accumulation of 
soluble chemical oxygen demand (sCOD) patterns by shifting microbial communities. Different pH levels and 
pretreatment times led to positive and negative effects on methane yield. A 12-h pretreatment of substrate at pH 
8 prior to AD increased the methane yield by 16.6% in comparison with the un-pretreated sample.   
1. Introduction 
China has strived to vigorously develop the anaerobic digestion (AD) 
of agricultural wastes to produce bio-natural gas since 2015 for 
environmental protection, renewable energy alternatives, and CO2 
emission reduction. Corn stover, accounting for about 32.5% of agri­
cultural straw produced in China, was regarded as a good candidate. 
Many biogas and bio-natural gas projects using corn stover as the main

structure of lignocellulose is one of the important limiting factors 
(Woiciechowski et al., 2020). 
It is well known that pretreatment is an effective measure for 
improving digestion rate, thereby enhancing methane generation from 
lignocellulosic substrates. Many pretreatment technologies, such as 
alkaline, acid and steam explosion, are investigated for improving the 
lignocellulosic biomass AD (Frigon et al., 2012), with good results 
achieved. However, these pretreatment technologies usually have spe­
cific drawbacks, such as increased energy consumption, inhibitor for­
mation, or scaling-up difficulties. As a result, few of them have been 
used in commercial production, because of negative economic profit or 
the introduction of pollution. 
Accordingly, enhanced microbial hydrolysis pretreatment under 
microaeration conditions is considered an effective method to improve 
the AD of lignocellulosic substances by promoting certain facultative 
and aerobic microbial activities, while this increases biomass dissolution 
(Botheju & Bakke, 2011). However, the effect of microaeration on the 
AD of lignocellulose substances remains controversial. It is extensively 
reported that microaeration has positive effect (Fu et al., 2016; Lim & 
Wang, 2013), but some studies found that the addition of oxygen dete­
riorated AD, leading to reduced methane yield (Johansen & Bakke, 
2006). The uncertain outcomes may arise from different microaeration 
strategies, techniques, or intensities. 
As reported in previous studies, microaeration improves the methane 
potential of biomass by effectively promoting hydrolysis and acido­
genesis of complex substrates into simple organic matter (Nguyen et al., 
2019). Hydrolysis, which is positive for AD, and consumption of sub­

be speculated that if oxygen is supplied improperly, or if the pretreat­
ment time is too long, then oxygen respiration is too high and the 
availability of substrates for AD is decreased too much, leading to an 
adverse impact on AD. To maximize methane yield, pretreatment should

Coal gasiﬁcation wastewater (CGW) contains several types of aromatic pollutants, which impart high biotoxicity
and reduce the quality of anaerobic treatment. Two types of hydrolysis acidiﬁcation processes, namely
microaerobic hybrid reactor (HA-1) and upﬂow anaerobic sludge blanket reactor (HA-2), were developed for
pre-treatment before the anaerobic treatment. The changes in the dissolved organic matter and biotoxicity
were investigated to comprehensively understand the degradation process. The results showed that HA-2
coupled with an anaerobic reactor achieved a 12.3% and 13.4% higher removal efﬁciency for chemical oxygen de-
mand and total phenols, respectively, compared with the coupled process with HA-1. Furthermore, HA-2 could
transform macromolecules into small molecules more efﬁciently and produce fewer intermediates. The coupled
process with HA-2 preferentially removed complex aromatic substances with absorption wavelengths of 285 and
254 nm, according to the sequential orders interpreted from two-dimensional correlation spectroscopy. In addi-
tion, the results of ﬂuorescence excitation-emission-matrix with regional integration analysis revealed that the
contents of typical cyclic compounds in CGW, such as phenolic, heterocyclic, and polycyclic aromatic compounds
were remarkably reduced by HA-2. In addition, HA-2 reduced the toxic unit value of CGW by 67.5% and increased
the resazurin dehydrogenase activity of the sludge by 37.5% during CGW treatment, thus improving the
biotoxicity removal and biodegradability. However, the coupled process with HA-2 did not signiﬁcantly affect
the “indirect estrogenic activity” of CGW. A Pearson correlation analysis indicated that spectral indicators, such
as UV254 and ΦT,n, presented a high positive correlation with the reduction of acute toxicity and organics.

1. Introduction
Coal gasiﬁcation is a clean and efﬁcient energy-conversion method,
and plays an important role in adjusting the energy structure, particu-
larly regarding the situation in China of “rich coal, less oil, lack of gas”
(Shi et al., 2019a). However, a large amount of wastewater is produced
from the coal gasiﬁcation process, containing high concentrations of re-
fractory and toxic compounds, such as phenols, polycyclic aromatic hy-
drocarbons, nitrogen heterocyclic compounds, long chain n-alkanes,
and thiocyanate, among others (Ma et al., 2018a; Zhao and Liu, 2016).
The existence of hazardous compounds in coal gasiﬁcation wastewater
(CGW) constrains industrial development due to its adverse effect on
environmental safety and public health.
In general, CGW is treated successively through the phenol and am-
monia recovery process, biological treatment process, and advanced
treatment process (Ji et al., 2016). Among these, anaerobic treatment
is an indispensable process in which refractory compounds can be de-
graded or converted to easily biodegradable compounds, thus reducing
the toxicity and improving the biodegradability of CGW (Fuchs et al.,
2011; Meckenstock and Mouttaki, 2011; Shi et al., 2019b). However,
for chemical oxygen demand (COD) and total phenols (TPh), a removal
efﬁciency of only 20–30% has been achieved during the anaerobic treat-
ment of CGW with conventional mesophilic upﬂow anaerobic sludge
blanket (UASB) reactors (Wang et al., 2011). The hydrolysis acidiﬁca-
tion (HA) process has been widely used as a pre-treatment process for
various industrial wastewaters (Song et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2014;
Wu et al., 2016) to improve the wastewater-treatment process. In the-
ory, HA can remove toxic compounds, change the composition of refrac-
tory organics, and reduce the concentration of pollutants in CGW, thus
creating suitable conditions for the subsequent anaerobic process (Xu
et al., 2015). However

A B S T R A C T   
Separated hydrolysis and acidification is an effective pretreatment method for anaerobic digestion of lignocel­
lulose. However, excess consumption of soluble substrates remains a problem. Rice straw and pig manure were 
used as substrates with biogas slurry as the inoculum, combined with aerobic and microaerobic conditions in the 
14-day hydrolysis and acidification. Aeration can significantly accelerate volatile solid degradation (38.25%), 
especially the lignocellulose. Soluble chemical oxygen demand (29157 mg/L) and volatile fatty acids (13219 mg/ 
L) of the group with 4 days aerobic treatment, reached their peaks on day 5, obtaining a balanced insoluble 
substrate degradation and soluble substrate consumption. Candida, Lactobacillus, Bifidobacterium, and Acetobacter 
were enriched at the balanced point for positive contribution to the degradation of the insoluble substrate and 
the generation of soluble substrate. This study not only reveals the balance between degradation and con­
sumption, but also provides new insight into biogas slurry recycling and anaerobic digestion precursor substrate 
production.

1. Introduction 
Every year, China generates approximately 48 million tons of rice 
straw (RS) and 240 million tons of pig manure (PM) (Shaheen et al., 
2022; Xiao et al., 2022), and its resource efficiency remains insufficient. 
There are various resource recovery technologies available to reduce the 
amount of solid waste to avoid a large amount of CO2 emissions caused 
by direct combustion, such as anaerobic digestion (AD), pyrolysis, 
composting, and others. AD is a better treatment option for these 
biomass resources because of its multiple properties, such as energy, 
fertilizer, and positive contribution to “carbon neutral” (Gross et al., 
2021; Rodin et al., 2020). Anaerobic co-digestion (co-AD) of RS and PM 
to produce biogas is currently a popular treatment method because it 
can compensate for the imbalance in the carbon to nitrogen ratio 
compared to a single substrate, as well as reduce ammonia inhibition in 
PM and increase microbial abundance (Xu et al., 2018). However, co-AD 
has yet to overcome the time constraint (Qu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 
2020; Zhang et al., 2019), and it takes longer compared to other tech­
niques of waste reduction. 
The hydrolysis stage is the time-limiting stage in AD of lignocellulose 
substrates, and pretreatments are required before AD. Biological pre­
treatment is less expensive and more environmentally friendly than 
physical or chemical methods, but it has a longer cycle time and a more 
complex operation. The composite microbial community, which in­
cludes paddy soil microorganisms (Wang et al., 2021a), biogas slurry 
(Wang et al., 2020), and self-screened mixed strains (Yu et al., 2016), 
has demonstrated significant advantages in the hydrolysis and acidifi­
cation (HA) process of lignocellulosic raw materials, which is based on 
the synergy of diverse microorganisms. The composite microbial com­
munity secretes extracellular enzymes to promote the hydrolysis of 
complex insoluble substrates (ISS) into soluble substances (SS), resulting 
in the production of volatile fatty acids (VFAs) (Hua et al., 2014), and 
the accumulation that could be used for methane production (especially 
in two-stage or three-stage AD reactor) or platform compound refine­
ment (Fu et al., 2020). However, due to the simultaneous generation and

Synergistic promotion of straw anaerobic digestion by a composite 
microbial consortium and micro-aeration: Enhancing lignocellulose 
decomposition and methanogenesis
Junyi Zheng , Xuepeng Wang , Yaobin Zhang *
a Dalian University of Technology, School of Environmental Science and Technology, No. 2 Linggong Road, Ganjingzi District. Dalian, Liaoning, 116024, China
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Reactive oxygen species
Intermittent micro-aeration
Composite microbial consortium
Anaerobic digestion
A B S T R A C T
The stable structure of lignocellulose is the main obstacle to the anaerobic digestion of agricultural straw. In this 
study, a composite microbial consortium composed of Phanerochaete chrysosporium and Aspergillus niger, coupled 
with intermittent micro-aeration, was employed to enhance lignocellulose decomposition and methanogenesis. 
Under an optimal micro-aeration intensity of 4 % (Vair:Vreactor/day), methane production was 22.57 % higher 
than that under strict anaerobic conditions. A higher aeration intensity (6 %) further improved organic matter 
removal, but decreased methane production. Micro-aeration induced periodic fluctuations in oxidation-reduction 
potential during anaerobic digestion to form reactive oxygen species, which significantly enhanced the activities 
of lignin peroxidase (2.92-fold), manganese peroxidase (1.99-fold), and laccase (2.83-fold), thereby accelerating 
lignin decomposition and humus formation. The resulting humic substances acted as natural electron shuttles, 
facilitating microbial electron transfer and elevating intracellular NADH/NAD+ ratios, which ultimately stimu­
lated methanogenesis. Microbial community analysis confirmed that the inoculated fungi survived and remained 
metabolically active under micro-aerobic conditions, effectively degrading lignocellulose to provide accessible 
substrates for methanogens. This study demonstrated that integrating a composite fungal consortium with 
controlled micro-aeration could be a robust and efficient strategy for valorizing straw waste.
1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion is an efficient approach for agricultural waste 
management by converting organic solids into methane or valuable 
chemicals such as fatty acids. However, agricultural residues like crop 
straw mainly consist of lignocellulose—a complex and chemically stable 
mixture of lignin, cellulose, and hemicellulose—which resists microbial 
breakdown and thus limits the digestion efficiency [1,2]. Phanerochaete 
chrysosporium, an aerobic lignin-decomposing fungus, secretes extra­
cellular enzymes such as lignin peroxidase (LiP), manganese peroxidase 
(MnP), and laccase (Lac) to decompose lignin [3]. Specifically, oxidases 
and dismutases in P. chrysosporium catalyze oxygen reductions: first, O2 
accepts two electrons to form superoxide anions (•O2
−; O2 + 2e−→ •O2
−), 
which then disproportionate in the presence of protons to generate 
hydrogen peroxide (2•O2
−+ 2H+ → H2O2 + O2). This initiates Fenton- 
like reactions (Fe2+ + H2O2 → Fe3+ + •OH + OH−) [4], where hy­
droxyl radicals (•OH) cleave aromatic structures and β-O-4 ether bonds 
in lignin, disrupting its protective matrix and improving the accessibility 
of cellulose for enzymatic hydrolysis [5–7]. Additionally, phenolic 
compounds derived from lignin decomposition undergo enzyme- 
catalyzed polymerization and humification [8,9]. Owing to these 
properties, Phanerochaete chrysosporium has been widely applied in 
aerobic composting and anaerobic pretreatment processes [10,11].
Methanogenesis requires strict anaerobic conditions. However, 
recent research has demonstrated that controlled micro-aeration in 
anaerobic digestion systems can promote the enrichment of hydrolytic 
and acidogenic microorganisms (including actinomycetes and fungi) 
without inhibiting methanogens [12–14]. Notably, Gong et al. recently 
reported that Phanerochaete chrysosporium secreted ligninolytic enzymes 
under intermittent micro-aeration, thereby accelerating straw decom­
position and enhancing digestion efficiency [15].
While Phanerochaete chrysosporium primarily targets lignin decom­
position, its effectiveness on cellulose and hemicellulose is limited. 
Aspergillus niger, however, is capable of breaking cellulose into

toxic and refractory organic wastewater 
Zhuowei Zhang a,b,c, Yin Yu a,b, Hongbo Xi a,b,**, Yuexi Zhou a,b,c,*

Handling editor. Zhen Leng  
Keywords: 
Hydrolysis acidification 
Micro-aeration 
Pretreatment 
Toxic and refractory organic wastewater 
Application 
A B S T R A C T   
Micro-aeration (dosing tract air or oxygen) is an effective method to promote hydrolysis acidification (HA). In 
recent years, the pretreatment of toxic and refractory organic wastewater has attracted increasing attention. As 
micro-aeration in the HA process accelerates hydrolysis, improves volatile fatty acid production, increases 
biodegradability, scavenges hydrogen sulfide, promotes enzyme activity, and facilitates the diversity of func­
tional microbes, this review evaluated the underlying mechanisms for each of these processes. Furthermore, by 
summarizing the process parameters and control strategies, the factors involved in the implementation of the 
micro-aeration HA process were revealed. In addition, we summarized previous applications of various toxic and 
refractory organic wastewater pretreatments to provide guidance for potential large-scale implementation. 
Finally, the challenges and future perspectives of using micro-aeration HA to pretreat toxic and refractory 
organic wastewater were highlighted. Further scope of the study includes removal mechanisms of toxic and 
refractory organic matter, the development of automatic processes with intrinsic control and long-term stability, 
development of new antifouling and economical microaerobic membrane materials, CFD simulations for the 
evaluation of micro-aeration transfer of different aeration methods, and mathematical modeling describing 
micro-aeration effects in HA.   
1. Introduction 
In recent years, with rising concerns regarding environmental pro­
tection and sustainable development, treating wastewater contaminated 
with toxic and refractory organic matter is gaining increasing interest. 
Toxic and refractory organic wastewater mainly refers to recalcitrant 
wastewater containing toxic and refractory compounds, such as petro­
chemical wastewater, chemical and mining industry wastewater, and 
pharmaceutical wastewater. Refractory and toxic organics, including 
benzene, aldehydes, phenols, aromatic hydrocarbons, and heterocyclic 
compounds, contained in the effluents of these polluting industries are 
potential carcinogens and endocrine disrupters and are toxic to living 
organisms; therefore, their presence in aquatic environments, even to a 
small extent, can significantly affect public health (Malik et al., 2020). 
Compared with physical and chemical treatment methods, biological 
treatment methods have been widely used in recent decades owing to 
their high degradation efficiency and uncomplicated pretreatment and 
extraction processes. However, when untreated toxic and refractory 
organic wastewater, containing benzene, aldehyde, and phenol com­
pounds, is directly discharged into a biological treatment system, it 
could have an inhibitory effect on the activated sludge, resulting in the 
deterioration of the effluent quality (Wu et al., 2015; Song et al., 2017). 
Therefore, effective technologies for the pretreatment of toxic and re­
fractory organic wastewater are pertinent. 
Hydrolytic acidification (HA) is an economical and effective pre­
treatment method that involves biological hydrolysis and acid produc­
tion.

A B S T R A C T   
Lignocellulosic biomass (LCB) presents a promising feedstock for carbon management due to enormous potential 
for achieving carbon neutrality and delivering substantial environmental and economic benefit. Bioenergy 
derived from LCB accounts for about 10.3 % of the global total energy supply. The generation of bioenergy 
through anaerobic digestion (AD) in combination with carbon capture and storage, particularly for methane 
production, provides a cost-effective solution to mitigate greenhouse gas emissions, while concurrently facili­
tating bioenergy production and the recovery of high-value products during LCB conversion. However, the 
inherent recalcitrant polymer crystal structure of lignocellulose impedes the accessibility of anaerobic bacteria, 
necessitating lignocellulosic residue pretreatment before AD or microbial chain elongation. This paper seeks to 
explore recent advances in pretreatment methods for LCB biogas production, including pulsed electric field 
(PEF), electron beam irradiation (EBI), freezing-thawing pretreatment, microaerobic pretreatment, and 
nanomaterials-based pretreatment, and provide a comprehensive overview of the performance, benefits, and 
drawbacks of the traditional and improved treatment methods. In particular, physical-chemical pretreatment 
emerges as a flexible and effective option for methane production from straw wastes. The burgeoning field of 
nanomaterials has provoked progress in the development of artificial enzyme mimetics and enzyme immobili­
zation techniques, compensating for the intrinsic defect of natural enzyme. However, various complex factors, 
such as economic effectiveness, environmental impact, and operational feasibility, influence the implementation 
of LCB pretreatment processes. Techno-economic analysis (TEA), life cycle assessment (LCA), and artificial in­
telligence technologies provide efficient means for evaluating and selecting pretreatment methods. This paper

A B S T R A C T
To address the challenges associated with the large-scale production and difficult disposal of biogas slurry in 
conventional high-solid anaerobic digestion, this study developed a three-stage integrated co-digestion (TSAD) 
process integrated with biogas slurry reflux (BSR), and assessed its feasibility for stable semi-continuous oper­
ation over a 120-day period. Results demonstrate that TSAD enables targeted enrichment among functional 
microbial communities—achieved through spatially segregated operational stages: aerobic hydrolysis, micro­
aerobic acidification, and anaerobic methanogenesis. Under an appropriate hydraulic retention time (HRT) of 20 
days, the system achieved sustained high biogas production stability (with a final methane yield of 218 mL/g 
COD). Crucially, relying on the comprehensive strategy of high-solid feedstock, staged separation and BSR, it 
enhanced overall treatment efficiency by approximately 2.8-fold relative to conventional single-stage system, 
while reducing daily water consumption per unit substrate by 83.3 %, thereby substantially mitigating slurry 
emission. In contrast, reducing the HRT to 10 days boosted short-term biogas production, but also enhanced the 
mobilization of copper and zinc into the liquid phase and caused rapid accumulation of ammonia nitrogen (up to 
4855.1 mg/L) during prolonged operation, ultimately increasing the risk of process instability and potential 
system failure. These findings provide a theoretical basis for achieving process optimization through staged

for biomass treatment, enables the conversion of organic matter into 
clean biogas through microbial synergism. This process offers dual 
benefits—effective waste management and renewable energy produc­
tion, and plays a significant role in advancing carbon emission re­
ductions (Awodun et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2019).

in recent years, it has seen stagnation or even negative growth in project

ever, it may also contain potential contaminants including heavy metals 
and antibiotic residues (Liu et al., 2021). Although stringent emission

Abstract
Aerobic treatment of olive mill wastewater (OMW) is a promising technique for biogas recovery using anaerobic digestion, 
in the case of OMW it is possible to reduce polyphenols and TCOD concentration which undesirable by microorganism 
metabolism. OMW was subjected to the aeration process over different periods to detect the removal efficiency of polyphenols 
and TCOD. During this study, anaerobic co-digestion of OMW without pretreatment and activated sludge (AS) was inhibited 
due to the presence of a high inhibitors concentration. While anaerobic co-digestion of aerated OMW–AS were achieved 
TCOD removal 56.34%, 70.32%, 52.81% and polyphenols removal 42.69%, 60.45%, 63.51% when the OMW aerated for 
2, 4 and 6 days respectively. The highest biogas production 0.473 ­Nm3/kg VS was achieved by OMW aerated for 4 days in 
conjunction with 68.39% CH4, 55.85% VS removal, 10.91 g/l of TCOD and 4.23 g ­CaCO3/l.

Introduction
Among the possible renewable energy sources, biowaste 
from activated sludge (AS) is a promising resource [1]. 
An attractive process solution for cancelling accumulation 
of active sludge is the anaerobic digestion (AD) process 
[2–5]. Therefore, AD of the AS with higher volatile solids 
(VS) content has been considered to be an alternative to 
biomass digestion without competition to food production 
[6, 7].
Thus, VS content higher than 4% in comparison to the 
conventional AD processes from other sources which have 
TS 0.5–3%, could operate by using existing AD infrastruc-
ture at wastewater plants [2–4]. Moreover, the short resi-
dence time for complete digestion of AS from 16–46 days 
were reported when total solid (TS) with removal rate 32% 
of VS increased from 1.79 to 15.67% [8].
The AD inhibitors AS were believed to be directly 
related to the decreased capacity of functional microor-
ganisms. Microbial communities may also differ due to 
the accumulation of volatile Fatty Acids (VFA) combined 
with high, thus leads to alternation in metabolic pathways 
and decrease AD performance. On the other hand, various 
suggestions were presented to avoid inhibition through co-
digestion technology [3, 6, 7, 9, 10]. In practical, using AD 
to co-digest AS with other biowaste materials to improve 
biogas production has been proposed and implemented at 
the wastewater plant [2–5], that can be achieved by using 
existing infrastructure at the wastewater plant without 
extra capital cost.
The world production of olive oil in 2017 about 2.945 
million tons and according to provisional figures by the 
International Olive Council (IOC), the Global olive oil 
production is increased to rise by 28% for 2018. The by-
products of Olive oil mills such as olive mill wastewaters 
(OMW), could be considered as suitable feedstock for the 
AD process. Actually, those by-products of Olive oil mills 
pose a serious risk, where the organic compounds meas-
ured as 40 g/l to 220 g/l [11, 12]. However, OMW was 
subjected to many treatment studies in terms of physical 
and chemical treatment [13–17], one of the satisfactory 
solutions to dispose of these organic pollutants is the AD 
process [18, 19].
However, the AD of OMW suffered low pH value, high 
content of phenolic, and ammonium nitrogen lack, which 
lead to inhibition. Currently, to overcome these limitations, 
pretreatments for OMW have been reported such as aerobic 
process and evaporation in storage ponds. In order to encour-
age bacterial growth, aeration as a pretreatment process had 
been applied with different technologies. That approves 
digestion process efficiency and high polyphenols rates [20]. 
The Polyphenol molecular structure is concerned as one 
of the main toxicity reasons. When the Hydroxyl Number 
Group (HNG) decreases the inhibitory effect is increased, 
HNG is associated with polyphenols concentration [21].
Many studies showed that OMW could be improved with 
low dilution by drying without adding chemical substances, 
also could be subject to co-digestion process with AS which 
contains a high level of ammonium nitrogen. Co-digestion of 
AS with OMW provides the necessary nutrients and buffer 
capacity also decrease potential inhibitors of the AD process 
[16–22].

The application of microaerobic conditions during sludge digestion has been proven to be an efﬁcient
method for H2S removal from biogas. In this study, three microaerobic treatments were considered as
an alternative to the technique of biogas desulfurization applied (FeCl3 dosing to the digesters) in a

1. Introduction
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is widely employed in wastewater
treatment plants (WWTPs) in order to reduce excess sludge pro-
duction from the activated sludge process, and generate an
energy-rich gas called biogas. Among other applications, biogas
can be burnt in combined heat and power (CHP) generation plants
for the production of heat and electricity by combustion engines.
Therefore, AD can improve the economic balance of WWTPs
(Appels et al., 2008).
Besides CH4 and CO2, which are its main components, biogas
also contains several trace compounds that must be removed
before combustion. H2S is the most relevant of these pollutants,
which is produced during sludge digestion as a result of reduction
and fermentation of inorganic and organic S-containing com-
pounds (respectively) present in both primary and secondary
sludge (Lens and Hulshoff Pol, 2000). It is a toxic malodorous com-
pound, highly corrosive to many types of steel, and considerably
shortens the lifetime of the installations for biogas utilization.
Therefore, for trouble-free operation of CHP generation plants,
H2S concentrations of less than 100–500 mg/N m3 must be main-
tained (Deublein and Steinhauser, 2008).
Several techniques can be applied in order to achieve the
required H2S concentration in biogas, including physical, chemical,
or biological, or combinations of these three alternative methods.
Despite their high chemical requirements, energy and disposal
cost, physicochemical technologies are widely implemented at
industrial scale due to extensive experience in design and opera-
tion. Biological processes have the potential to overcome some or
all the disadvantages of physicochemical technologies (Syed
et al., 2006). In fact, there are several technical solutions offered
commercially worldwide for biogas desulfurization involving bio-
logical removal mechanisms, such as the combination of chemical
scrubbing
with

ABSTRACT: An integrated anaerobic digestion system for the
simultaneous removal of carbon and nitrogen from fish sludge was
developed by coupling iron sludge supplementation with
intermittent aeration. In terms of nitrogen removal, Fe(III) in
iron sludge could trigger Feammox reactions and intermittent
aeration could drive the Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycle to sustain continuous
ammonia removal. Mass balance analysis suggested that nitrate was
the main product of Feammox, which was subsequently removed
through heterotrophic denitrification. In terms of carbon removal,
the Fe(III)-induced dissimilatory iron reduction (DIR) process
significantly promoted fish sludge hydrolysis and provided more
simple organics for methanogens and denitrifiers, but aeration
showed a negative impact on methanogenesis. To promote
nitrogen removal and avoid serious methanogenesis inhibition,
different aeration intensities were studied. Results showed that compared with the control without aeration or iron sludge addition,
aeration for 5 min every 3 days (150 mL/min) contributed to a 29.0% lower NH4
+-N concentration and a 12.1% lower total
chemical oxygen demand level on day 28, and the decline in methane yield was acceptable (only 13.5% lower). Simultaneous
methanogenesis, Feammox, and denitrification in a single reactor treating fish sludge were achieved, which provides a simple and
low-cost strategy for the treatment of organic wastewater.
KEYWORDS: fish sludge, nitrogen removal, carbon removal, CH4 recovery, Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycle, metagenomic analysis
1. INTRODUCTION
Huge amounts of fish sludge, consisting of fecal solids and
undigested feed, are generated each year from the freshwater
aquaculture industry globally and require proper treatment and
utilization. Anaerobic digestion (AD) is an environmentally
friendly process that converts organic matter into combustible
methane (CH4), and has long been practiced for the treatment
of fish sludge.1 However, the digestates containing high levels
of ammonia require further treatment before discharge. The
normal practice is to set up biological nitrogen (N) removal
units after AD, which not only complicates the treatment
procedure but also increases the energy consumption, land use,
and construction cost.2,3 Therefore, it is necessary to develop
integrated anaerobic treatment systems for the simultaneous
removal of carbon (C) and N.
In recent years, researchers have successfully coupled
methanogenesis and denitrification in a single reactor,
achieving simultaneous removal of organic C and nitrate/
nitrite.4,5 The small molecular organic substances produced
from the fermentation process can provide carbon sources for
the denitrifiers, and the alkalinity generated during the
denitrification reactions can create a more stable environment
for the methanogens.4,5 Despite the merits of simultaneous
methanogenesis and the denitrification process, the organic N
rich in fish sludge is mainly decomposed to ammonia during
AD, which cannot be directly utilized by denitrifiers. The
conventional ammonia oxidation and nitrite oxidation
processes generally function at a dissolved oxygen (DO)
concentration no less than 0.4 and 3.0 mg/L, respectively,6
which are difficult to occur in AD reactors. Therefore, finding
effective strategies to convert ammonium-nitrogen (NH4
+-N)
into nitrite-nitrogen (NO2
−-N) or nitrate-nitrogen (NO3
−-N)
under anaerobic environments is the key to simultaneously

The effects and underlying mechanisms of composting and extrusion 
pretreatment on anaerobic biogas production from wheat straw
Guangyin Chen 
a,b, Ya-Ge Lia, Guang-Cai Gea, Yu-Juan Suna and Yu-Xin Zhanga
aSchool of Ecology and Environment, Anhui Normal University, Wuhu, People’s Republic of China; bAnhui Engineering Laboratory of Soil and 
Water Pollution Control and Remediation, Wuhu, People’s Republic of China
ABSTRACT  
The effects of moisture + extrusion and composting + extrusion treatments on the production of 
biogas from the anaerobic digestion (AD) of wheat straw (WS) were systematically investigated. 
The results showed that when the moisture content of WS was adjusted to 55% before 
extrusion and maintained for 24 h, the biogas production of both the unextruded and extruded 
samples reached the highest levels, which were 130.48 and 158.41 mL/g, respectively. Based on 
these results, the WS was further aerobically composted after adjusting its moisture content to 
55%, and then extruded for biogas production. The biogas production of unextruded WS 
initially increased and then decreased, reaching the maximum of 129.40 mL/g when the 
composting temperature rose to 55°C. In contrast, the biogas production of extruded WS 
increased at all composting temperatures and reached the maximum of 150.83 mL/g at 55°C, 
which is 19.49% higher than the initial biogas production of extruded WS at the start of 
composting. Mechanistic analyses indicated that extrusion reduced particle size, increased 
specific surface area, and disrupted lignocellulosic structure, while composting promoted partial 
degradation of hemicellulose and lignin. These structural modifications enhanced substrate 
accessibility and microbial degradation, thereby boosting biogas production. In conclusion, the 
combination of composting and extrusion pretreatment can significantly improve the biogas 
production performance of anaerobic digestion of WS, with an increase ranging from 20.76% to 
43.45%, which is worthy of further research.

1. Introduction
In recent years, there has been a growing focus on the 
environmental pollution caused by agricultural waste. 
China produces approximately 900 million tons of crop 
straw annually [1]. Rice straw, maize stalks, and wheat 
straw constitute the primary categories of straw, 
accounting for about 90% of the global total [2]. The 
treatment, recovery, and resource utilization of straw 
remain 
pressing 
challenges 
in 
environmental 
management.
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a biological process in 
which organic substances are decomposed by a consor­
tium of microorganisms working synergistically. Briefly, 
AD consists of four stages: hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acet­
ogenesis, and methanogenesis [3]. AD treatment of 
straw has been adopted in many countries, and AD tech­
nologies for straw are well-developed in developed 
countries. For example, in Europe, biogas production 
from energy crops constitutes a significant portion 
(30–40% wet weight basis of total mixed feed) in agricul­
tural biogas plants [4]. In contrast, the application of AD 
technology for straw in China is still in the developmen­
tal stage.
Although AD is an effective approach to straw treat­
ment, direct AD has limitations regarding the degra­
dation efficiency of raw straw and biogas production

Recent Advances in Applying Nanobubbles for Enhanced Anaerobic 
Digestion: Fundamentals, Challenges, and Future Prospects
Alsayed Mostafa1 · Ahmed Elsayed2 · Rasha Maal‑Bared3 · Elsayed Elbeshbishy2 · Bipro Ranjan Dhar1
Received: 14 April 2025 / Accepted: 16 August 2025 
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2025
Abstract
In recent years, the use of nanobubbles (NBs) in anaerobic digestion (AD) has received significant research attention, with 
numerous studies reporting notable improvements in AD efficiency when nanobubble water (NBW) is introduced in digest-
ers. The improvements are often attributed to more efficient substrate degradation, higher activity of key enzymes, and the 
more complex and diverse microbial communities associated with NBW-integrated AD. Despite these promising results, 
detailed explanations of the mechanisms and modes of action behind NBW, particularly its impact on each step of the AD 
process—hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis, methanogenesis—are still limited. This paper aims to provide a compre-
hensive review and critical assessment of NBW’s impacts on AD, with a particular focus on how operational conditions 
can influence NBW-related effects on AD performance. Finally, energy efficiencies, future opportunities and challenges of 
expanding NB technology to boost AD efficiency are discussed.

Introduction
Given the significant global interest in green energy pro-
duction, resource recovery, and sustainable practices, 
anaerobic digestion (AD) has emerged as a promising 
technology for addressing various challenges, including 
the management of organic waste and associated green-
house gas emissions. The AD process comprises four suc-
cessive steps, i.e., hydrolysis, acidogenesis, acetogenesis 
and methanogenesis [1, 2]. By treating organic wastes, the 
AD not only minimizes waste but also produces renewable 
biogas, which contributes to carbon neutrality and serves 
as a sustainable alternative to fossil fuels [3]. Also, AD 
enables nutrient recovery, minimizes energy demand and 
offers economic and environmental benefits [4]. Despite 
its multiple advantages, AD process still faces some chal-
lenges in terms of instability at high organic loading rates 
[5]. Challenges also include accumulation of volatile fatty 
acids (VFAs) when using easily biodegradable feedstocks 
[2], slow hydrolysis of complex substrates [6], produc-
tion of inhibitory products such as hydrogen sulfide (H₂S)/
bisulfide ion (HS⁻) and ammonia (NH₃) [7, 8], and ulti-
mately the inhibition of microbial community leading to 
process instability [9, 10]. Various sludge pre-treatment 
approaches, including thermal hydrolysis, chemical oxi-
dation, alkaline treatment, and ultrasonic disintegration, 
have been employed to address these drawbacks. How-
ever, these approaches often involve high chemical/energy 
consumption, high capital investment, and may produce 
additional inhibitory by-products [11–13].
An innovative approach used to overcome some of these 
shortcomings is microaeration, which involves introducing 
a small amount of oxygen ­(O2) or air into digesters [14]. 
The required gas dosage for maintaining microaerobic 
conditions has been reported as 0.005 ~ 5 L ­O2/Lreactor/day 
[15], or maintaining dissolved oxygen (DO) levels between 
0.1 ~ 1 mg/L [16]. Microaeration intervals reported in 
literature vary widely, ranging from intermittent [17] to 
continuous injection of air or oxygen [18, 19]. Microaera-
tion enhances the abundance of facultative bacteria, as 
well as acidogenic and hydrolytic microbes, in digesters, 
thereby improving substrate degradation [20]. Neverthe-
less, safety concerns, particularly the risk of explosion 
due to excess oxygen, remain a significant barrier to the 
widespread implementation in full-scale AD facilities 
[21]. Unlike conventional microaeration, which involves 
introducing microbubbles of air or oxygen into digesters, 
nanobubble (NB) technology involves introducing the gas 
in nano-sized bubbles, providing better distribution and 
utilization efficiencies [22].
The concept of NBs was first introduced in 1994 to 
explain attractive forces observed between hydrophobic 
surfaces in water [23]. The first image of nano-sized bub-
bles was captured using atomic force microscopy (AFM) 
in 2000 [24]. Over the last two decades, NB technology 
has been applied in biomedical engineering [25], agricul-
ture [26], and environmental remediation [27]. Recently, 
the application of this technology in AD systems has 
attracted growing interest [28, 29]. Supplementing NBs 
in AD enriches hydrolytic bacteria and methanogens, 
improving hydrolysis and methanogenesis [30, 31]. Fur-
ther, NBs promote the generation of reactive oxygen spe-
cies (ROS), which at optimal levels enhance microbial 
metabolism [30]. In addition, NBs possess unique phys-
icochemical properties, such as high surface charge, large 
surface area-to-volume ratio, high negative zeta potential, 
long residence time, weak floating features,

Effect of organic compositions of aerobically pretreated municipal solid waste
on non-methane organic compound emissions during anaerobic degradation
Yuanyuan Zhang a, Dongbei Yue a,⇑, Jianguo Liu a, Liang He b, Yongfeng Nie a
a Key Laboratory for Solid Waste Management and Environment Safety, Ministry of Education of China, Tsinghua University, Beijing 100084, China
b BESG Environmental Engineering Co. Ltd., Beijing 100101, China
a r t i c l e
i n f o

Received 15 November 2011
Accepted 3 January 2012
Available online 14 February 2012
Keywords:
Non-methane organic compounds
Organic composition
Aerobically pretreated municipal solid
waste
Anaerobic degradation
a b s t r a c t
Odor pollution caused by municipal solid waste (MSW) treatment plants has become a growing public
concern. Although aerobic pretreatment of MSW has advantages in accelerating landﬁll stabilization,
the property of non-methane organic compound (NMOC) emissions from aerobically pretreated MSW
(APMSW) during landﬁlling is unknown. To investigate NMOC emissions from anaerobic degradation
of APMSW and to study the impact of organic compositions of APMSW and their decomposition stages,
ﬁve simulative anaerobic bioreactors (R1–R5) were ﬁlled up with APMSW of different original organic
compositions in a laboratory. For NMOC analysis, samples were collected from the gas that accumulated
separately during two successive independent stages of the whole experiment. The results showed that
the cumulative quantities of NMOCs from R1 to R5 were 1.11, 0.30, 0.18, 0.28, and 0.31 mg/kg DM,
respectively, when volatile solid was degraded by 34.8–47.2%. As the organic content of the original
waste was lower, the proportion of NMOCs generated in the early stage of anaerobic degradation became
higher. Multiple linear regression analyses of the relationship between the quantities of degraded organ-
ics and generated NMOCs showed that lipid and protein have a strong effect on NMOC amount. The effect
of lipid on NMOC quantity lasts longer than that of protein. This observation suggests that controlling the
lipid and protein contents in MSW can reduce the odor from landﬁlls.

1. Introduction
Conventional landﬁlling is a common method adopted world-
wide to dispose of municipal solid waste (MSW). During the anaer-
obic degradation of MSW, most organic matter is broken down by
microorganisms into simple compounds, leading to the formation
of landﬁll gas. CO2 and CH4 are the dominant components in land-
ﬁll gas. Trace species, such as mercury, arsenic, and some organic
compounds, are often found abundantly in landﬁll gas relative to
other environmental sources (Kim and Kim, 2002; Feng et al.,
2004; Huang et al., 2009). Although non-methane organic com-
pounds (NMOCs) comprise less than 1% (V/V) of landﬁll gas, they
may create a disproportionate environmental burden and potential
risk to human health (Allen et al., 1997). For example, emissions of
carcinogens, such as benzene and vinyl chloride, pose a potential
threat to workers and local inhabitants (El-Fadel et al., 1997;
Durmusoglu
et
al.,
2010).
Furthermore,
chloro-
and
ﬂuoro-
hydrocarbons emitted from landﬁlls seriously corrode combustion
engines that utilize landﬁll gas (Dernbach, 1985), deplete the
ozone layer, and cause climate change (Molina and Rowland,
1974; Wallington et al., 1994).
The reported yields of NMOCs varied widely according to the
nature of waste and the experiment condition (Thomas and Barlaz,
1999; Smet et al., 1999; Staley et al., 2006; Wang and Wu, 2008).
The yield of total terpenes from orange wastes was up to
11,000 mg/kg DM (Wang and Wu, 2008), and the NMOC yields of
refuse, paper, yard waste, and food waste were investigated to be
151, 16, 38, and 221 mg C/kg DM, respectively (Staley et al.,
2006). It was also found that NMOC release during aerobic decom-
position of refuse and yard waste was larger than that in anaerobic
systems (Staley et al., 2006). However, Komilis et al. (2004)
detected a VOC yield of food waste as low as 0.33 mg/kg DM under
controlled aerobic conditions, approximately four orders of magni-
tude less than values reported by Staley et al. (2006).
Knox (1990) compared NMOCs released from three main phases
of decomposition, and found that total NMOC concentration ini-
tially increases and then steadily decreases. Moreover, the author
also investigated some categories of NMOC concentrations among
waste degradation processes. Alcohols and halogenated hydrocar-
bons are the main components of NMOCs emitted from young
refuse (Knox, 1990). Deipser and Stegmann (1994) found that the
highest concentrations of volatile chlorinated and ﬂuorinated
hydrocarbons occur during the acid phase in a landﬁll. Kim
(2006) similarly concluded that the proportion of reduced sulfur
compounds is larger in young landﬁlls than in old landﬁlls.

A B S T R A C T   
Micro-aeration is considered a new strategy for improving volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production of agricultural 
waste. This study investigated the effect and mechanism of micro-aeration of air and oxygen (O2) on VFAs 
production from swine manure. The results showed that Air-micro-aeration had the most significant improve­
ment effect, with the highest VFAs of 8.21 g/L, which was increased by 22.4%. Moreover, the mixing effects of 
different micro-aeration were limited, and the microbial communities significantly varied. Firmicutes and Bac­
teroidota were the dominant hydrolytic and acidogenic bacteria, and Air-micro-aeration preferentially promoted 
electron transfer activity and energy generation. Methanosarcina, Methanocorpusculum, and Methanobrevibacter 
can adapt to environmental changes according to their different oxygen tolerance, and the consumption and 
conversion of VFAs by methanogens were slow under Air-micro-aeration condition. This study revealed mech­
anism of micro-aeration for improving VFAs production from swine manure, providing a theoretical basis for 
micro-aeration regulation optimization.

1. Introduction 
Micro-aerobic environment is a state between aerobic and anaerobic 
conditions with a low dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration, that is 
created by injecting a trace amount of air or oxygen (O2) (DO range of 
0.1-1.0 mg/L) into an anaerobic bioreactor (Wu et al., 2015; Chen et al., 
2020; Zhang et al., 2021). Recent studies have shown that micro- 
aeration is an effective approach that facilitates anaerobic digestion 
(AD), such as improving hydrolysis rate and enhancing methane pro­
duction (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018; Wang et al., 2020). The hydrolysis 
stage is generally regarded as a rate-limiting step of AD, especially when 
recalcitrant lignocellulosic biomass, such as straw, are used, and hy­
drolysis rates under aerobic and anoxic conditions are significantly 
higher than those under anaerobic conditions (Shrestha et al., 2017; 
Wang et al., 2020). 
Given that AD system has a certain tolerance to O2, micro-aeration 
can have a positive impact on microbial metabolism and energy trans­
fer. Lim et al. (2014) studied the co-digestion characteristics of brown 
water and food waste at a micro-aeration intensity of 5 and 7 mL O2 
L−1d−1, and the results showed that micro-aeration enhanced microbial 
diversity and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production, and the hydrolysis 
rate and methane yield also increased. Microbial analysis indicated that 
micro-aeration can promote the proliferation of diverse bacterial pop­
ulations and increase the proportion of Firmicutes clones related to hy­
drolysis in contrast to anaerobic conditions (Lim et al., 2014). Yu et al. 
(2020) found that hydrolytic/fermentative bacteria and acetoclastic 
methanogens (e.g., Methanosaeta) were in higher abundances with 
controlled micro-aeration (5 and 10 mg O2/L-reactor), which facilitated 
syntrophic interactions between microorganisms. The relative abun­
dance of dominant bacterium Firmicutes increased from 58% to 72%, 
and the relative abundance of methanogenic archaea Methanosarcina 
and Methanobacterium with certain oxygen tolerance also increased (Fu 
et al., 2016). 
VFAs are the intermediate products and can be consumed at the 
methanogenic stage in AD. When air or O2 is introduced into an 
anaerobic reactor, the proliferation of strictly anaerobic methanogens is 
inhibited to a certain extent due to the enhanced activity of facultative 
hydrolysis bacteria and fermentation bacteria, and thus VFAs may 
accumulate. Lim and Wang et al. (2013) reported that VFAs concen­
tration increased from 1.69 g COD/L to 5.57 g COD/L after 4 days of 
micro-aeration pretreatment, and methane production increased by 
21%, but long-term experiment is needed to verify.

A B S T R A C T
High-solids anaerobic digestion sustainably converts organic waste into methane-rich biogas and nutrient-rich 
biomanure, offering dual benefits. This study assessed poultry litter (PL) digestion at 10 %, 30 %, and 60 % 
total solids (TS) under three setups: (i) PL alone, (ii) co-digestion with food waste hydrolysate (PL + FH) to 
improve carbon/nitrogen (C/N) ratio, and (iii) in situ desulfurization (St-PL) using sulfur-oxidizing bacteria 
(SOB) with micro-aeration to reduce H2S. The highest biogas yields were obtained at 30 % TS: 12.4 L (PL + FH), 
9.9 L (PL), and 8.9 L (St-PL). Methane content was highest in St-PL (68 %) with H2S removal of 80–92 %. 
However, slight sulfate accumulation was detected in the digestate, attributed to the metabolic activity of sulfur 
oxidizing bacteria (SOB). Microbial analysis revealed the dominance of Firmicutes, Bacteroidetes, Methanosaeta, 
and Methanobacterium. This study demonstrates a scalable strategy in which micro-aeration combined with SOB 
enhanced methane yield and biogas quality while effectively mitigating H2S during high-solids poultry litter 
digestion.

1. Introduction
The accumulation of poultry litter, a major by-product of the poultry 
industry, poses significant environmental challenges due to its high ni­
trogen content which leads to ammonia emissions, nutrient leaching and 
groundwater pollution, the release of greenhouse gases (GHGs), and the 
spread of pathogens. It is estimated that in 2024, the global chicken 
meat production was ~103,046 tons, which is associated with the 
generation of approximately 68 billion tons of poultry waste annually 
(Coˆelho et al., 2025). Over the past five decades, the production of 
poultry litter (PL) has increased by an average of 5 % per annum, along 
with other associated wastes, including droppings; bedding materials 
such as straw, sawdust, wood shavings, and rice hulls; hatchery waste; 
feathers; and processing wastewater generated during and after the 
production period (Beausang et al., 2020; Moreki & Keaikitse, 2013; 
Mottet & Tempio, 2017).
These waste materials possess properties that can substantially 
exacerbate pollution, leading to health hazards. Current treatment 
methods for poultry litter include biological, physico-chemical and 
thermal methods. However, most of these approaches are not cost- 
effective and are complex to implement, whereas biological treatment 
through the anaerobic digestion (AD) approach offers the dual benefit of 
cost-effectiveness and the generation of biogas and biomanure, 
contributing to the circular bioeconomy. AD is widely utilised for the 
treatment of a diversity of organic wastes, including cattle and pig 
manure, which share similar characteristics with poultry litter, partic­
ularly the hazardous emissions of H2S and ammonia (NH3). These wastes 
cause contamination through pathogens, odours, and pests, while 
manure facilities emit CO2, CH4, and N2O, contributing to global 
warming. The sulfur content in poultry litter hinders the metabolism and 
growth of methanogenic archaea by promoting toxic sulfide production 
and by allowing sulfur-reducing bacteria (SRB) to compete for essential 
substrates. Poultry farms supplement feeds with sulfur-containing 
amino acids like methionine and cysteine, as chicks cannot synthesize 
them; these are essential for protein synthesis, feather growth, and 
improved egg production (Capson-Tojo et al., 2017). PL, rich in sulfur 
amino acids and organics, generates sulfur by-products during AD, 
creating microbial competition that lowers biogas yield and methane 
production (Mahdy et al., 2020).

A B S T R A C T   
Air-nanobubble water (NBW) was applied to pre-acclimate anaerobically digested sludge that was then used as 
the inoculum in the two-stage anaerobic digestion (AD) of high saline (20 g NaCl/L) food waste (FW) to optimize 
NBW application in the AD of high saline FW. K+ was simultaneously supplemented during the methanogenic 
stage to resist the inhibition of salt on methanogens. Results showed that after the second pre-acclimation cycle, 
the inoculum activity was increased 27% in the Air-NBW supplemented reactor in comparison to the deionized 
water (DW) supplemented one. In the first-stage AD, H2 yield was enhanced by 46% in the Air-NBW pre-accli­
mated sludge reactor compared with the DW pre-acclimated sludge reactor. Besides, supplementation of KOH in 
the methanogenic stage could enhance methane production by 17–25% in the DW reactors at initial pH 7.5, 8.0, 
and 9.0 when compared to the control reactor (using NaOH adjusted initial pH to 7.5), respectively.   
1. Introduction 
Salinity is one of the most stressful abiotic factors that limit hydrogen 
and/or methane production in the anaerobic digestion (AD) process, 
which has attracted much attention of researchers. On the other hand, 
food waste (FW) is becoming an increasingly preferred feedstock for AD, 
which normally contains a high salinity because salt is extensively used 
as a food flavoring agent, especially in Japan. Asakura et al. (2014) 
pointed out that a much higher level of Na+ than the world health or­
ganization (WHO) recommendation was consumed by most Japanese 
due to the Japanese diet. As known, high salinity (>10 g NaCl/L) usually 
increases the osmotic pressure outside the cells and causes the outflow of 
intracellular water or even the cell rupture, which strongly inhibits the 
metabolism of non-halophilic bacteria (Li et al., 2018). Therefore,

excessive salt present in organic wastes, i.e., FW, could inhibit the ac­
tivities of microorganisms in all stages (hydrolysis/acidification and 
methanogenesis) of AD to varying degrees, resulting in a lower AD 
performance and even process failure. Among them, high salinity may 
more remarkably inhibit methane production than hydrogen and vola­
tile fatty acids (VFAs) production because the methanogens are more 
sensitive to environmental factors like high salt concentration than the 
hydrolytic bacteria (Wang et al., 2018a). Additionally, it has been found 
that anaerobic microbes need some time to accommodate the hypersa­
line environments when dealing with the highly saline FW, which is 
probably the main reason for a longer startup time (about 20 days) at 20 
g NaCl/L in a previous study (Hou et al., 2021b). Hierholtzer and 
Akunna (2014) also found a similar phenomenon that methane pro­
duction was delayed by about 15 days in the AD of saline-rich macro­
algae system. These observations suggest that high salinity could 
strongly inhibit microbial activity during the early stage of methano­
genesis. Therefore, some strategies for addressing this problem though 
improving microbial activity are recommended. 
In general, the tolerance of microorganisms to high salinity could be 
improved by the synthesis of themselves or adding external osmopro­
tectants, allowing microorganisms to accumulate osmolytes (compatible 
solutes) and balance their cytoplasms (Salma et al., 2020). Amino acids 
and quaternary ammonium compounds, including proline, choline, 
glycine betaine, carnitine, and trehalose, have been adopted as common 
osmoprotectants in the AD of high saline organic wastes to recover 
methanogenic activity and increase methane production (Oh et al., 
2008; Liu et al., 2019b; Zhang et al., 2016). However, Liu et al. (2019b) 
reported that excessive addition of osmoprotectants had an adverse ef­
fect on methane production. Apart from this, the osmoprotectants are 
organic substances that may be consumed by microorganisms as carbon 
or nitrogen sources, resulting in instability in continuous

Effects of nano-bubble water on anaerobic co-digestion of cabbage waste and 
cow manure under mesophilic and thermophilic conditions
Youfei Zhoua, Peilin Guob, Yi Liub,c, Weijie Hua and Tianfeng Wangb
aDesign Institute No.3, Shanghai Municipal Engineering Design and Research Institute (Group) Co., Ltd., Shanghai, People’s Republic of China; 
bCollege of Petrochemical Engineering, Lanzhou University of Technology, Lanzhou, People’s Republic of China; cSchool of Environmental and 
Municipal Engineering, Xi’an University of Architecture and Technology, Xi’an, People’s Republic of China
ABSTRACT  
The impact of four nano-bubble water (NBW) additions on the hydrolysis rate, methane yield, and 
microbial community of co-digestion of cabbage waste (CW) and cow manure (CM) under 
mesophilic and thermophilic conditions were investigated. Adding NBW under mesophilic 
conditions promoted hydrolysis, and the highest soluble chemical oxygen demand of the 
mesophilic digesters with the addition of CO2-NBW increased by 15.86%. Methane yield in the 
mesophilic digesters with Air-NBW and CO2-NBW increased by 17.54% and 14.72%, respectively. 
Moreover, the addition of NBW further accelerated the methane yield rate under mesophilic 
conditions. Due to the influence of thermophilic temperature, the impact of NBW addition on 
hydrolysis, methane yield, and methane yield rate in the thermophilic digesters did not differ 
significantly from the control. The addition of Air-NBW and N2-NBW in the thermophilic 
digesters resulted in only marginal increases in methane yield, by 1.09% and 5.61%, 
respectively. NBW addition enhanced both the abundance and diversity of microbial 
communities in both mesophilic and thermophilic digesters. The addition of NBW represents a 
promising technological advancement for enhancing the efficiency of anaerobic co-digestion of 
CW and CM.

1. Introduction
As a predominantly agricultural nation, China generates 
an estimated 360 million tons of vegetable waste 
annually [1]. Cabbage waste (CW), a common food 
waste in China, is characterized by its high biodegrad­
ability [2]. Improper management of CW may result in 
significant health and environmental risks [3]. Anaerobic 
digestion (AD) offers an effective solution for treating 
CW by decomposing the organic matter in vegetables 
to produce biogas, while the resulting digestate serves 
as a valuable fertilizer [4]. The high volatile solids (VS) 
content (approximately 75%) and low total solids (TS) 
content (below 10%) in CW can lead to the accumulation 
of volatile fatty acids (VFA), which in turn may inhibit 
methanogenic activity and potentially result in the 
failure of the AD [3].
Co-digestion of CW and cow manure (CM) presents a 
promising strategy for stabilizing the AD process and 
enhancing methane yield [5]. Integrating CW and CM 
can effectively balance the water content, biodegrad­
able organic matter, and buffering capacity within the 
AD [3]. Vegetable peels were combined with CM under 
mesophilic anaerobic co-digestion conditions, achieving 
a methane yield of 170 mL g−1-VSadded [6]. However,

Submicron magnetite-enhanced
tribromophenol removal and methanogenesis
under microaerobic condition
Fan Yang, Jing Wang,*
Chen Gu, Ying Han, Guang-fei Liu and Hong Lu
Abstract
BACKGROUND: To accelerate direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET), magnetite is supplemented in anaerobic activated
sludge (AS). However, it is usually reduced by dissimilatory iron reducing bacteria (DIRB). Therefore, an AS system supplemented
with submicron magnetite particles (Fe3O4/AS) in an up-ﬂow microaerobic sludge reactor was established, aiming to remove
tribromophenol (TBP) eﬃciently and alleviate the magnetite dissolution.
RESULTS: Under microaerobic condition (DO, 0.6 mg L−1), the eﬃciencies of removal of COD, TBP, and methane production
in Fe3O4/AS system were, respectively, 14.3%, 16.7%, and 27.2% higher than those of the AS system. Correspondingly,
the dehydrogenase (DHA) and Coenzyme F420 (CoF420) activities were separately 1.38-fold and 1.41-fold enhanced. The
enhanced biodegradation was via potential DIET, as visualized by microbes and magnetite particles, Geobacter enrichment and
c-type cytochromes (c-Cyts) increasement. Notably, magnetite majorly maintained an intact structure. In eﬄuents, the Fe(II)
concentrations were maintained at less than 10 mg L−1 under microaerobic conditions, far less than the amount under anaerobic
conditions, which might be due to the in situ redox cycle of Fe(III)-reduction and Fe(II)-reoxidation.
CONCLUSION: Signiﬁcant enhancements in removal eﬃciencies of TBP and COD and methanogenesis were demonstrated
in a Fe3O4/AS system, indicating intrinsically faster electron transfer via electrical conduction. Putative oxidation of dissolved
Fe(II) in situ occurred in microaerobic environments, which could protect magnetite in the system without extra magnetite
supplementation.

INTRODUCTION
Tribromophenol (TBP) is widely used as a synthetic intermediate
of brominated ﬂame retardants (BFRs), pesticide, and the replace-
ment of pentachlorophenol in wood preservation. TBP has devel-
opmental neurotoxicity, embryotoxicity, and fetotoxicity eﬀects,
and this compound has been detected in various environmen-
tal matrices throughout the world, including marine and fresh
waters, sediments, soil, sewage sludge, and organisms.1–5 Notably,
wastewater containing TBP has attracted considerable concern
due to long-term residual and bioaccumulative properties, and the
developmentofeﬃcientandcost-eﬀectivetechniquestotreatTBP
wastewater is needed.
To date, limited physicochemical methods (phototransforma-
tion, chemical catalysis, etc.) have been reported to remove TBP,
while biodegradation is the eco-friendly and economical approach
for removal of TBP.6 However, TBP is resistant to aerobic biodegra-
dation due to the electron-withdrawing properties of bromine.
But anaerobic dehalogenation via dehalorespiration using halo-
genated compounds as terminal electron acceptors occurs more
easily.7 Previous studies have reported that both activated sludge
(AS) and pure strains exhibit anaerobic biodegradability of TBP.8,9
Lei et al. isolated Bacillus sp. GZT isolate, which was capable of
debrominating and mineralizing TBP, inferring that anaerobic
reductive debromination could act as the major degradation
pathway in the process of mineralizing TBP.10 However, the elec-
tron transfer rate is relatively low under anaerobic conditions,
which limits the rate of the dehalogenation process. To solve this
problem, diﬀerent mediators have been applied in biodegrada-
tion processes as electron shuttles to accelerate electron transfer,
such as vitamin B12 (VB12) and anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonate
(AQDS).11,12 Recently, it has been documented that nanoparticle
magnetite (Fe3O4) and other conductive minerals can promote
direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) in a range of metabolic
processes, including a syntrophic metabolism between dehalo-
genating and non-dehalogenating bacteria under anaerobic

Upgrade the high-load anaerobic digestion and relieve acid stress through 
the strategy of side-stream micro-aeration: biochemical performances, 
microbial response and intrinsic mechanisms 
Wen Li a, Yongli Liu a, Baocun Wu a, Li Gu a,*, Rui Deng b 
a Key laboratory of the Three Gorges Reservoir Region’s Eco-environments, Ministry of Education, Institute of Environment and Ecology, Chongqing University, 174 
Shapingba Road, Chongqing 400045, PR China 
b School of Architecture and Urban Planning, Chongqing Jiaotong University, Chongqing 400074, PR China   
A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
High-load anaerobic digestion 
Acid stress 
Side-stream micro-aeration 
Metagenomic analysis 
A B S T R A C T   
In high-load anaerobic digestion such as in kitchen waste, side-stream micro-aeration (SMA) shows excellent 
operational performance to direct micro-aeration (DMA). It immediately restores the acidification to stability. 
Methanogenic performance remained stable when organic load ratios (OLR) was further increased to 5.5 g VS/L. 
Enhanced enzyme activity, microbial aggregation, and proliferation of bacteria and archaea were observed in 
SMA. The results indicates that SMA enriched Methanosaeta (relative abundance exceeded 93%) and induced the 
change of the main methanogenic pathway to acetoclastic methanogenesis. Mechanisms was further explored by 
using metagenomic analysis, and the results show SMA avoids mass formation of ROS (reactive oxygen species) 
by cycling the aerated slurry, and retains benefits of trace O2 on material and energic metabolism, which poses 
great application potentials and deserves further investigation.   
1. Introduction 
Urban food waste (FW) is an important part of household waste that 
is rich in nutrients, which can be utilized via anaerobic digestion (AD). 
However, the high proportion of easily biodegradable organic matter in 
FW commonly results in rapid acidification, as well as subsequent 
acidity accumulation in its AD, especially when high feed load is 
applied. The acidity accumulation deteriorates systematic stability by 
inhibiting anaerobic microbes, and if not properly treated, system fail­
ure occurs. However, AD with high organic load ratios (OLR) presents 
the advantage of high volume gas yield and small reactor volume, which 
have great potential for AD-engineered treatment of different kinds of 
organic wastes (Li et al., 2022). Therefore, it is of great significance to 
effectively maintain the stability of such a AD system. Effectively 
diluting the adverse effects of inhibitors during high-load anaerobic 
digestion is a key hurdle. 
Several studies have explored to handle acid inhibition, including the 
use of exogenous alkaline (Chen et al., 2019), cultivating acid-resistant 
strains via pre-inoculation, gradient culture, or using trace elements to 
enhance microbial activity (Zhang and Loh, 2019), and accelerating the 
transfer of electrons from syntrophic oxidation bacteria to methanogens 
through exogenous conductors (Zhao, 2020). In these processes, the 
fundamental goal is to effectively reduce the accumulation of fatty acids, 
such as propionate and butyric acid, which cannot be directly used by 
methanogenic archaea. 
In recent years, micro-aeration has attracted much attention in 
ameliorating these challenges. In such processes, a small amount of air is 
injected into the anaerobic digestive system to induce the fluctuation of 
the digestive ORP (Oxidation Reduction Potential). Trace oxygen acts as 
an electron receptor to capture/shunt excess electrons produced in AD of 
perishable organics, alleviating acid inhibition and promoting meth­
anogenesis. Yu et al.(2020) observed that during AD of black water, an 
appropriate micro-oxygen supply improved hydrolysis, acidification and 
even methanogenic efficiency, and the abundance of hydrogenotrophic 
methanogens significantly increased. According to Nguyen et al.(2019), 
intermittent micro-aeration rapidly decreased the total VFA concentra­
tion in the reactor from 9.2 to 3.0 g HAc/L and induced the recovery of 
methane production, thereby improving overall stability of the AD 
system. 
Recently, direct introduction of air into the digester is the most 
common form of intervention used. This kind of micro-aeration is 
impractical for engineering application due to the high cost of full-scale

Air Supplement as a Stimulation Approach for the In Situ
Desulfurization and Methanization Enhancement of Anaerobic
Digestion of Chicken Manure
Yunlong Song, Ahmed Mahdy, Zhen Hou, Min Lin, Walter Stinner, Wei Qiao,* and Renjie Dong
Cite This: Energy Fuels 2020, 34, 12606−12615
Read Online
ACCESS
Metrics & More
Article Recommendations
ABSTRACT: Anaerobic digestion of chicken manure produces biogas with an extreme H2S content (5000−6000 ppm), which
greatly weakens the economic viability of biogas plants. In this study, in situ desulfurization through supplying limited air into the
headspace of a digester and the impact upon the process performance were evaluated under diﬀerent oxygen loads (1.4, 2.8, and 4.2
mL/gVSin) and injection approaches (single pulse and continuously). The results showed that an oxygen load at 4.2 mL/gVSin with
continuous injection removed 99.7% of H2S (reduced to 10−15 ppm) and simultaneously increased the methane yield by 6.4%.
Sulﬁde-oxidizing bacteria enrichment and the increased concentration of soluble iron were the main features of the air supplement
system. The 16S rDNA results explained the attached growth of sulfur-oxidizing bacteria on the headspace carriers and the
enrichment of Methanobacterium and Methanoculleus under the microaerated system. The obtained results suggest that in situ
desulfurization technology could be applied more widely.
1. INTRODUCTION
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a promising solution for
stabilizing organic waste, reclaiming bioenergy, and producing
digestate as organic fertilizer. In 2019, China issued a policy
aiming to accelerate the development of bionatural gas,
through the AD of waste, to 20 billion m3 by the end of
2030 (www.nea.gov.cn). In China, around 155 million tons of
chicken manure are produced annually, and regarding its
higher potential biogas production (794 mL/gVS),1 chicken
manure is deemed to be a suitable substrate for AD treatment.
In addition, recent studies indicated that the AD of chicken
manure was successful even under stressed conditions such as
high ammonia level.2,3 However, AD of chicken manure
generates biogas with H2S as high as 5000−6000 ppm, which is
much higher than that produced from the AD of diary manure
(2000−4000 ppm) and sewage sludge (2500−4900 ppm).4,5
Biogas containing high concentrations of H2S could corrode
gas pipes, mechanical devices, and engines, and thus, it must be
puriﬁed before its further utilization.6 A wide range of
desulfurization techniques have been applied, but the
signiﬁcant drawbacks with maintenance complexity, high
cost, and the secondary pollution have restricted their
application.7 So far, a cost-eﬀective approach for removing
H2S from the AD of chicken manure has remained a challenge.
In situ desulfurization technology is proposed as a way of
removing H2S by supplying a limited amount of air/oxygen
into the headspace of an anaerobic digester in which the
growth of sulﬁde oxidizing bacteria (SOB) is sustained. Under
microaerated conditions, SOB biologically oxidizes H2S to
sulfur or sulfate, depending on the O2 dosage (in eqs 1 and 2).8
A wide range of in situ H2S removal eﬃciencies have been
reported for dairy manure (68%; from 4000 to 1120 ppm),4
agricultural waste (88%; from 2500 to 300 ppm),9 and
synthetic waste (99%; from 680 to 10 ppm).10 Recently, H2S
removal from biogas of chicken manure through in situ
desulfurization technology was reported in a batch experi-
ment.11 However, the performance of the in situ H2S removal
in a long-term AD of chicken manure has been scarcely
studied, and the underlying mechanism is still unclear. On the
other hand, improper air dosage may not only result in a lower
H2S removal eﬃciency but also increase the risk of disturbing
the anaerobic environment.12 Balancing the air dosage for
simultaneous H2S removal and an eﬃcient AD performance is
therefore still a challenge. In addition, a stable habitat with
available wetted area is necessary for the bioﬁlm activity,
guaranteeing the eﬃcient H2S removal.13 However, hitherto,
there is little research about the installation of carrier for
bioﬁlm growth during the in situ desulfurization process, and
the microbial features of the bioﬁlm are still lacking and not
quite clear.

Technical, Economical, and Microbiological Aspects
of the Microaerobic Process on H2S Removal for Low
Sulfate Concentration Wastewaters
M. R. Sousa1 & C. J. S. Oliveira1 & A. C. Lopes1 &
E. R. Rodríguez1 & G. B. M. Holanda1 &
P. G. C. Landim1 & P. I. M. Firmino1 & A. B. Dos Santos1
Received: 21 March 2016 /Accepted: 20 June 2016 /
Published online: 30 June 2016
# Springer Science+Business Media New York 2016
Abstract We studied the feasibility of the microaerobic process, in comparison with the
traditional chemical absorption process (NaOH), on H2S removal in order to improve the
biogas quality. The experiment consisted of two systems: R1, biogas from an anaerobic
reactor was washed in a NaOH solution, and R2, headspace microaeration with atmo-
spheric air in a former anaerobic reactor. The microaeration used for low sulfate
concentration wastewater did not affect the anaerobic digestion, but even increased
system stability. Methane production in the R2 was 14 % lower compared to R1, due
to biogas dilution by the atmospheric air used. The presence of oxygen in the biogas
reveals that not all the oxygen was consumed for sulfide oxidation in the liquid phase
indicating mass transfer limitations. The reactor was able to rapidly recover its capacity
on H2S removal after an operational failure. Bacterial and archaeal richness shifted due
to changes in operational parameters, which match with the system functioning. Finally,
the microaerobic system seems to be more advantageous for both technical and econom-
ical reasons, in which the payback of microaerobic process for H2S removal was
4.7 months.
Keywords Anaerobic . Biogas desulfurization . DGGE . Hydrogen sulfide .
Microaerobic process

Introduction
Anaerobic digestion is presented as an attractive technology in wastewater treatment, which involves
the biological degradation and stabilization of organic matter and transformation into biogas. The
biogas quality is very important when its potential for energy use is considered.
The biogas contains considerable amounts of pollutants, which are produced during anaerobic
digestion. Among these pollutants, hydrogen sulfide deserves major attention because it is highly
toxic and can cause problems in the nervous system, eyes, and respiratory tract [1]. In addition to
public health problems, hydrogen sulfide can cause an inhibitory effect in several microorganisms,
including methanogens, which will result in a decrease in the methane production and, consequently,
decrease the energy potential production. Moreover, hydrogen sulfide is very corrosive, which
reduces the lifetime of pipework and other installations needed for biogas utilization [2–5]. Therefore,
the sulfide content in the biogas is important to be controlled to prevent damage and fulfill the quality
standards for biogas use [6].
In order to prevent a high concentration of hydrogen sulfide in anaerobic reactors, some
investigations have been performed introducing a limited amount of oxygen/air to anaerobic
bioreactors as a strategy to lower the levels of sulfide. This technique involves the oxidation of
sulfide by sulfur-oxidizing bacteria (SOB) under limiting oxygen conditions [7]. Several
studies have shown that microaeration of wastewater or solid wastes containing high sulfate
concentration is a promising technology, which promotes the oxidation of the generated sulfide
in elemental sulfur [8–12].
It was proved in a mixed culture that even strict anaerobes are not inhibited by oxygen, assuming
that facultative microorganisms are able to consume this oxygen quickly and completely [8]. This
technology brings many benefits, mainly related to the excellent efficiency of treatment, no necessity
of a specific unity and a subsequent reduction in energy consumption [13]. Currently, microaerobic
systems have been used for efficient removal of hydrogen sulfide from biogas, mainly in anaerobic
digesters treating both domestic and agroindustrial wastes [2, 4, 9]. Therefore, low concentrations of
dissolved oxygen play an important role on sulfide oxidation to elemental sulfur according to the
following equation (Eq. 1) [14]:
2HS‐ þ O2→2S0 þ 2OH‐
ð1Þ
However, literature lacks an investigation of microaerophilic treatment for low sulfate concentra-
tion wastewaters (e.g., sewage), especially analyzing all technical, economical, and microbiological
aspects. Therefore, this study evaluated the feasibility of the microaerobic process, in comparison with
the traditional chemical absorption process (NaOH), for H2S removal in order to improve the biogas
quality and minimize odor generation in anaerobic reactors. Moreover, the impact of microaeration
over the anaerobic system stability was evaluated. The microorganisms change in both systems was
analyzed by using molecular biology tools such as DGGE. Finally, a technical and an economical
analysis were performed after scale-up of the systems.

Sludge Source

Corporation (EMBRAPA) from an anaerobic reactor used in the treatment of banana

a b s t r a c t
Characteristics of non-methane organic compounds (NMOCs) emissions during the anaerobic decom-
position of untreated (APD-0) and four aerobically pretreated (APD-20, APD-39, APD-49, and APD-63)
samples of municipal solid waste (MSW) were investigated in laboratory. The cumulative mass of the
NMOCs of APD-20, APD-39, APD-49, and APD-63 accounted for 15%, 9%, 16%, and 15% of that of APD-0,
respectively. The intensities of the NMOC emissions calculated by dividing the cumulative NMOC
emissions by the quantities of organic matter removed (QVS) decreased from 4.1 mg/kg QVS for APD-0 to
0.8e3.4 mg/kg QVS for aerobically pretreated MSW. The lipid and starch contents might have signiﬁcant
impact on the intensity of the NMOC emissions. Alkanes dominated the NMOCs released from the
aerobically pretreated MSW, while oxygenated compounds were the chief component of the NMOCs
generated from untreated MSW. Aerobic pretreatment of MSW prior to landﬁlling reduces the organic
content of the waste and the intensity of the NMOC emissions, and increases the odor threshold, thereby
reducing the environmental impact of landﬁlls.
